case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated November 12, 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3339 of 1992).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by leave is against the judgment dated November 12, 1998 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3339 of 1992 making the Rule absolute and thereby allowing the prayer for rejection of the plaint of Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Iswarganj, Mymensingh. The suit was filed seeking declaration that the order dated January 25, 1989 passed in Second Certificate Appeal No.88 of 1984 by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, order dated August 22, 1989 passed in Certificate Review Case No.16 of 1989 by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division Dhaka and the order dated March 14, 1991 passed in Certificate Appeal Case No.2-42/89 passed by the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka are illegal, void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff.

2. The Second Certificate Appeal No. 88 of 1984 was filed against the order dated February 9, 1984 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh in Certificate Appeal No. 3/77- 78 dismissing the same. The Certificate Appeal No.3/77-78 was filed for setting aside the auction sale of September 17, 1964 in Certificate Case No.1 723(1 )63-64. The auction sale was confirmed on November 30, 1964 and the possession was delivered to the auction purchaser i.e. plaintiff, herein appellant, on January 17, 1966. The Certificate Case No.1 723(1)63-64 was started in respect of the land of plot No. 1503 of Mouza Dattapara, Police Station-Iswarganj, Mymensingh. The aforesaid plot was listed in CS Khatian No.264 and later on in SA Khatian No.595.

3. It is the case of the plaintiff that after purchase of the land of plot No.1503 of SA khatian No.595 (CS khatian No.264) of Mouza Dattapara, Police Station Iswarganj, Mymensingh he got delivery of possession of the auction purchased land on January 17, 1966 and since then possessing the land so purchased by himself and his licensees.

4. The licensees of the plaintiff approached the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh for setting aside the auction sale of the land of plot No.1503 in Certificate Case No. 1723(1) 63-64 and thereupon Certificate Appeal No.3/77-78 was registered. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dismissed the said appeal. The licensees of the plaintiff ie. respondent Nos. l and 2 herein, went on appeal before the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the appeal was registered as Second Certificate Appeal No.88 of 1984. The appeal was heard by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the same was allowed upon setting aside the order dated February 9, 1984 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner. The plaintiff filed a review application and thereupon Certificate Review Case No.16 of 1989 was registered. The review was rejected. Then the plaintiff went on appeal before the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka in Certificate Appeal No.2-42/89, Mymensingh. The Land Appeal Board dismissed the said appeal on January 14, 1991. Thereafter, plaintiff filed the suit seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore. In the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Iswarganj, Mymensingh the suit was numbered Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991. The defendants, i.e. respondent Nos. 1 and 2, entered appearance and filed written statement and thereafter, filed an application on November 16, 1992 under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure with the prayer for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was not maintainable and that barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the suit was also barred under section 37 of the Public Demands Recovery Act (PDR Act) as well as under sections 48 and 49 of the PDR Act. The learned Assistant Judge upon hearing the parties by the order dated November 16, 1992 (Order No.35 dated 11-16-1992) rejecting the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the observation that in the suit serious question of law is involved and that without hearing the suit finally it would not be possible to arrive at a correct decision as regard the point of law involved in the suit and that as the suit is ready for hearing, as such point of law involved in the suit should be decided and disposed of at the final hearing.

5. As against the order of the learned Assistant Judge the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. In support of the Rule it was contended that the suit was wrongly entertained by the Court of Assistant Judge since the orders as against which relief sought were passed by the Revenue Authority in connection with the sale held in execution of the order passed in the Certificate Case as per provision of the PDR Act and, as such. the learned Assistant Judge was in error in rejecting the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as in view of the provision of section 37 of the PDR Act the suit filed was not maintainable. As against the aforesaid contention of the defendant-petitioners, it was contended on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party that the suit filed by him is very much maintainable as setting aside of auction sale was "sought by the persons" who are not of the category of the persons as in section 37 of the PDR Act. The High Court Division rejected the contention of the plaintiff-opposite party upon observing as the suit has been filed challenging the orders of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the order of the Land Appeal Board provision of section 37 of the PDR Act puts bar in filing a suit like the category of plaintiff's suit. The High Court Division also observed as the case of the plaintiff is not "that the certificate proceeding are unauthorised and fraudulent and that the revenue authority acted without jurisdiction" and, as such, the suit so filed by the plaintiff was not entertainable by the civil Court. The High Court Division finally observed "Since the OP No.1 plaintiff filed the Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 challenging the orders passed by the Additional Commissioner and Member, Land Appeal Board as an appellate authority in setting aside the auction held in a certificate case, so the learned Assistant Judge should have allowed the petition of the petitioner-defendants under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint instead of going into the question of law at the time of hearing of the original suit on the principle that the parties should not be dragged unnecessarily in a suit which is barred by law. Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 filed by the OP No.1 plaintiff is found to be barred under section 37 of the PDR Act for which this revision should be allowed setting aside the impugned order of the learned Assistant Judge".

"In view of the facts and circumstances and the law bearing on the subject, I find that the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law in not allowing the application of the petitioners defendants (sic) for rejection of the plaint as being barred by law. So, I find that there is merit in this revision and as such it should be allowed.

6. In the result, the Rule is made absolute on contest against the opposite party No.1 and ex parte against the rest without any order as to costs.

7. The impugned order of the learned Assistant Judge is set aside and the plaint of Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 is rejected as being barred by law".

8. On the aforesaid finding and observation the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and thereupon rejected the plaint of Title Suit No. 82 of 1991 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Iswarganj, Mymensingh.

9. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division misread or misconceived the statement made in the plaint and that also misconstrued the section 37 of the PDR Act and consequent thereupon was in error in rejecting the plaint of Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991, that averments having been made in the plaint alleging fraud and malafide and that in the light thereof relief having been sought civil Court is quite competent to investigate the question of fraud and malafide and the said allegation as can only be finally adjudicated upon full dress hearing of the suit, the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the plaint upon an erroneous view that the suit is barred under section 37 of the PDR Act, that the provision of section 37 of the PDR Act bars suit either by the certificate- holder, the certificate-debtor or by their representative and the plaintiff being not anyone of them the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the plaint of Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Iswarganj, Mymensingh on the view suit was barred under section 37 of the PDR Act.

10. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute and thereupon rejected the plaint of the Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 on the view that the suit filed by the plaintiff was not maintainable as per provision of section 37 of the PDR Act. The appellant has obtained the leave on contending that the plaintiff being not a certificate-holder, or the certificate-debtor or not being a representative of anyone of them his suit was not barred because of the provision of section 37 of the PDR Act.

11. To appreciate the contention of the appellant and for examining the correctness of the judgment of the High Court Division the provision of section 37 of the PDR Act is reproduced below:

"37. General bar to Jurisdiction of Civil Courts, save where fraud alleged : Except as otherwise expressly provided in this Act every question arising between the certificate-holder and the certificate-debtor, or their representatives, relating to the making, execution, discharge or satisfaction of a certificate duly filed under this Act, or relating to the confirmation or setting aside by an order under this Act or a sale held in execution of such certificate, shall be determined, not by a suit, but by order of the Certificate-officer before whom such question arises, or of such other Certificate-officer as he may determine. Provided that a suit may be brought in a Civil Court in respect of any such question upon the ground of fraud".

12. The plaintiff is the auction purchaser of land measuring.47 acre of plot No.1503 listed in SA khatian No.599 (CS khatian No. 264) of Mouza Dattapara, Police Station Iswarganj, Mymensingh sold in Certificate Case No.1723(1)63-64. The auction sale having been affirmed on November 30, 1964, possession of the land so sold in auction and purchased by the plaintiff was delivered to the plaintiff on January 17, 1966. It is the case of the plaintiff that after taking delivery of possession of the land purchased by him in the auction he was possessing the same with his licensees.

13. It appears from the materials on record that the licensees approached the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh for setting aside the auction sale and thereupon Certificate Appeal No. 3/77-78 was registered. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh dismissed the said certificate appeal on February 9, 1984. The licensees went on appeal before the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka and the said appeal was heard by the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Di is ion and the same was allowed. Thereupon the plaintiff filed a review application but without any success and then the plaintiff moved the Land Appeal Board as against the order of the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the Land Appeal Board dismissed the case filed by the plaintiff. After all those efforts the plaintiff filed the aforementioned suit seeking declaration that the order of the office of the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the order of the Land Appeal Board are illegal, void and not binding upon him. The question in the suit framed by the plaintiff whether a person who is neither a certificate-holder, or certificate-debtor or their representative is incompetent as per provision of section 37 of the PDR Act to challenge legality of the orders as mentioned hereinbefore. From the reading of section 37 of the PDR Act it is seen that jurisdiction of the civil Court has been ousted to entertain a suit relating to the certificate proceeding initiated under the provision of PDR Act and sale held in the said certificate case except when a suit is filed alleging fraud in conducting the proceeding of the certificate case and the sale held in pursuant to the proceeding of the certificate case. The provision of section 37 of the PDR Act contemplates that every question arising between the certificate holder and certificate-debtor or their representatives, relating to the making, execution, discharge, satisfaction of a certificate duly filed under the PDR Act or relating to the confirmation or setting aside by an order under the PDR Act or a sale held in execution of the certificate shall be determined not by a suit but by order of the Certificate officer before whom such question arises, or of such other certificate officer as he may determine.

14. The suit, plaint of which has been rejected by the High Court Division, has been filed by the plaintiff impleading his licensees at whose instance Certificate Appeal No.3/77-78 was registered in the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh and the government functionaries dealing with land revenue and matter relating to land administration questioning legality of the orders of Government functionaries passed in connection with auction sale held in certificate Case No. 1723(1 )/63-64 at the instance of the persons stranger in the certificate case and not as to the correctness of the proceedings of the certificate case and the sale held thereunder. The plaintiff did not question the proceedings of the certificate case as the certificate-debtor, certificate-holder or of being their representative. The respondent Nos.1 and 2, who are 3rd party in the certificate proceeding or, in other words, nobody in the certificate proceeding and that also not an auction purchaser, approached the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh for setting aside the sale held in Certificate Case No. 1723(1)/63-64. The Additional Deputy Commissioner dismissed the said appeal but on second appeal the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division set aside the auction sale and then plaintiff tried to get the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division set aside by filing review petition and appeal before Land Appeal Board but was not successful. In the background of the aforesaid state of the matter the plaintiff filed the suit questioning legality of the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and the order of the Land Appeal Board.

<u>15. The question as appears to us, involved in the suit is how far the Revenue authority on the application of third persons, whom the plaintiff claimed as his licensees in the land purchased by him in the auction sale held in Certificate Case No.1 723(1)/63-64, is legally competent to set aside an auction sale which has not been questioned by the certificate-holder, certificate-debtor and their representative. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division while making the Rule absolute placed reliance on the decision in the case reported in 43 DLR, 242 (Marida Begum and others vs Moulavi Md Hasan and others). The fact of the case so relied upon' by the High Court Division is quite different from the facts of the instant appeal. In the reported case the certificate-debtor took objection to the certificate sale and thereupon the revenue authority on examination of the materials on record set aside the auction sale and thereupon the auction purchaser filed revision which was dismissed and then the auction purchaser moved the Board of Revenue but without any success. Thereafter, one of the auction purchasers filed Writ Petition No. 435 of 1967 before the High Court of the then East Pakistan challenging the aforesaid orders of the Revenue authority setting aside the auction sale. The Rule obtained in the writ petition was discharged. The writ petitioner filed petition for leave to appeal in the Supreme Court but the same was dismissed. Thereafter, some other auction purchasers filed the suit. In the background of the said facts it was held that after exhausting the procedure as provided in PDR Act the auction purchaser is prec1udedfrom resorting to the Civil Court for the relief which he could not have from the Revenue authority.</u>

16. In the instant case third person in the certificate case and also third person in the certificate proceeding i.e. auction proceeding and that who also was not an auction purchaser moved the revenue authority for setting aside the auction sale and the Revenue authority set aside the auction sale. The plaintiff is the auction purchaser. The point involved in the suit filed by the auction purchaser is whether third person in the auction proceeding and that also not being the representative of the parties in the auction proceeding and also not being an auction purchaser can move the Revenue authority seeking setting aside of the auction sale and thereupon how far the Revenue authority is competent to set aside the auction sale or, in other words, how far the Revenue authority is/was within its jurisdiction in setting aside the auction sale at the instant of a stranger to the certificate proceeding.

<u>17. As stated hereinbefore respondent Nos. 1 and 2, whom the plaintiff claimed his licensees in respect of the property purchased in Certificate Case No. 1723(1)/6364, moved the Revenue authority for setting aside the auction sale, which was confirmed on 17-1-1966, almost after lapse of about 12 years. These 2 respondents as already mentioned were strangers to the certificate proceeding. The action of the Revenue authority at the instance of aforesaid category of person in the background of the provision of PDR Act how far is competent in law came up for consideration in the case of Monirunnahar Begum and others vs Shahed Ali and others reported in 1981 BCR 43.</u>

18. In the reported case in a certificate proceeding property belonging to the member of the Hindu community was sold and after 5 years, as it appears, a tenant of the holding approached the Revenue authority for setting aside the auction sale and the application was allowed by the Additional Deputy. Commissioner and the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner was maintained by the Additional Commissioner and Joint Secretary (appellate and revisional authority respectively). The said action of the Revenue was challenged by the auction purchaser by filing writ petition. The High Court Division on consideration of different provisions of the PDR Act observed "Although the power conferred upon the revisional authorities mentioned therein under section 53 of the Act is .in general terms, it is always conditional upon the various provisions of the Act itself. Consequently, the provisions of sections 7, 22, 23, 25, 36, 37 of the Act as mentioned and discussed hereinbefore have mandated the revisional authorities under section 53 of the Act to act according to the provisions of the act mentioned hereinbefore. It appears in the present case that the authorities mentioned in section 53 of the Act have acted in clear and gross violation of the various mandatory provisions of sections 7, 22, 23, 25,36,37 of the Act".

19. It has further been observed in the background of the facts of the reported case "Such person not claiming any title under certificate debtor as such could not, be treated as a person whose interests had been affected by the sale. Thus the application for setting aside the sale having been made by respondent No.1 who has been found to be a person not legally interested in the property as such, the revisional authorities could not set aside the auction at the instance of a person who had no locus standi to apply in that regard------that the respondent No.1 being a monthly tenant in the premises of the property without claiming any title under the certificate debtor is not a. person having any interest in the auction of the property as such and consequently could not invoke sections 22,23, M the Act and thereby the auction became absolute under section 25 of the Act. That being so, the revisional authorities under section 53 of the Act could not set aside the sale upon the ground of nonservice of notice under section 7 of the Act- which in turn comes in direct conflict with the provision of section 36 of the Act". In the reported case the action of the Revenue authority was held illegal. In the aforesaid case the Revenue authority was moved for setting aside the auction sale, as in the instant case, by a person having no interest in the land sold or in any respect interest of the respondent Nos.1 and 2 was affected by the auction sale. It appears from the papers on record that the Revenue authority was of the view that there was no existence of Certificate Case No. 1723/63-64. It is the definite case of the plaintiff that he purchased the land sold in Certificate Case No.1723(1)/63-64 but the authorities placing reliance on the local revenue office set aside the auction sale taking the view there was no Certificate Case No.1723/63-64. Along with other contentions of the plaintiff the contention as to Certificate Case number was required to be adjudicated by the civil Court on consideration of the evidence that would be adduced by the parties as regard that vital contention.

<u>20. As stated hereinbefore the High Court Division set aside the order of the trial Court rejecting the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the view that the suit filed by the plaintiff, the auction purchaser, was barred under section 37 of the PDR Act. The provision of section 37 of the PDR Act is that every question arising between the certificate-holder and the certificate-debtor or their representatives, relating to the making, execution, discharge or satisfaction of a certificate duly filed under said Act, or relating to the confirmation or setting aside by an order under that Act or a sale held in execution of such certificate, shall be determined by the certificate-officer concerned and not by a suit, but a suit can always be brought in a civil Court challenging such sale on the ground of fraud. In the suit in question the situation contemplates in section 37 of the PDR Act and to be determined by the certificate-officer alone while there is. no allegation of fraud since the respondent Nos.1 and 2 are totally strangers in all respect to the certificate proceeding or; in other words, they are neither certificate- holder, certificate-debtor or their representatives. This being the position the High Court Division was in serious error in arriving at a finding that the suit i.e. Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991, was barred as per provision of section 37 of the PDR Act and thereupon in rejecting the plaint of the said suit upon setting aside the order of the trial Court rejecting the prayer for rejection of the plaint. It has already been stated hereinabove point involved in the suit is how far the Revenue authorities were within their jurisdiction in setting aside the auction sale at the instance of a person who has not claimed title in the property sold in auction in the certificate proceeding initiated as per provision of PDR Act after lapse of about 12 years. In the background of the said moot point for decision in the suit, we are of the view the suit so filed is very much maintainable and can legally be proceeded.</u>

21. In the background of the discussion made hereinbefore the appeal is allowed. The order dated November 12, 1998 passed in Civil Revision No.3339 of 1992 is set aside and the order dated November 16, 1992 (order No.35 dated 16-11-1992) of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Iswarganj, Mymensingh passed in Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 is restored. The Other Class Suit No.82 of 1991 is restored to its file and number. The trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (On appeal from the judgment and decree dated 28th June, 1968 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 138 of 1972).
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J.-This appeal raises a complex question of interpretation of Section 20(5)(c)(ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. The facts are that the plaintiff-respondents instituted a title suit for declaration of title and for khas possession of the suit lands after evicting the defendants therefrom and further for declaring the decision by the Revenue Officer dated 23.12.54 in Misc. Case No. 2 of the R.O.S. Court Barisal a nullity Their case in short in that Kemaluddin Sardar predecessor of the plaintiffs created a Wakf of the suit property by a Wahfnama of 28.12.1891. The plaintiff No. 1 is managing the Wakf property as Mutwalli of the Wakf estate. In terms of the Wakfnama the plaintiffs as the heirs of three sons of Kemaluddin Sardar are entitled to enjoy the usufruct of the wakf property after meeting expenses for charitable, religious and other purposes, Thus leaving aside the land for the expenses for charitable purposes, the balance of the Wakf properties are to be divided into three parts representing the heirs of the three .sons of Kemaluddin Sardar. It is alleged that there was a proceeding before the Revenue Officer; Barisal who directed acquisition of Schedule 'Kha' properties which were found to be in excess under the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. The Revenue Officer treated the all Wakf properties as one unit belonging to one family instead of treating the properties belonging to three families of the heirs of three sons of the Wakf.

2. The Province of East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) Contested the suit asserting that the impugned order of the Revenue Officer under section 20 of the Act is well founded in law and binding upon the Wakf Estate and the plaintiffs. The Revenue Officer on taking accounts from the Mutwalli of the Wakf Estate and on consideration Of the terms of wakf deed has allowed 17'65 acres of land for religious and charitable purposes out of the total Wakf land of 72'20 acres, 33'66 acres of Nalland for Mutwalli of the Wakf Estate and 3'31 acres of land as homestead The rest 18'18 acres is considered "excess" under the Act and had been directed to be acquired.

The learned Subordinate Judge, found the decision of the Revenue Officer valid and the plaintiffs had no cause of action and so he dismissed the suit on contest with costs.

3. On appeal the learned Judges of the High Court construing s. 20(5)(c)(ii) of the Act held that two consequences of the law is that, it first bifurcates a mixed wakf-al-alaulad into public and private wakf and then converts the private portion into secular property. After so holding they concluded that the secular part will be distributed to the present beneficiaries of the wakf according to section 20(2) of the Act.

This order is challenged by the Government. The question set out above is whether the High Court put a correct interpretation on the provisions of section 20(5)(c)(ii) of the Act.

The learned Attorney General and Mr. Pal have given their rival interpretations on the section and they will be dealt with in due course. We are not very much impressed by any of their rival contentions. We therefore, propose to give our construction on the section.

<u>4. The scheme of section 20 may be looked at. The section contemplates the sequel to the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests." The section covers the holders of all categories of land, not only the rent-receiver but cultivating riyat, cultivating under raiyat and non-agricultural tenant. The section also defines the quality and quantity of the land each of them can hold. Sub-section (1) of section 20 days that on the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests, no rent-receiver, agricultural or non-agricultural tenant shall be entitled to retain possession of any of his khas lands in such area except as provided in the suit-section (2). This sub-section divides all khas lands into retainable and non-retainable. Retainable khas land is again subject to quantitative ceiling fixed by it.</u>

<u>The sub-section says, a person allowed to retain khas land shall be entitled to retain as tenant under the (Provincial) Government, homestead, land used for agricultural or horticultural purposes including tanks, land cultivable or capable of cultivation on reclamation and vacant non-agricultural lands. These are retainable khas land: Any land or building in a hat or bazar, fishery, forest and ferry are excluded from the category of retainable khas lands they are non-retainable khas land. The sub-section fixes a quantitative ceiling to the retainable khas land. While fixing the quantity the measure is the holder of the land and the members of his family. It says, any one of the allowable person shall be entitled to retain 100 standard beghas or ten standard beghas for each member of the family, whichever is greater. An explanation has been appended describing the family. According to the explanation 'family' shall mean any person under sub-section (1) and .all persons leaving in the same mess and dependent upon him but does, not include any servant or hired labourer.</u>

5. Other provisions of this section are not relevant for our purpose excepting those relating to wakf. They have been set out in sub-section (5) clauses (c) and (c)(ii). The interpretation of the sub-clauses require a closer study and may be set out:-

(5)(1) Nothing in sub-sections (1)(2) and

(3) of this section shall apply to

(c) to so much of the lands held under debater wakf, wakf-al-alaulad or any other trust as is exclusively dedicated and the income from which is exclusively applied to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual.

(ii) Where, under any debuttor, wakf, wakf-al-aulad or any other trust, the income from the lands covered by such trust is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes and partly reserved for the pecuniary benefit of any individual, only such portion of the lands, as may be selected in accordance with the rules to be made in this behalf by the Provincial Government, shall come within the purview of sub-clause (c) of clause (i),

<u>6.Clause (c) does not pose any complication. All wakf which are exclusively for religious or charitable purposes will be allowed to retain all retainable khas land. But complexity arises with clause C(ii). It says among others that any wakf-al-aulad the income from the land covered by such wakf is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes, and partly for pecuniary benefit of any individual, only such portion of the land, as may be selected in accordance with the rules framed by the Government, shall come within the purview of the retainable khas land of the wakf. This clause is silent how the land is covered by charitable or religious purposes but meant for pecuniary benefit of any individual is to be dealt with. The silence indicates that such land will be governed by the genus I provision of S. 20. It will be subject to the quantitative limitation set by sub-section (2).</u>

7. The High Court in construing clause (c)(ii) has held that the clause has bifurcated a mixed wakf into charitable and secular and has thus partially destroyed such, a wakf. The secular portion will be treated as outside wakf and it is to be divided among the beneficiaries of the wakf. The view of the High Court seems to be that when the property of the wakf has been divided into Charitable and non-charitable part, the wakf itself has been bifurcated thereby. Lands for Charitable purposes could be retained in the wakf land but non-charitable wakf lands is susceptible to quantitative restriction of sub-section (2) Thus the land is converted into secular land.

<u>8. In our opinion the reasons cannot be accepted, if the true character of Wakf under Mohamadan law is taken into consideration Clause (c)(ii) is totally silent about any indication of destruction of the wakf character of non-charitable wakf land. Wakf is the permanent dedication of any property for any purpose recognised by the Mohamadan Law as religious, pious or charitable. Provision for the maintenance of the members of wakf's family under the Muhammad  Law is a valid purpose., When a wakf is created all rights of property pass out of the wakf and vest in the Almighty Allah. The Income of the wakf properties can be distributed either purely for charitable purposes or wholly for the benefit of the heirs of the wakf with ultimate benefit to charity, or a combination of the two, and each one of them is a valid wakf. When a wakf is made it becomes indestructible as the ownership is tied to the eternal Almighty. Wakf is a religious Institution under Mohamadan Law. It has its notional or justice existence. It is perpetual. However, the corpus of the wakf property has Its physical existence and like all physical things it is subject to change, decay and destruction. When any change or partial destruction takes place in the corpus of the wakf, the wakf is neither changed nor destroyed thereby. Mutwalli is required to apply the changed or surviving property for the purposes of the wakf as nearly as possible, applying the doctrine of cypres.</u>

<u>9. If we now revert to clause C(ii) of the Act, we find the legislature has divided the corpus and not the wakf into two, Charitable and non-charitable, where the pecuniary benefit is for any individual. The Charitable part shall continue under the original wakf deed in all retainable khas land. The non-charitable part of the wakf property will be subject to the quantitative ceiling fixed by sub-section (2) for the retainable khas land. The land in excess of quantitative ceiling, no doubt, will stand acquired to the Government but the wakf estate shall get compensation for it. This part of corpus of the wakf estate is altered from land into cash money. This money is wakf. The Mutwalli, under the doctrine of cypres is bound to invest it in such other property as would yield income equal as nearly as possible to the original wakf deed. Interpreted in the way we do, there is neither bifurcation of wakf, nor its destruction nor conversion of a part of wakf property into secular property.</u>

10. We are now left to construe a wore equivocal provision of sub-section (2) with reference to the wakf, via who is a rent-receiver We have already referred to it and found that the provision is that a rent-receiver and each member of his family shall be entitled to retain a total quantity of land fixed under the sub-section Rent-receiver in the & lib section has been conceived as a natural person fie is the owner of the land. The question is how a rent-receiver under sub-section (2) can be conceived as a wakf estate  It is true, that for the purposes of sec. 3 of the Act, a Mutwalli in Tihendra Kishore's case (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 21. PLD 1957 (SC) 9 he has been held to be a rent-receiver. Whether Mutwalli could be said to be a rent-receiver for section 20(1) 45t (2) as well is to be seen. For the purpose of acquisition of rent-receiving interest, it is to be seen who cap be a rent-receiver for the purpose of wakf. In other words, who can represent the wakf estate Mutwalli, according to Mohamadan law, is a manager of the wakf estate and may represent the estate. For the purpose of acquisition of the rent receiving interest Mutwalli does represent the wakf estate and so he fully answers the description of a rent-receiver for the purposes of S. 3 of the Act. We think is Jibendra Kishore's case the standing of the Mutwalli proceeded on the consideration whether he represented the wakf estate for the purpose of the acquisition of rent-receiving interest under S. 3 of the Act, though reasons were not collaborated. The test, therefore, is not whether Mutwalli is a rent-receive but whether he represents the wakf estate as a rent receiver.

<u>11. Turning to sub-section (2), we find rent-receiver has been conceived as a natural person and an owner of the land. The section is silent as to the wakf estate or the Mutwalli. Could he for the purpose of this section represent the wakf estate? Mutwalli is the Manager. He can never be equated with the owner of the land Mutwalli way he a stranger. There may he joint Mutwallis, there any be a committee of Mutwallis, and there may he ex-officio Mutwalli, there may be Mutwalli by rotation. In such circumstances a Mutwalli cannot represent an owner. He cannot there-fore represent the wakf estate for the purpose of sub-section (2). And obvious illustration will clarify the point. If a stranger is the Mutwalli, land of the wakf estate will be allotted to him and his family. The land of the wakf will pass out of the wakf and go to a stranger and his family. Could such an absurd situation be allowed to occur which is alien both to the Act and the purpose of the wakf.</u>

<u>12. Who can then be treated a rent-receiver under section 20(2) of Act for a wakf estate The sub-section allows 100 standard beghas to a family or 10 beghas to each member, of a family whichever is greater. We have held earlier that the test is who can represent the wakf estate for the purpose of this section. Mutwalli though he represents the wakf estate for the purpose of S. 3, cannot so represent for the purpose of this section. It is to Le remembered that this section not only covers the case of a rent-receiver but all agricultural and non-agricultural tenants. A tenant, agricultural or non-agricultural, can equally make a valid wakf of his tenanted land. We are therefore, to give a meaning to the sub-section which will govern all categories of persons, rent-receivers and tenants. The test of representations of wakf estate, according to us, best satisfy the requirement of the law, capable of governing the case of both rent receiver and tenant. In our view the wakf estate for this sub-section is truly represented by heirs of the wakf alive on the date when the section comes into operation. This interpretation comes nearest to the true import of the rent receiver or the tenant and the members of his family provided in sub-section (2) in case of wakf. The interpretation in our judgment harmonizes with the purpose of the Act which is land reform, and the purpose of the wakf which the maintenance of a religious institution. On this interpretation both the Act and wakf co-exist and one does not destroy the other.</u>

13. It is further to be remembered that the heirs of the wakf come to represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity and not in their personal capacity. The land so allotted will ensure to the benefit of the wakf estate It will subsist as part of retainable khas land of the wakf estate. Mutwalli will in his managerial capacity administer the land as" part and parcel of the wakf estate.

<u>14. In our opinion any wakf al-al-aulad which is dedicated party for charitable purpose and partly for individual benefit or wholly for benefit of any individual the khas land of such wakf-al-al-aulad estate should be retained on the footing of the living heirs representation the wakf state on the date the section came into operation. The heirs of the wakf in the aggregate will represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity but not in their personal capacity. Calculated on this basis, the wakf-al-al-aulad estate will retain as much as it will be possible to retain above 100 beghas by as many number as the heirs will be in existence above ten.</u>

15. We now turn to the contentions of the learned counsel on either side. First we refer to the submission of the learned Attorney-General, who appeared for the Government So much of his contention that the High Court was in error in construing the provision of cause C(ii) to mean bifurcation of the wakf into charitable and secular and secular portion will go to beneficiaries is well founded. We have given our reasons and no further discussion is called for.

<u>16. His next contention is that, we should apply the test of Mutwalli as rent-receiver held in Jibendra Kishore's case for the purpose of S. 20 as well The Revenue Officer according to him rightly allotted the land on the footing of Mutwalli as rent-receiver. We have already held that a Mutwalli cannot represent the wakf estate for purpose of section 20. The reasons need not be repeated over again. The learned Attorney-General has referred to two decisions for our consideration. They are Golam Hossain Sherazee Vs. Province of East Pakistan (1966) 18 DLR 52= PLD 1967 Dacca, and Khawaja Maynuddin Vs. Province of East Pakistan 21 DLR 886.</u>

17. In the case of Golam Hossain Sherazee, a Division Bench of the Dacca high Court has held that on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest of a wakf estate, the proceeds of the wakf whatever form they had taken must be made over to the Administrator of wakf. The decision says that the changed corpus of the wakf remains a wakf.

18. In Khawaja Maynuddin, another Division Bench of the Dacca High Court held that on the acquisition of rent-receiving interest of Wakf estate, there is no authority in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for the distribution of the khas land among the beneficiaries.

The cited decisions are not very much relevant to the' point in issue before. No further discussion is called for.

19. We now turn to the contention of Mr. Pal. He refers to sections 3(i), 3(4)(e) and 20(5)(c)(ii), and says that the total effect of these provisions is that the law first acquires all rent receiving interests, makes all persons statutory tenants of the Government for retainable khas land, and then for the retainable khas land bifurcates the wakf into charitable and non-charitable one and by implication converts the non-charitable part into a secular estate and so the beneficiaries are entitled to allotment of this secular land in their individual capacity. He, in short, adopts the conclusion of the High Court. We have already held against this contention with reasons. In addition to those reasons it may be added that Mr. Pal's contention that the secular part of the wakf estate will go to the beneficiaries suffers from inherent contradiction. If he concedes that part of the wakf estate has become secular, then the secular part will be treated as secular property of the wakf and in that event the heirs of the wakf and not the beneficiaries of the wakf will get the land. In the present case the beneficiaries do not include the heirs of the daughters of the wakf. Mr. Pal's contention does not stand.

<u>20. We now turn to the merits of the appeal. It is not disputed that the wakf of late Kemaluddin Sardar is a mixed wakf, partly dedicated to the charitable purposes and partly dedicated to the individual benefit of some of the heirs of wakf. The total khas land of the wakf estate is 72.20 acres Upon calculation the Revenue Officer found that 17'65 acres of land is required for the maintenance of charitable purposes. It is not in dispute. The dispute is now the balance of 54.55 acres of land is to be allotted. The Revenue Officer and the Trial Court allotted the land treating Mutwalli as the rent-receiver. The High Court has set aside the finding of the trial court holding this land as secular and the beneficiaries entitled to its allotment. None of the decisions is correct. According to our judgment, the heirs of the wakf will represent 4he wakf estate and land will be allotted to the wakf estate on that basis. The land so allotted will be khas land of the wakf estate. If sortie land in excess is left over on calculation, it will vest in the Government, but the compensation money for the excess land will be wakf, and the Mutwalli will be found to reinvest the same in any other suitable property. In this view of the matter, we set aside the decisions of the courts below and send the case back on remand to the Trial Court to dispose of the suit in the light of the observations made above. He will be at liberty to take such additional evidence as may be required for the disposal of the suit over and above the evidence already on record.</u>

<u>The appeal is allowed with the modification set out above but without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J: This Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned act of the respondents illegally including the Pipya Village under Ward No. 6 of No 1 Rajargaon (Uttar) Union Parishad under Hajiganj Upazila, District Chandpur and publishing the same in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 12-10-1996 (Annexure-G) by ignoring the investigation report dated 11-9-1996 (Annexure-F) of the Delimitation Officer should not be declared to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The facts, as stated in this petition, in short, are that respondent No. 8, the Thana Nirbahi Officer of Hajiganj, Chandpur by his Memo No. 9-5/96-308/dated 24-6-1996 referring Memo No. PROJE-3/Misc.-37/941 307(64) dated 16-5-1996 issued by respondent No. 3, the Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives, Local Government Division, instructed Proforma respondent No. 10, the then Chairman, No.1 Rajargaon (Uttar) Union Parishad to divide existing three wards of his Union Parishad into 9 Wards and send a list of village-based wards to him by 30-6-1996. Proforma respondent No. 10 called for a meeting in the Union Parishad Office on 8-7-1996 and in presence of eight elected Union Parishad members divided the three existing wards into nine wards upon thorough and detailed discussion and considering territorial unity, distribution of population and administrative convenience in accordance with the prescribed form sent to him by respondent No. 8 and forwarded the same together with minutes of the meeting, List of newly constituted 9 wards showing number of voters, names of the villages and a sketch map showing their geographical location, vide Annexure-C, C-1, and C-2 to respondent No. 8 on 10-7-1996.

3. Respondent No. 8 thereafter referred the matter to respondent No. 9, the delimitation officer and respondent No. 9 informed proforma respondent No. 10 that a meeting would be held on 24-8-1996 in the Union Parishad office to finalise the delimitation/reconstitution of wards and hear objections, if any, and under his instructions proforma respondent No. 10 made publicity by miking to make sure of the presence of the local people and Union Parishad members.

4. In Annexure-C-1, i.e, List of newly constituted 9 wards the village named Pipya was included in ward No. 4 along with villages named Menapur and Niraine.

5. One Lokman Patwari, former Chairman of the said Union Parisad, took an objection to respondent No. 9 on 4-9-1996 about inclusion of the village Pipya with ward No. 4 and respondent No. 9 by Annexure-E notified Lokman Patwari that a discussion meeting would be held on 9-9-1996 in the said Union Parisad office about inclusion of the Pipya village with newly constituted wards and that he will physically visit the Pipya village after the said meeting requesting him to attend the meeting with documents and witnesses in his support also instructing proforma respondent No. 10 to prepare a list of male female inhabitants and number of voters in each village and also ensure attendance of the members of the Union Parisad in the meeting.

6. The discussion meeting was held on 9-9-1996 in the Union Parisad Officer wherein one Mr A Kadar was present as representative of Lokman Patwari. After the meeting respondent No. 9, the delimitation officer had gone to the Pipya village for local inspection, heard opinion of the representatives of all the houses. He thereafter by Annexure-F has recorded the following findings:

“বিষয়ঃ নতুন ওয়াড পূর্নগঠনে পিপিয়া গ্রামের অন্তুর্ভূক্ত প্রশ্নে সরেজমিনে তদন্তের পরবর্তী কার্যক্রম।

উল্লেখিত বিষয়ের প্রেক্ষিতে আপনার আবেদনের উপর নিম্ন স্বাক্ষরকারী অত্র কার্যালয়ের ৫-৯-৯৬ ইং তারিখের ৫৪০ নং স্বারক নোটিশের মাধ্যমে ৯-৯-৯৬ ইং তারিখ বেলা ১১-০০ টায় ইউ/পি কার্যালয়ে আপনার প্রতিনিধি জনাব আঃ কাদের এর উপস্থিতিতে আলোচনা সভা শেষে পিপিয়া গ্রাম পরিদর্শনে যাই। পরিদর্শন কালীন পিপিয়া গ্রামের অন্তর্ভুক্ত প্রশ্নে উক্ত গ্রামের সকল বাড়ীর প্রতিনিধিত্বকারীদের অভিমত গ্রহন করি। মেনাপুরের সাথে থাকার জন্য অভিমত প্রদানকারী প্রতিনিধিত্বকারীগণ নিম্ন লিখিত যুক্তি উপস্থাপন করেন।

১। পূর্ব থেকেই পিপিয়া গ্রামের লোকজন মেনাপুরে ভোট দিত। পরে স্থানীয় রাজনৈতিক কারণে তাদেরকে রাজারগাঁও কেন্দ্রে ভোট দেওয়ার ব্যবস্থা করা হয়।

২। তাদের জমিজমার বিভিন্ন কাগজপত্র মেনাপুর মৌজার সাথে সংশ্লিষ্টতা ছিল এবং বর্তমানে আছে বলে জানান। পিপিয়া গ্রামটি মেনাপুর মৌজার একই নম্বর ১৭৯ তে অবস্থিত।

৩। যাতায়াতের প্রশ্নে রাজারগাঁও এর সাথে তাদের তেমন কোন সুবিধা নাই।

৪। সামাজিক ভাবে তাহারা মেনাপুরের সাথে সম্পৃক্ত।

৫। ভোটার সংখ্যায় সামঞ্জস্যতার ক্ষেত্রে মেনাপুরের সাথে থাকা বাঞ্চনীয় বলে জানান।

৬। পিপিয়া গ্রামবাসী তাদের পক্ষে কোন অভিযোগ দাখিল করেননি বলে জানান।

অতএব, উক্ত গ্রামের নির্বাচিত ইউ/পি সদস্য সহ অন্যান্য ইউ/পি সদস্য ও ইউ/পি চেয়ারম্যানের মাধ্যমে আপনার আবেদন ও অত্র পত্রের মতামতে প্রয়োজনীয় সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ পূর্বক পত্র প্রাপ্তির ৩ (তিন) দিনের মধ্যে স্ব-শরীরে নিম্ন স্বাক্ষরকারীর কার্যালয়ে হাজির হয়ে চেয়ারম্যানের সুপারিশকৃত সংশোধিত সিদ্ধান্ত দাখিল করার জন্য বলা হইল। অন্যথায় চেয়ারম্যান কর্তৃক পূনগঠন সংক্রান্ত কাগজপত্র ও সরেজমিনে তদন্তের আলোকে প্রাথমিক বিজ্ঞপ্তি প্রকাশ করা হইবে।

(মোঃ আলী আকবর)

ডেলিমিটেশন অফিসার”।

The delimitation officer has communicated these findings to Lokman Patwary by Memo. No. 551/1(1) dated 11-9-1996, vide Annexure-F. He has also communicated the same to respondent No. 8, the Thana Nirbahi Officer.

7. It is alleged that the said Lokman Patwari did neither appear before the delimitation officer nor substantiate his objection. He rather approached the Thana Nirbahi Officer, respondent No. 8, who most illegally excluded the Pipya village from ward No. 4 and included it with ward No. 6 and sent the list of 9 newly constituted wards of respondent No. 2 for publication in the Bangladesh Gazette. In the Bangladesh Gazette published on 12-10-1996 (Annexure-G) the Pipya village was included with the ward No. 6 behind the back of the petitioner and people of the Pipya village. The petitioner is an intending candidate for the post of Union Parisad member from this Pipya village. For the first time on 11-10-2002 the petitioner came to learn about the Gazette notification and inclusion of Pipya village with ward No. 6 instead of ward No. 4. He then made representations in writing to respondent No. 8 and respondent No. 5, the District Election Officer, chandpur on 13-10-2000, vide Annexure-I and J stating that the villages of ward No. 6 are far away from the Pipya village and that the communication system is not good. On the other hand, other two villages in ward No. 4 situate next to the Pipya village, communication is good, all the villagers are living in the same society.

8. It is stated that there is a Bil known as 'Chawk' in between ward Nos. 4 and 6 apparent from the sketch map, Annexure-C-2 and whereas the Jurisdiction List (JL) number of Pipya village and Menapur village is 179 and they both are contiguous. For going to ward No. 6 the people of the Pipya village have to cross over ward No. 5 which will cause serious inconvenience in casting their valuable votes for there is no direct pathway to ward No. 6 from this village. The villagers of the Pipya village were used to cast their votes in Meenapur Centre for long but due to political reasons their centre has been rearranged with Rajargaon under Ward No. 6. The objector Lokman Patwari is a permanent inhabitant of ward No. 5 and a life convict in a murder case. No one from the Pipya village ever raised any objection about inclusion of the village with ward No. 4 and previously they were under this ward.

9. Mr NH Khandakar, Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that division of existing three wards into 9 wards is legal, valid and lawful but inclusion of the Pipya village with ward No. 6 instead of ward No. 4 is illegal, arbitrary and malafide. The voters of the Pipya village will have to go to the vote centre in ward No. 6 by crossing through the chowk and during the rainy season the chowk goes under water. The Pipya villagers are closer from all respects to Menapur village under ward No. 4. Inclusion of the Pipya village with ward No. 6 was done in violation of section 20 of the Local Government (Union Parisad) Ordinance, 1983.

10. Mr SM Emdadul Hoque, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondents, submits on the other hand, that due to various objections/disputes election of this Union Parisad is being withheld from 1992 frustrating the very purpose of the delimitation and the election process. He further submits that the Government has no objection if the Pipya village is included in ward No. 4 with the villages named Menapur and Neraine according to wishes of the inhabitants of the village.

11. Section 19 of the Local Government (Union Parisad) Ordinance, 1983 provides for appointment of delimitation officer by the Thana Nirbahi Officer from amongst persons in service of the Republic. The delimitation officer shall follow the procedure laid down in section 20 of the Ordinance in delimiting the wards. Section 20 of the Local Government (Union Parisad) Ordinance, 1983 is quoted below.

"20. Delimitation wards-(1) The wards shall be delimited having regard to territorial unity and, so far as practicable, to distribution of population and administrative convenience.

(2) A delimitation officer may, for the purpose of delimiting the wards, make such enquiries and examine such records as he may deem necessary and consider such representations as may be received by him, and shall publish at his office and at the office of the Union parisad and at such other place or places as he considers necessary a preliminary list of wards specifying the areas proposed to be included in each such ward together with a notice inviting objections or suggestions within fifteen days from the date of publication of the notice.

(3) The objection or suggestion, if any, received under sub-section (2) shall be forwarded to the Thana Nirbahi Officer who, after making such enquiries as he considers necessary, shall give his decision within a period not exceeding fifteen days from the date of receipt of the objections or suggestions from the delimitation officer.

(4) The delimitation officer shall make such amendments, alterations or modifications in the preliminary list published under sub-section (2) as may be required by any decision on any objection or suggestion given by the Thana Nirbahi Officer, under sub-section (3) and may also make such other amendments, alterations or modifications in the said list as may be necessary for correcting any error or omission.

(5) After making amendments, alteration of modifications, if any, under sub-section (4), the delimitation officer shall publish at his office and at the office of the Union Parisad and at such other place or places as he considers necessary the final list of wards, specifying the areas included in such ward and shall forward attested copies thereof to the Thana Nirbahi Officer, who shall publish the list of wards in the official Gazette."

12. It appears from Annexure-C-2 that the Pipya village is adjacent to Menapur village under ward No. 4 and the people of Pipya village have exercised their right of franchise in the Menapur polling centre for long as per finding of respondent No. 9 vide Annexure-F. During the division of the three wards into 9 wards this Pipya village was placed under ward No. 4 along with Menapur and Niraine villages by the Chairman and members of the Union Parisad. A former Chairman, who is an inhabitant of Ward No. 5, raised an objection to inclusion of the Pipya village with Menapur under ward No. 4 and, according to him, it should be included with ward No. 6 The delimitation officer made an enquiry into the matter on 9-9-1996 and in local inspection found that the people of the Pipya village would cast their votes in Menapur village centre from before. Mouza Number of Pipya and Menapur villages is one and same, i-e, 179. There is no good communication between Rajargaon, i.e ward No. 6, and the Pipya village, socially they are co-related with Menapur village and that from the point of distribution of population i-e, voter-consistency, it is convenient for them to remain with the Menapur village and no one from the Pipya village ever raised any objection to inclusion of the village to ward No. 4.

13. Under sub-section (3) of section 20 of the Ordinance the Thana Nirbahi Officer may make an inquiry if he receives any objection or suggestion about delimitation and shall give his decision within 15 days and send it to the delimitation officer and under sub-section (4) the delimitation officer shall make such amendments, alterations or modifications in the preliminary list as may be required by any such decision. Thereafter the delimitation officer shall publish final list at specified places and shall send attested copies thereof to the Thana Nirbahi Officer who shall publish the list of wards in the official Gazette in accordance with sub-section (5). But in the instant case, the Thana Nirbahi Officer, respondent No. 8, in violation of procedure laid down in section 20 included the Pipya village with ward No. 6 behind the back of the villagers and without making any inquiry or suggestion whatsoever and before publication of final list according to the procedure, sent the same to respondent No. 2 for publication in the Bangladesh Gazette and the impugned Gazette notification was thus published.

14. Under section 20 of the Local Government (Union Parisad) Ordinance, 1983 only the delimitation officer is responsible for making preliminary and final list of wards. After publishing preliminary list he can make amendment, alteration, modification, if any. The Thana Nirbahi Officer may give his decision on specific matter to the delimitation officer owing to which the delimitation officer may make an amendment, alteration or modification or necessary correction of any error or omission in the preliminary list and shall thereafter publish the final list in the manner prescribed in sub-section (5) and only after that the Thana Nirbahi Officer shall publish the final list in the official Gazette.

<u>15. In the instant case there is nothing to show that the Thana Nirbani Officer ever made any inquiry, decision or suggestion to the delimitation officer and the delimitation officer ever made any amendment, alteration modification in the preliminary list. It appears that bypassing the delimitation officer and denying sentiment of the inhabitants of the Pipya village, ignoring their communication and other social and practical inconveniences and territorial unity the Thana Nirbahi Officer, respondent No. 8 sent the list of 9 wards to respondent No. 2 for publication in the Bangladesh Gazette including the Pipya village in ward No. 6 to utter disappointment of the inhabitants of that village and paving ways for litigation's resulting in impasse in the elections of that Union Parisad. No election was held in his Union Parisad, according to the Learned Assistant Attorney General, after 1992. The Thana Nirbahi Officer has acted beyond his jurisdiction and pangs have drawn the people up to this court.</u>

16. In the case of Abdul Wahab Chowdhury vs Md Abu Taher and others, reported in 6 BLC (AD) 151 their Lordships held that It is absolutely within the province of the delimitation officer to include a village in any ward taking into consideration all the three factors viz; territorial unity, administrative convenience and distribution of population as far as practicable.

<u>17. In a democratic society it is the convenience of the villagers and voters that shall be honoured in matters relating to delimitation or polling centre and not of any chairman, official or individual. Well linked communication, territorial unity and distribution of population are preconditions in these matters which have been violated by the official with impunity.</u>

18. It further appears that the Election Commission by Memo No. NIKS/Stha" Ni-I/E" PA/2(56)96/751 dated 9-10-2000 instructed respondent No. 5, the District Election Officer, Chandpur to hold General Election in this Union in view of disposal of Writ Petition No. 6772 of 1992, vide Annexure-H. Though there was no order of stay of election from this Court in this Writ Petition but still the District Election Officer did not arrange for holding election in accordance with Annexure-H for reasons best known to him.

19. Therefore inclusion of the Pipya village in ward No. 6 of No.1 Rajargaon (Uttar) Union Parisad under Hajiganj Upazila, District Chandpur and publishing the same in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 12-10-1996 (Annexure-G) is declared to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The respondent are directed to exclude the Pipya village from ward No. 6 and include the same in ward No. 4 and publish necessary Gazette Notification accordingly.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.
