full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: The propriety and legality of concurrent decisions recorded by Courts below have been called in question by pre-emptee petitioner in invoking this Court's Civil Revisional Jurisdiction on laying a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Opposite party No.1 of this Civil Revision petition in the capacity of a co-sharer by inheritance as pre-emptor impleading petitioner as pre-emptee laid a case being Miscellaneous case No.6 of 1986 in the Fourth Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge Narayanganj under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for an order of pre-emption with respect to land described in schedule to Miscellaneous case. The said Miscellaneous case was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1990 on transfer to second Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Narayanganj Pre-emptee-petitioner was a stranger to the case holding.

3. Petitioner of Civil Revision petition as pre-emptee resisted Miscellaneous Case on presentation of a written objection taking stand that pre-emption proceeding holding had been sub-divided and new Jama had been created in the name of seller-opposite party No. 2 and also in the name of pre-emptee-petitioner and pre-emptor opposite party ceased to be a co-sharer in pre-emption proceeding holding.

4. The legal battle between pre-emptor-opposite party and pre-emptee-petitioner centred round the question of co-sharership of pre-emptor-opposite party on pre-emption proceeding holding.

5. Evidence both oral and documentary had been led in support of the respective contentions of the parties.

6. Two witnesses had been examined in support of the case of pre-emptor-opposite party. Pre-emptor-petitioner examined himself as OPW 1 in support of his case.

7. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court, Narayanganj by judgment and order dated 24-6-1992 allowed pre-emption Miscellaneous case. In allowing the case learned Senior Assistant Judge as trial Judge considered evidence both oral and documentary and other materials brought on record and recorded decision that mutation and sub-division proceeding with respect to pre-emption proceeding holding had not been done properly and legally. Learned trial Judge further held that pre-emptee-petitioner failed to substantiate his case that mutation and sub-division proceeding had been done within the knowledge of pre-emptor-opposite party.

8. Pre-emptee-petitioner felt aggrieved of the above adjudication and sought setting aside the same through a medium of appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 43 of 1992 before the Court of District Judge, Narayanganj. Learned Subordinate Judge, Narayanganj heard the appeal and by judgment and order dated 17-8-1993 dismissed the appeal. In recording dismissal, learned Subordinate Judge as appellate Judge as well as the final judge of fact also considered evidences and other materials on record and came in full agreement with the decision rendered by learned trial Judge.

9. Feeling still dissatisfied, pre-emptee-petitioner approached this court in this Civil Revision petition and obtained present Rule.

10. Basic ground pressed into service in this Civil Revision petition is that courts below failed to consider that suit land stood recorded in the name of seller opposite party and separate Jama was created in his name prior to sale of the suit land to pre-emptee-petitioner and, pre-emptor-opposite party not being a co-sharer of the holding was not entitled to pre-empt suit land.

11. The fact of Civil Revision petition hinges on answer to the following question whether pre-emptor-opposite party ceased to be a co-sharer to exercise right of pre-emption on the basis of alleged sub-division of pre-emption proceeding holding.

<u>12. In approaching the said question provision contained in section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act may conveniently be noticed. Section 117 (1)( c) enshrines that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent and for effecting a sub-division of a joint tenancy an application is required to be filed and notice is required to be given to all the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter and notice having not been served upon co-sharers, mutation and sub-division effected behind their back cannot said to be valid sub-division or splitting up of jama and in such case co-sharer in the joint tenancy cannot be said to have lost their right of pre-emption.</u>

13. Pre-emptee-petitioner claimed that joint tenancy had been sub-divided and new jama had been created in the name of the seller and also in the name of pre-emptee-petitioner. This contention of the pre-emptee-petitioner has been negatived by pre-emptor-opposite party raising contention that joint tenancy or holding was not sub-divided and she did not cease to be a co-sharer in holding and the pre-emptee-petitioner remains to be a stranger to case holding.

14. Exhibit-ka and ka(1) are mutated khatians in the name of Golam Mustafa Bhuiyan, seller opposite party No. 2 and Exhibit-kha (1) is a Rent Receipt manifesting payment of rent by pre-emptee petitioner and Exhibit-kha (2) is a niutated Khatian in the name of pre-emptee-petitioner, Except those documents no other documents had been produced from the side of pre-emptee-petitioner evidencing that for sub-division of the joint tenancy application was filed before Revenue Officer and notices upon co-sharers had been issued and co-sharers had been heard in the alleged sub-division matter. In the absence of those it cannot be at all suggested that the joint tenancy had been sub-divided and a separate Jama and tenancy had been created in the name of seller opposite party and pre-emptee-petitioner. There cannot be any sub-division of holding and splitting up of Jama unless requirements of law embodied in section 117 (1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been complied with.

15. Courts below also duly considered this aspect of the matter and allowed pre-emption Miscellaneous Case. No exception can be taken to the decisions rendered by courts below. In agreement with the decisions recorded by courts below I am also of this view that pre-emptor-opposite party did not cease to be a co-sharer in the case holding and pre-emptee-petitioner is a stranger.

16. This takes me to the, propriety of decisions rendered by courts below. On examination of the decisions, reason and. conclusion reached by courts below it is not at all possible to hold that those were not backed by substantial evidence and went against evidence and materials on record and suffer from patent illegality, legal infirmity, perversity and flagrant error of law warranting any interference by this court in the exercise of Civil Revisional Authority under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. Resultantly, this Rule arising out of Civil Revision petition got not merit and Rule stands discharged, however, without any order as to costs.

18. The order dated 8-11-1993 recorded at the time of issuance of Rule staying the judgment and order dated 17-8-1993 passed by learned Subordinate Judge, Narayanganj till disposal of the Rule stands vacated.

Lower court Records be sent down as immediate as possible.

End.

parties:
Shahriar Rashid Khan ----- Petitioner
Vs
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Parliamentary Affairs and others -----Respondents [In WP No. 5321 of 1996

Mahmuda Rahman ----- Petitioner.
Vs
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Parliamentary Affairs and others ----- Respondents [In WP No. 5313 of 1996]
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: Since in these two Writ Petition Nos. 5321 of 1996 and 5313 of 1996 the constitutional validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, has been challenged, the same were heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment.

2. Rules were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, should not be declared void, illegal, ultra vires the Constitution and are of no legal effect and as to why the Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)/1996 dated 2-10-96 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11 (11)/5 dated 4-11-75 should not be declared illegal, unlawful and void.

3. In Writ Petition No. 5321 of 1996 Colonel (Retd.) Shahriar Rashid Khan is the petitioner. He has been implicated as an accused in Dhanmondi Thana Case No. 10 (10)/1996 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11)/1975. In this Writ Petition the validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, and the legality of the institution of the aforesaid two criminal cases have been challenged.

4. In Writ Petition No. 5313 of 1996 Mrs. Mahmuda Rahman mother of Colonel (Retd.) Syed Faruqur Rahman, is the petitioner. In this writ petition the validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, and the institution of Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)/1996 have been challenged. It is stated in the application that the accused Colonel Faruqur Rahman is in custody and the petitioner-mother tried her best to get the vokalatnama from him from the jail, but she was unsuccessful. Since the petitioner being mother could not obtain the vokalatnama from her son (in jail), she had no other alternative but to file the present Writ Petition on behalf of her son challenging the validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, No. 21 of 1996 and the criminal proceeding as stated above.

5. In this connection a short background of the occurrence requires to be stated. By virtue of Constitution (4th Amendment) Act, 1975, the Constitution of Bangladesh was amended and the then Prime Minister Shaikh Mujibur Rahman became the President of Bangladesh. In the morning of 15th August, 1975 the President Shaikh Mujibr Rahman and his family members and some others were killed by a group of army people who committed a coup and these army people, after killing the President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman, brought Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed, one of the Cabinet Members of President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman, and put him in the office of the President of Bangladesh. Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed assumed the power of the Government as President on 15-8-75 and proclaimed Martial Law on 20th August, 1975, with effect from 15th August, 1975, throughout the country. Though Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed proclaimed Martial Law all over the country by his proclamation dated 20th August, 1973, he maintained the Constitution of Bangladesh with a condition that 'subject to the Martial Law Proclamation, Martial Law Regulation and Martial Law Orders, the Constitution of Bangladesh would continue to remain in force. On 26th of September, 1975 Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed as President of Bangladesh promulgated an Ordinance which was called 'Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 and by that Ordinance indemnity was granted to all those people responsible for killing the President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and others on 15th August, 1975, restricting from taking any legal or other proceeding in respect of certain acts or things done in connection with, or in preparation of execution of any plan, or steps necessitating, the historical change and the proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of 15th August, 1975.

6. In the night following 2nd November, 1975 (3-11-75) four national leaders, namely, Vice-President Syed Nazrul Islam, Prime Minister Captain Mansur Ali, Mr. Tajuddin Ahmed and Mr. Qumruzzaman were killed in the Dhaka Central Jail. In connection with that jail killing, Jail Authority lodged FIR in Lalbagh Police Station which was registered as Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11)/1975. The said case was pending in the Lalbagh Police Station and no further step was taken so far. With regard to the killing of the President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and others, on 2nd of October, 1996 an FIR was lodged in Dhanmondi Police Station being Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10 (10)/1996. Colonel (Retd.) Shahriar Rashid Khan along with others has been made accused in both the aforesaid criminal cases and Colonel (Retd.) Faruqur Rahman along with others has been made accused in Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)/1996.

7. As the Parliament thought it necessary to repeal the said Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, it passed the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 repealing Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 14-11-96. Section (1) (2) of the aforesaid Indemnity(Repeal) Act, 1996, runs as follows:

"2(1) The Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (L of 1975, যাহা XLX of 1975 নম্বরে মুদ্রিত), অতঃএব CO Ordinance বলিয়া উল্লেখিত, এত দ্বারা রহিত করা হইল।

(২) এই আইন বলবৎ হইবার পূর্বে যে কোন সময় উক্ত Ordinance এর অধিনকৃত কোনকার্য্য, গৃহিত কোন ব্যবস্থা, প্রদত্ত কোন সার্টিফিকেট বা আদেশ-নির্দেশ অথবা অর্জিত কোন অধিকার বা সুযোগ-সুবিধা অথবা সরকার বা কোন কর্তৃপক্ষের জন্য সৃষ্ট কোন দায়-দায়িত্ব, যদি থাকে এর ক্ষেত্রে General Clauses Act, 1887 (X of 1987) এর Section 6- এর বিধানাবলী প্রযোজ্য  হইবেনা এবং উক্ত রুপ কৃতকার্য্য, গৃহীত ব্যবস্থা, প্রদত্ত সার্টিফিকেটবা আদেশ-নির্দেশ বা অর্জিত অধিকার বা সুযোগ-সুবিধা বা সৃষ্ট দায়-দায়িত্ব উপ-ধারা (১) দ্বারা উক্ত Ordinance রহিত করণের সংগে সংগে এইরুপে অকার্য্যকর বাতিল ও বিলুপ্ত হইয়া যাইবে যেন উক্ত Ordinance জারী করা হয় নাই এবং উক্ত Ordinance এর কোন অস্তিত্ব ছিলনা ও নাই।

8. Challenging the validity of the aforesaid Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 and also challenging the legality of the institution of the aforesaid two criminal cases the present two writ petitions were moved by the petitioners who thereupon obtained two instant Rules from this Court.

9. In these two cases the petitioners brought several allegations which were denied by the respondents by filing affidavit-in-opposition. Affidavits-in-reply have also been filed. In the instant cases the facts are not required to be stated in details in view of the fact that mainly the constitutional validity of Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 is under challenge in both the writ petitions and we are to consider as to whether this Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 is a valid piece of legislation or not and as to whether the institution of the aforesaid two criminal cases is constitutionally barred or not.

10. Mr. KS Nabi, the learned Attorney-General for Bangladesh, has raised the following preliminary objections:

(a) The petitioners have no locus-standi to file the instant writ petitioners.

(b) Previously on behalf of both the accused, namely, Colonel (Retd.) Shahriar Rashid Khan and Colonel (Retd.) Faruqur Rahman two writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition Nos. 4297 of 1996 and 4334 of 1996 were moved before this Court, but the same were summarily rejected holding that the petitioners in those two writ petitions had no locus-standi to file the writ petitions and that they might seek alternative remedy under the Criminal Procedure Code. So, the two writ petitions were not maintainable. He further submits that against the orders passed in those two writ petitions the petitioners went before the Appellate Division and preferred appeals. But, ultimately, during hearing of the leave petitions the learned Advocate for the petitioners had withdrawn the aforesaid two appeals from the Appellate Division. So the instant two writ petitions cannot be entertained.

(c) On behalf of the present two accused two writ petitions were also filed challenging the orders of their detention under the Special Powers Act. In the said two writ petitions, both the Rules were made absolute and they were directed to be released. In those writ petitions moved, challenging the detention made under the Special Powers Act, in fact, the petitioners had not denied the grounds of detention. Since the grounds of detention were, in fact, admitted, the present two writ petitions are not maintainable.

11. Mr. Muhammad Korban Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that in the instant Writ Petition No. 5321 of 1996 Shahriar Rashid Khan himself is the petitioner. He signed the vokalatnama from the jail and filed this writ petition. Only with the permission of the Court the affidavit was sworn by his wife. In Writ Petition No. 5313 of 1996 Mrs. Mahmuda Rahman, the mother of accused Faruqur Rahman, is the petitioner. In the Writ Petition she has explained the position stating that her son Colonel (Retd.) Faruqur Rahman was in custody since 13-8-96. She tried her best to get the vokalatnama executed by her son from jail, but he was not allowed to execute the vokalatnama by the Jail Authority. Since the accused Faruqur Rahman was not allowed to execute the vokalatnama in order to file a writ petition, the mother, namely, the petitioner on behalf of her son, filed the writ petition. Further, Mr. Korban Ali submits that onbehalf of her son the petitioner Mrs. Mahmuda Rahman challenged the vires of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 and the criminal proceeding started against her son. So, Mr. Korban Ali submits, both the Writ Petitions are maintainable in the present form.

<u>12. In Writ Petition Nos. 4297 of 1996 and 4334 of 1996 the wife of Shahriar Rashid Khan and mother of Faruqur Rahman respectively challenged the detention of the two accused (in custody), but in the prayer portion the petitioners challenged the validity of the aforesaid two criminal proceedings praying for a declaration that the aforesaid two criminal proceedings should be declared to have been instituted without lawful authority and were of no legal effect. This Court summarily rejected those two writ petitions on the ground that by the application under Articles 102(2)(b )(i) of the Constitution the criminal proceedings as stated above could not be challenged in view of the fact that there was an alternative remedy for quashing the proceedings under the Criminal Procedure Code. Further, both the petitioners, in fact, were not the aggrieved persons and, as such, the two writ petitions were summarily rejected. But in the present two writ petitions the constitutional vires of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, along with it, the very legality of institution of the aforesaid two criminal proceedings has been challenged. So, in our view, the orders by which we summarily rejected the previous two writ petitions cannot be a bar for institution of the present two writ petitions inasmuch as the cause of action of the previous two writ petitions was quite distinguishable from the cause of action as taken in the present two writ petitions. Challenging the detention of two detenus two writ petitions were also filed on behalf of the present two accused. After hearing, this Court made both the Rules absolute and directed the detenus to be released forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case. In view of the above we hold that the present two writ petitions are maintainable and as such the preliminary objections raised by the learned Attorney-General cannot be accepted.</u>

13. Mr. Korban Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioners in both the writ petitions, has raised the following points:

(A) Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 is ultra vires the Constitution offending paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution.

(B) Since the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was protected and saved under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, the same cannot be repealed by simple majority of the members of the Parliament. Rather in order to repeal such an Ordinance the Constitutional amendment by two third majority of the members of Parliament is necessary, but is was illegally passed by the simple majority.

(C) Even if it can be repealed by simple majority, its effect, consequence, benefit, result and legal right accrued to the accused will remain in force as the same have been saved and protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and under section 6 of the General Clauses Act and such effect, consequence, benefit, result and legal right derived from the aforesaid Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 cannot be taken away without amending the provisions of paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution as per Article 142 of the Constitution by two-third majority of the members of Parliament.

(D) Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 is nothing but a colourable legislation inasmuch as Constitution, in fact, was amended indirectly by this Act which cannot be done directly.

(E) Since the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 has been protected under the Constitution, the two impugned criminal proceedings cannot be instituted against the accused of the two criminal cases as the accused of these two criminal cases are entitled to be protected constitutionally.

14. Mr. Korban Ali submits that the occurrence that took place on 15th August, 1975, was nothing but a revolution and through such revolution the existing Government was changed and the new Government took over the power. By way of revolutionary process Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed took over the power of the country which was ultimately protected and saved by Proclamation No. 1 of 1977 vide Para 3A and by Constitution (5th) Amendment) Act No.1 of 1979 vide Para 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. He submits that whatever was done in between 15th August, 1975 and 9th April, 1979, were protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. As such, anything done by the Government in between the said period cannot be called in question in any manner whatsoever. Mr. Korban Ali further submits that Martial Law was proclaimed by Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed on 20th August, 1975, all over the country with effect from 15th August, 1975 which was withdrawn on 9th of April, 1979. So, anything done in between the said period cannot be challenged. In this connection he has referred to the case of State vs. Dosso, 11 DLR (SC) 1.

15.Mr. Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the occurrence which took place in the morning of 15th of August, 1975, was not a revolution, rather a group of army people being armed with sophisticated weapons attacked the house of the then President Bangabandhu Shaikh Mujibur Rahman, the father of the nation, and killed him and all his family members and others including a ten years old child. It was nothing but a simple killing of the President and his family members and usurpation of power by Khondkar Moshtaque Ahmed with the help of a group of army personnel and thereby he illegally and unconstitutionally proclaimed himself as President and took over the power of the country. So, Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed was an usurper and unlawful ruler and, as such, his regime as well as his rule was wholly unconstitutional and the activities of an usurper like Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed cannot be protected and saved under the constitution. So, the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, promulgated by Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed, had no legal existence and as a result the criminal proceedings started against the two accused and others cannot be called to be constitutionally barred.

16. It is difficult for us to accept the above emotional contentions of either the learned Advocate Mr. Korban Ali or Mr. KS Nabi, the learned Attorney-General, in view of the fact that we are not called upon here to consider and judge the constitutional validity of the regime prevailing from 15th August, 1975 upto 9th April, 1979. Both the learned Advocates of both sides appeared to be swayed by emotions. During the above period so many Martial Law Proclamations were issued, Martial Law Regulations were made, Martial Law Rules and orders were passed and so many ordinary laws like Ordinances, Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws, etc. were passed by the authority for running the administration. Not only that, several provisions of the Constitution of Bangladesh were amended or repealed by Martial Law Proclamations at different times and ultimately, the Parliament passed the Constitution (5th Amendment) Act on 6th April, 1979 protecting and saving the effects of the Martial Law Proclamations, Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law orders and other laws made during the aforesaid period. Since this Constitution (5th Amendment) Act had been passed by two-third majority of the members of the Parliament and since that has been incorporated into the Constitution as a part of the Constitution, we are not in a position to re-open the passed and closed issue and consider the constitutional validity of the aforesaid Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979. As an existing and continuing law this Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 was running in the statute book of this country and on 14th November, 1996, that Ordinance was repealed by Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 and since the validity of this Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 has been challenged. in both the writ petitions, we are required to consider what is the law passed on 14th of November, 1996 as Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 and also what was the Constitution as stood on that very day, that is, on 14-11-96. We are of the view that we cannot go beyond that in the instant two writ petitions.

17. Mr. Korban Ali has referred to paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution along with the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975. The Indemnity Ordinance, No. 50 of 1975 and paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution run as follows:

"GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH MINISTRY OF LAW, PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND JUSTICE"

(Law and Parliamentary Affairs Division)

NOTIFICATION

Dacca, the 26th September, 1975

No.692. Pub: The following Ordinance made by the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, on the 26th September, 1975, is hereby published for general information:

THE INDEMNITY ORDINANCE, 1975

Ordinance No. L of 1975

AN ORDINANCE

To restrict the taking of any legal or other proceedings in respect of certain acts or things done in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or steps necessitating, the historical change and the proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of the 15th August, 1975.

Whereas it is expedient to restrict the taking of any legal or other proceedings in respect of certain acts or things done in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or steps necessitating, the historical change and the Proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of the 15th August, 1975;

And whereas Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary;

Now, therefore, in pursuance of the Proclamation of the 20th August, 1975, and in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of Article 93 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the President is pleased to make and promulgate the following ordinance:

1. Short title:- This Ordinance may be called the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975.

2. Restrictions on the taking of any legal or other proceedings against persons in respect of certain acts and things-(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any law, including a law relating to any defence service, for the time being in force, no suit, prosecution or other proceedings, legal or disciplinary, shall lie, or be taken, in, before or by any Court including the Supreme Court and Court Martial, or other authority against any person, including a person who is or has, at any time, been subject to any law relating to any defence service, for or on account of or in respect of any act, matter or thing done or step taken by such person in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or as necessary step towards, the change of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of the 15th August, 1975.

(2) For the purposes of this section, a certificate by the President, or a person authorised by him in this behalf, that any act, matter or thing was done or step taken by any person mentioned in the certificate in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or as necessary step towards, the change of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of the 15th August, 1975, shall be sufficient evidence of such act, matter or thing having been done or step having been taken in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or as necessary step towards, the change of such Government and the Proclamation of Martial Law on that morning.

Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed

President

MH Rahman

Secretary.

Dacca

26th September, 1975

Paragraphs 3A(I) and (2) and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution:

"3A.(1) The Proclamations of the 20th August, 1975, and 8th November, 1975, and the Third Proclamation of the 29th November, 1976, and all other Proclamations and Orders amending or supplementing them, thereinafter in this paragraph collectively referred to as the said Proclamations and all Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law Orders and all other laws made during the period between the 15th day of August, 1975 and the date of revocation of the said Proclamations and the withdrawal of Martial Law (both days inclusive), hereinafter in this paragraph referred to as the said period, shall be deemed to have been validly made and shall not be called in question in or before any Court or Tribunal on any ground whatsoever.

(2) All orders made, acts and things done, and actions and proceedings taken, or purported to have been made, done or taken, by the President or the Chief Martial Law Administrator or by any other person or authority during the said period, in exercise or purported exercise of the powers derived from any of the said Proclamation or any Martial Law Regulation or Martial Law Order or any other law, or in execution of or in compliance with any order made or sentence passed by any Court or authority in the exercise or purported exercise of such powers, shall be deemed to have been validly made, done or taken and shall not be called in question in or before any Court or Tribunal on any ground whatsoever."

"18. All Proclamations, Proclamation Orders, Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law Orders and other laws made during the period between the 15th August, 1975, and the 9th April, 1979 (both days inclusive), all amendments, additions, modifications, substitutions and omissions made in this Constitution during the said period by any such Proclamation, all orders made, acts and things done, and actions and proceedings taken, or purported to have been made, done or taken, by any person or authority during the said period in exercise of the powers derived or purported to have been derived from any such Proclamation, Martial Law Regulation, Martial Law Order or any other law, or in execution of or in compliance with any order made or sentence passed by any court, tribunal or authority in the exercise or purported exercise of such powers, are hereby ratified and confirmed and are declared to have been validly made, done or taken and shall not be called in question in or before any Court, tribunal or authority on any ground whatsoever."

18. Relying on the aforesaid provisions of law Mr. Korban Ali submits that the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 or 1975 was promulgated on 26-9-75 and as the same was protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, without amending paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, the Indemnity Ordinance, No. 50 of 1975 cannot be repealed. Since this Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 offend paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, the same is ultra vires of the Constitution and, as such, it is liable to be struck down. Mr. Korban Ali has alternatively argued that even if by ordinary legislation the Indemnity Ordinance, (No. 50) of 1975 can be amended or repealed, its effect, consequence, benefit, result and legal right accrued out of the Ordinance will remain in force in view of the provisions of paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and also of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. Since all those who took part in the occurrence of 15th August, 1975, are entitled to the effect, consequence, benefit, results and legal right of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, that cannot be taken away by ordinary legislation without amending paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. He submits that the Ordinance may be repealed, but its consequence will remain and since the right accrued under the aforesaid Indemnity Ordinance (No. 50) of 1975 on and from 15th August, 1975 in favour of the two accused in the instant two writ petitions, the same cannot be taken away by ordinary legislation, namely, the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996.

19. He further submits that as per section 6 of the General Clauses Act which was incorporated in the Constitution itself, the right accrued to the accused persons with effect from 15th August, 1975 cannot be taken away in any manner whatsoever. So, the accused in the aforesaid criminal cases have got constitutional protection and the institution of the two criminal proceedings against them is constitutionally barred.

20. Mr. Korban Ali further submits that this Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 is nothing, but a colourable legislation in view of the fact that since the repeal of the Indemnity Ordinance (No. 50 of 1975) could not be done directly without amending the Constitution, it was done indirectly through Ordinary Law. This means, in the colour of this repealing Act, namely, Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 the Constitutional provisions, in fact, have been amended. Such a colourable legislation is ultra vires of the Constitution.

21. Learned Attorney-General submits that by Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979, the Martial Law Orders and "all other laws" made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79 were protected and saved under the Constitution, namely, Paragraph 3A and Paragraph 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. Though Martial Law was promulgated all over the country with effect from 15th August, 1975, by a proclamation dated 20th August, 1975, a provision was made in paragraph (e) of the aforesaid proclamation to the following effect:

"The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, subject to this proclamation and the Martial Law Regulations and Orders and other orders made by me in pursuance thereof, continue to remain in force."

22. It is submitted that though Martial Law was promulgated all over the country, yet the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh remained in force side by side, only subject to the provisions of the Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations and Orders. This Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was promulgated by Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed as President of this country in exercise of this power conferred by Clause (1) of Article 93 of the Constitution as the Parliament was then not in session. Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed did not promulgate that law as a Martial Law Administrator, or that law was neither a Martial Law Proclamation nor a Regulation nor an Order. Usurping the power of the President of Bangladesh Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed promulgated the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 under Article 93(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Since the Constitution was in force, this Court should consider as to whether that Ordinance was promulgated in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. This Ordinance was not made a part of the Constitution. If that Ordinance infringes any provisions of the Constitution, then it would be ultra vires of the Constitution. If any law is found ultra vires of the Constitution, that law cannot be saved by the Constitution itself inasmuch as a void law repugnant to the Constitution cannot be saved by or under any other law.

23. In this connection learned Attorney-General has referred to Article 93(1) of the Constitution which runs as follows:

"At any time when (Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session), if the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary, he may make and promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require, and any Ordinance so made shall, as from its proclamation, have the like force of law as an Act of Parliament."

Together with the aforesaid Article 93(1) learned Attorney-General has also referred to Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution which run as follows:

7(2) "This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution, that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void."

Article 26(2):

"The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provision of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void."

24. Learned Attorney-General submits that under Article 93(1) of the Constitution the President is competent to promulgate Ordinance, but such Ordinance will take effect from the date of its promulgation. In the instant cases occurrence took place on 15-8-1975, but the Ordinance was promulgated on 26-9-1975. Such a subsequent Ordinance could not be given retrospective effect from 15-8-75 inasmuch as the effect of this Ordinance will take place on the very day of its promulgation, that is, on 26-9-75. Since this Ordinance was not in force on 16-8-75 and since retrospective effect has been given to it, it offends Article 93(1) of the Constitution and, as such, it is void. He further submits that the Ordinance No.50 of 1975 provided something which could not be provided by the Parliament itself and, as such, it offends Article 93(1)(i) of the Constitution.

25. This Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is ultra vires of the Articles 31, 32 and 46 of the Constitution. Articles 26 to 47 of the Constitution are the fundamental rights of the citizens. Article 31 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"To enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law."

Article 32 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law."

26. Mr. Attorney-General submits that these Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution are fundamental human rights guaranteed by our Constitution. So, right to life and body is protected under the fundamental rights which cannot be taken away except in accordance with law. On the fateful day, that is, 15-8-1975 the lives of the then President Bangabandhu Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and others were taken away by a group of army people without any sanction of law. In our ordinary laws, namely, the Penal Code or Army Act and in some other laws life of a person can be taken away by holding a trial in accordance with law. But in the morning of 15th August, 1975, the President along with his family members and others were killed by some army people and such an action of taking away life was not permitted by any law. If any person takes away life of another person, he must be tried in accordance with the existing law of the land. This Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 put restriction on taking any legal proceeding against the killers and though they committed the offence of murder, they were made immune from being tried under the ordinary laws of the land. Since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 has made provision for not trying the army people or any person who committed murder, for which the normal law was in force for trial, such an Ordinance, in fact, offends Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution inasmuch as, although without any sanction of law the President and his family members were killed, the killers were given protection by the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. Though the killers were liable for trial under ordinary laws of the land for killing several persons as stated above, by promulgating such Ordinance the killers were made impugned from facing the trial under the laws of the land. So, this Ordinance, in fact, offends and infringes the provisions of Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution and, as such, the Indemnity Ordinance is void being ultra vires the Constitution.

27. Learned Attorney-General has also referred to Article 46 of the Constitution which runs as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, Parliament may by law make provision for indemnifying any person in the service of the Republic or any other person in respect of any act done by him in connection with the national liberation struggle or the maintenance or restoration of order in any area in Bangladesh or validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted, forfeiture ordered, or other act done in any such area."

As such, it was void ab-initio. He further submits that void means non-existent from its very inception and a ban against its recognition. Even in juristic writing expression void and ultra vires are used in different sense. A thing that is void in the strict sense of the word is merely a nullity and may be ignored even in collateral proceeding as it never were. Void ab-initio is the expression Court often used to take. The expression ultra vires strictly implies to an absence of the jurisdiction as well as the absence of the competency.
