He submits that Bangladesh Bar Council Lawyers' Conference was held on 2-4-1989 and it was presided over by him. In that meeting a resolution was taken condemning the killing of the then President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and all other killings. Such an inhuman and brutal killing could not stand the test of any human rights.

57. He submits that an Ordinance may be promulgated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution in normal time by the President. Mr. Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed with the help of some army people usurped the power of the President on 15th August, 1975 and made himself a self-proclaimed President of Bangladesh and he also proclaimed Martial Law on 20-8-75 all over the country with effect from 15th of August, 1975. The Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 dated 26-9-75 was promulgated in an abnormal situation. It might be that the self-proclaimed President Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed was surrounded by army people in Bangladesh with tanks and guns and he was forced to promulgate that Indemnity Ordinance in order to save the killers. Martial Law was continuing and side by side the Constitution was running subject to the Martial Law. He submits that the Indemnity Ordinance does not come within the purview of Article 46 of the Constitution and since it offended Article 46 of the Constitution, it was ultra vires that Article. This can be argued if the law was promulgated in a normal situation. Since the Indemnity Ordinance was promulgated in an abnormal situation being forced by the killers of President Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members, it should be looked at from a different angle.

58. He has referred to the preamble of Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 and submitted that in the preamble the President taking source of power from the Martial Law Proclamation and exercising his power conferred under Article 93(1) of the Constitution promulgated the aforesaid Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. He submits that it shows that he assumed power from both the sources, that is, from Martial Law proclamation as well as from the Constitution and since being President he was the Supreme Authority to make Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations and Orders as well as he could exercise his power under the Constitution of Bangladesh, the Ordinance in question should be characterisd as an Act of President Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed who passed it in the capacity of an Administrator under the Martial Law Proclamation and, as such, it is a valid piece of legislation notwithstanding Article 46 of the Constitution and since such an Act in the form of an Ordinance is protected and saved under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Constitution, it should be deemed to be a valid law and a part of the Constitution.

<u>59. It shows some departure from the earlier views expressed by Mr. Khondaker. In an abnormal situation then prevailing, he characterised the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, as a valid legislation. He submits that such a law was not permitted to be promulgated either under Martial Law Proclamation or under the Constitution, but he termed it as a contractual legislation which was made by the highest source of law giving authority at the relevant time. As such it must be taken as a valid law which had been ultimately made a part of the Constitution by protecting, affirming and ratifying it in the Constitution. If Khondaker Mostaque Ahmed was forced by the killers of the President and others to make such a legislation, it would be absolutely a malafide one which cannot be protected and saved by the Constitution. Further, such a theory of contractual legislation was neither in the Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations or Orders, nor in the Constitution. So, it was absolutely without jurisdiction to pass such a law as the so-called highest law giver was not authorised by the Constitution or by any Martial Law Proclamation, Regulation or Order to make such a contractual legislation. He might be the highest law giver, but he must have to act within the bounds of law then in force. If it was not so done, it would be absolutely without jurisdiction. The Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, ex-facie shows that it was made by the President in exercise of his power under Article 93(1) of the Constitution as the Parliament was not in session then. So, the new theory of Mr. Khondaker i.e. contractual legislation had no legal existence either during normal time or during abnormal time, either in the Constitution or in the Martial Law Proclamation, Regulation or Order. As such, this new theory as enunciated by Mr. Khondaker is not acceptable.</u>

60. Now, we are to consider the two words "other laws" incorporated in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. Paragraph 3A (1) of the fourth Schedule provides that "law includes Ordinances, rules, regulations, bye-laws, orders, notifications and other instruments having the force of law." Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was not specifically mentioned in paragraphs 3A or 18 of the 4th Schedule, rather it was in the category of "other laws." All "other laws" made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79, were protected, ratified and confirmed by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule. According to Mr. Khondker, since Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was approved, protected, ratified and confirmed by Proclamation No. 1 of 1977 and further by the Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979, vide paragraphs 3A and 18 respectively in the 4th Schedule, the Ordinance was made a part of the Constitution. If the above view of Mr. Khondaker is accepted, then all "other laws" viz, Ordinance, Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws, Orders, Notifications and other instruments having the force of law made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79 should be treated as parts of the Constitution, and even for amendment of full-stop and semi-colon of the above "other laws", two third majority of the members of the Parliament will be necessary. We say, such an absurd proposition was neither contemplated by the Constitution itself nor by any Martial Law Proclamation, Regulation or Order which stood in force up to 9-4-79 from 15-8-75. Such a proposition will lead to legal crisis and constitutional vacuum.

61. It is not disputed that Khandaker Moshtaque Ahmed, Justice AM Sayem and General Ziaur Rahman were the three de-facto rulers of the country in view of the fact that they were not constitutionally elected. During the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79, they were required to make so many Ordinances, Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws, Notifications, Orders, etc. for running the administration of the state. When constitutional Government came into existence and democracy was restored through general election in 1979, all the laws made by the three de-facto rulers during the  above period were required to be saved, protected, ratified and affirmed, otherwise country would have fallen into Constitutional crisis and legal vacuum and that was why the "other laws" were protected, ratified and affirmed under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, So the "other laws" incorporated in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule were not made parts of the Constitution, rather they were protected and continued as existing and ordinary laws of the country.

62. He has alternatively submitted that even if it is presumed that at the time of promulgating such an Ordinance there was some legal defect or lack of authority, but after the Proclamation No.1 of 1977 by which the paragraph 3A in the 4th Schedule of the Constitution has been inserted, this has become a valid piece of law inasmuch as it was protected by way of amendment of the Constitution. Whatever legal incompetency was there before hand was rectified by paragraph 3A of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. He further submits that on 6-4-79 the Parliament passed Constitution (5ih Amendment) Act by two-third majority and thereby saved and protected everything including all laws promulgated during the period from 15th August, 1975 to 9th April, 1979 and hereby paragraph 18 in the 4th Schedule was added which ratified and confirmed the "other laws" made during the above period. Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution provide that whatever laws were made during this period shall be deemed to have been made validly and same cannot be called in question in any Court on any ground whatsoever. As such, in the eye of law this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was protected in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule by way of constitutional amendment made by Proclamation No. 1 of 1977 and Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979. In this view of the matter, Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits, this Indemnity Ordinance, despite its original invalid character, was made valid and a part and parcel of the Constitution and, as such, it can be amended or repealed only by passing an Act by two-third majority members of the Parliament under Article 142 of the Constitution. Since the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, was passed by a simple majority, it offends paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and, as such, it is violative of the provisions of Article 142 of the Constitution. In a way the submission of Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed supports Mr. Korban Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

63. In the Indemnity Ordinance preamble portion speaks that in pursuance of the Proclamation of 20th August, 1975 and in exercise of power conferred by clause (1) of Article 93 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the President is pleased to make and promulgate the Ordinance. Relying on it Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and Mr. Korban Ali both submit that the President was exercising power both as Martial Law Authority as well as Constitutional President and since he exercised both the powers in promulgating this Ordinance, it cannot be touched. But it appears to us that the first sentence, that is, "In pursuance of the proclamation of 20th August, 1975' the de-facto Ruler Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed showed his source of power to act as President and by the subsequent sentence, in fact, he exercised his actual power under Article 93(1) of the Constitution as President of Bangladesh. It is already stated that Martial Law as well as the Constitution of Bangladesh were running side by side. Since Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed was not an elected President or a Constitutional Head of the State and since he usurped the power by force with the help of some army people and proclaimed Martial Law on 20th August, 1975, and proclaimed himself as self-made President. he had shown his source of power in making every law which he made during his regime. For this reason in the very first sentence of the preamble of Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, he disclosed his source of power to act as President and by the subsequent sentence he exercised his real power as President under Article 93(1) of the Constitution. Further, in the preamble it is stated that whereas the Parliament is not in session which is the prerequisite to promulgate an Ordinance under Article 93(1) of the Constitution.

<u>64. So, it appears that it was an ordinary civil legislation as an Ordinance promulgated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution. Further, it appears that it was issued from the Ministry of Law, Parliamentary Affairs and Justice Division; the heading speaks that the 'following Ordinance made by the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh on 26th September, 1975.' At the bottom of the Ordinance Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed himself put his signature as President. It is true that Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed after usurping power and proclaiming Martial Law did not declare himself as Martial Law Administrator. Rather he declared himself as a President and by virtue of his post as President he performed his constitutional and statutory functions and at the same time he performed his function as Martial Law Administrator. Even then the very piece of legislation clearly shows that Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed as a President of Bangladesh promulgated this Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, under Article 93(1) of the Constitution, but he did not exercise his power as Martial Law Authority in promulgating this Ordinance. So, this Indemnity Ordinance is an ordinary simple civil legislation and, as such, the same can be amended or repealed by ordinary legislation without recourse to Article 142 of the Constitution.</u>

65. In this connection it may be mentioned that the Ordinance promulgated during Martial Law period is to be treated as ordinary law after withdrawal of Martial Law. In the case of Monoranjan Mukharjee vs. Election Commission, 41 DLR 484, a Division Bench of this Court (Mustafa Kamal and MA Chowdhury, JJ) observed that after withdrawal of Martial Law in November, 1986, the Ordinance in question (Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983), is to be read as an ordinary law and when it refers to any criminal offence, and also speaks about conviction, it invariably refers to ordinary offences provided by the ordinary laws of the country and also refers to trial and conviction by an ordinary criminal Court with the judicial hierarchy or Special Tribunal created by ordinary law.

<u>66. It was further observed by their Lordships that it is well-settled that Martial Law is not a part of constitutional scheme of this country. It is an extra-constitutional dispensation. It is a temporary measure, a short term arrangement. It meets only an interim need. When it leaves, it usually legalises all past actions for the purpose of immunity, with the tacit acknowledgement that its interference with the constitutional process is an aberration and needs to be condoned. But while leaving, the Martial Law does not leave a trail of disqualification. It is good as long as it lasts, but with its departure it no longer casts a shadow upon the ordinary laws of the land. We respectfully agree with the above views of their Lordships and hold that the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was continuing as an existing law along with other laws, after withdrawal of Martial Law, being protected and saved within the terms "other laws" as contained in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and it is subject to judicial review of this Court whenever it is challenged.</u>

<u>67. According to Mr. Korban Ali and Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, this Ordinance was made a part of the Constitution by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. But it appears that neither the 4th Schedule nor any other provision of the Constitution provides that this Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 should be treated as a part of the Constitution. Rather, by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution it was protected and continued as existing law in the category of "other laws" which were promulgated in between the period from 15th August, 1975 and 9th April, 1979. Since it was an ordinary piece of legislation being saved, protected and is continued under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, it can be amended or repealed by simple majority members of the Parliament. In paragraph 3A(7) of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution a clear provision has been laid down to the effect that all laws made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79 were protected, but the same can be amended, altered and repealed by the authority. It means, the Parliament is the actual authority for repealing a law. Now here in the 4th Schedule or in any other provision of the Constitution it was stipulated that the laws which were continued and saved under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution would require two-third majority members of the Parliament for necessary amendment or alteration or repeal. Since there was no provision like that, we cannot import such a provision and, as such, we hold that the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 can be amended or altered or repealed by simple majority -members of the Parliament and two-third majority of the members of the Parliament was not at all required for the same. The learned Attorney-General as well as other five learned Amicus Curiae expressed their views that this Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 has been legally passed by a simple majority members of the Parliament acdjo pass such a law, two-third majority of the members of the Parliament was not at all necessary.</u>

68. In the affidavit-in-opposition, for example, the learned Attorney-General has shown 12 Ordinances which were passed during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79, but subsequently they were repealed by Act of Parliament by simple majority and even by Ordinances. Mr. Attorney-General has given another example showing that the Supreme Court and the High Court Judges (Remuneration and Privileges) Ordinance, 1976, (LXV of 1976) was repealed by Supreme Court Judges (Remuneration and Privileges) Ordinance, 1978, (Ordinance No.Xl of 1978). This Ordinance No.XI of 1978 was subsequently amended by several other Ordinances, from time to time. So, the submission to the effect that 'other laws' saved and ratified in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution requires to be amended or repealed by two third majority members of the Parliament has no legal basis.

<u>69. Learned Attorney General and the five learned Amicus Curiae expressed the view that since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was void being ultra vires the Constitution, it was void ab-initio and in the eye of the Constitution there existed no law like the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. They further submit that Indemnity Ordinance was born dead and it had no legal existence from its birth. Since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was void being ultra vires the Constitution, it cannot be considered as one of the 'other laws' as referred to in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. Since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was void ab-initio, it had no legal existence on 26th of September, 1975 and, as such, it can neither be a part of the Constitution nor it can be one of the existing 'other laws" as provided under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. So, it appears to us that a void law though not declared void by any Court so long was legally repealed by the Parliament and, as such, there was no illegality or unconstitutionality in passing the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996.</u>

<u>70. As regards ouster of jurisdiction arguments have been advanced by the learned Advocates stating that even if in the Martial Law Proclamation or Regulation there was ouster clause, even then our Appellate Division had decided in so many cases that this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.is competent to see as to whether there was actual ouster of jurisdiction or not and also as to what is the extent and scope of such ouster clause. As in the instant case the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, is found void ab-initio being ultra vires the Constitution, this Court has got the jurisdiction to consider the constitutionality of such a law.</u>

71. In this connection the following cases may be referred: "Secretary of State vs. Mask & Co., 44 CWN (PC) 709. Anismic Ltd. vs. Foreign Compensation Commission, (1969)(1) AER 208, Khandkar Ehteshamuddin Iqbal vs. Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 154, Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed vs. Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 222, Jamil Haq vs. Bangladesh, 34 DLR (AD) 125, Bangladesh vs. Md. Salimullah, 35 DLR (AD) 1 and Anwar Hossain vs. Government of Bangladesh, 41 DLR (AD), 165. In this connection the case of William Marbury vs. James Madison, reported in US Supreme Court Reports (1803), 2 Law Edition 135, has been cited from the Bar repeatedly as an assertion of the right of judicial review by the Supreme Court" In the above case the decision of the US Supreme Court, written by Chief Justice Marshall, was a masterpiece of both legal reasoning and political dexterity. The decision made as early as in 1803 laid down the principle of judicial review and power of the Supreme Court to exercise it in the following admirable terms:

"Thus, the particular phraseology of the Constitution of the United States confirms and strengthens the principle, supposed to be essential to all written Constitutions, that a law repugnant to the Constitution is void and that Courts, as well as other departments, are bound by that instrument"

72. Towards the close of his submissions Mr. Attorney-General referred to the celebrated decision given in the case of Miss Benazir Bhutto vs. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1988 (SC) 416. Eleven Judges of the Pakistan Supreme Court heard the case for eleven days and then passed this big judgment. From the above decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court we may got substantial support in the instant cases. Some amendments were made in Political Parties Act of 1962 during Martial Law providing for compulsory registration of political parties. Challenging such amendments made by the Martial Law Authority and ultimately protected, preserved, ratified and confirmed in the Constitution, Benazir Bhutta moved the Supreme Court, thereupon the Supreme Court of Pakistan gave the above judgment declaring section 3- B of the Political Parties Act, 1962, void in its entirety.

Their Lordships of the Pakistan supreme Court in this judgment expressed the view that validity of Martial Law Authorities for their acts though barred can be challenged and their actions are subject to judicial review. Adaption, affirmance, validation and confirmation of law coupled with the clause ousting jurisdiction sweepingly of Courts have no effect of either effacing or eclipsing or subordinating fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution. Affirmation and validation made by the amendment of the Constitution, though restricted, is subject to judicial review if it violates Fundamental Rights. Their Lordships held as follows:

"But it does claim and has always claimed that it has the right to interpret the Constitution and to say as to what a particular provision of the Constitution means or does not mean, even if that particular provision is a provision seeking to oust the jurisdiction of this Court. This is a right which it acquires not dehors the Constitution but by virtue of the fact that it is a superior Court set up by the Constitution itself as a result of the System of Division of power. It is not necessary for this purpose to invoke any divine or supernatural right but this judicial power is inherent in the Court itself. It flows from the fact that it is a Constitutional Court and it can only be taken away by abolishing the Court itself."

"The Court if left with no jurisdiction to strike off the laws without, in any way, affecting the judicial power to interpret the constitutional provision, which cannot be denied so long as the Court exists. Here I would add the admirable words of Chief Justice Hughes of the Supreme Court of the United States of America. We are under a Constitution, but the Constitution is what the Judges say it is ....................... "(Columbia Law Review, Volume 49, page 201,"

In this connection we may also profitably quote the famous words of Chief Justice Marshall which runs as under:

"Every branch of Government i.e. executive as well as legislature, has the right to look to the Constitution to find its meaning but the ultimate authority to say what the law is, is the Court and it is for the Court to say whether the executive or the legislature has overstepped its bounds."

<u>73. Answer to the question of ouster of jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. High Court Division, under Article 102 of the Constitution, is hidden in the judgment of the case of Khandkar Moshtaque Ahmed vs. Bangladesh, 34 DLR (AD) 222 where the learned Amicus Curiae Mr. Khondker himself appeared. In that judgment our Appellate Division declared the entire trial of Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed under Martial Law Regulation void and without jurisdiction on the ground of malafide. So, from the above judgment it appears to us that any act or thing done or any trial taken place even under Martial Law Proclamation, Regulation or Order, can be challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution if it is done or made without jurisdiction, coram non judice or malafide.</u>

<u>74. Mr. Rafiq-ul Huq has placed before us the copy of the original Constitution of Bangladesh of 1972. He submits that only under Article 142 of the Constitution when amendment is required to be made, it must be made by two-third majority members of the Parliament, but in all other ordinary legislation, the amendment or addition or repeal of any enactment can always be made by simple majority members of the Parliament. This is the, established law. If in the Constitution, excepting Article 142, it is provided that a particular law should be amended or repealed by two-third majority of the members of the Parliament, then and there the question of two-third majority of the members of the Parliament will arise to amend or repeal such a law. He has referred to Article 47(2) proviso of the Constitution of 1972 and submitted that in that Article for some particular law it was provided that the modification or repeal of such law would have to be made by two-third majority of the members of the Parliament. Excepting that, in all other ordinary amendments or repeals which are not covered by Article 142 of the Constitution, the simple majority of the members of the Parliament is competent to make amendment, addition, alteration or repeal of the law. Paragraph 3A(7) of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution provides for alteration, addition or repeal of the legislation and since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was protected and preserved in the form of ordinary civil legislation, its repeal was legally and rightly done by Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996. Question of two-third majority of the members of the Parliament will arise only when the law sought to be amendment or repealed is covered under Article 142 of the Constitution.</u>

75. In reply, the learned Advocate Mr. Korban Ali submits that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was promulgated in Martial Law dispensation and since it was done in supra constitutional dispensation, it was protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and, as such, two-third majority of the members of the parliament is required to repeal it. We have answered to the above submission of Mr. Korban Ali by our discussions made above and no new explanation is necessary.

<u>76. Mr. Korban Ali further submitted that by Act of 1975 the Emergency Powers Act was passed. In the Emergency Order the enforcement of fundamental rights were suspended. Before-hand Emergency Power Ordinance, 1974, was promulgated by the then President of Bangladesh which was subsequently made an Act of Parliament. Proclamation of Emergency was declared on 28th December, 1974 and an Order was issued on 28th of December, 1974, by the President in exercise of the powers conferred by Clause (1) of Article 142C of the Constitution and by that order the President suspended the enforcement of fundamental rights through Court and this emergency was withdrawn on 27-11-79. He submits that since the Indemnity Ordinance was promulgated on 26-9-75 and since at the relevant time the enforcement of fundamental rights through Court remained suspended, Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, cannot be made ultra vires of the fundamental rights of the Constitution. It is difficult to accept the above contention of Mr. Korban Ali in view of the fact that for certain period the enforcement of fundamental rights through Court remained suspended and subsequently it was withdrawn. Imposition of such emergency and suspension of fundamental rights for a certain period does not mean that an Act or Ordinance cannot be declared ultra vires of the Constitution. It was merely the enforcement of fundamental rights through court remained suspended for a limited period, and nothing more. So, we do not find any substance in the above contention of Mr. Korban Ali.</u>

<u>77. It is submitted that for change of Government the above incident took place on 15-8-1975. A question was put to Mr. Korban Ali that the then President was part and parcel of the Government, but the other persons who were killed by some people on 15-8-75 were not in any way connected with the Government and, as such, why the killers would not be liable for killing of other people excepting the President? Mr. Korban Ali submits that the incident of 15th August, 1975 was a revolution done through military coup d'etat and during commission of such army coup it could not be ascertained as to who killed whom. As such the other people cannot be isolated from the incident at the relevant time. Such an explanation is absolutely unfortunate and, as such, it cannot be accepted.</u>

<u>78. He further submits that this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was an ex-post facto legislation by which benefit or right can be given retrospectively, but no provision can be made for punishing a person retrospectively which was not a punishment at the time of promulgation of Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. By ex-post facto legislation the vested right of the persons who were connected with 15th August, 1975, incident, cannot be taken away. This theory of ex post facto legislation is not tenable in the instant case in view of the fact that the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 appears to be void being ultra vires of the Constitution. Agreeing with the decision reported in AIR 1956 (All) 684, we also hold that an unconstitutional Act is not a law: it confers no right; it imposes no duties; it affords no protection; it creates no office; it is, in legal contemplation as inoperative as if it has never been passed.</u>

79. The Court posed another question to Mr. Korban Ali stating that the Indemnity Ordinance came into force on 26th September, 1975 which allegedly protected the killers of former President and others on 15-8-75. But the jail killing incident took place on 3-11-75. In the prayer portion the validity of both the proceedings of two criminal cases, namely, Dhanmondi PS Case No.10(10)/1996 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11)/1975 have been challenged. But the jail killing incident took place on 3-11-73 and how could it be protected by the Indemnity Ordinance dated 26-9-75, since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 only relates to 15th August, 1975 incident?

80. In reply, Mr. Karban Ali submits that by promulgation of second proclamation dated 8-11-75 the incident of 3-11-75 was covered. He further submits that this jail killing incident on 3-11-75 was a consequence with regard to the incident dated 15-8-75 and as such it was covered by second proclamation dated 8-11-75. He further submits that this jail killing incident dated 3-11-75 was not only a consequence of 15-8-75 incident but also it should be treated as a part of the same transaction. This is an absurd proposition in view of the fact that this second proclamation dated 8-11-75 did not cover or give any immunity to the killers who committed murder on 3-11-75 of four national leaders in jail. No other immunity order or regulation was made with regard to jail killing incident. It is absurd to think that incident dated 3-11-75 was a part of the same transaction which took place on 15-8-75 in view of the fact that Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 relates to the incident of 15th August, 1975, only, and not the incident dated 3-11-75. Mr. Korban Ali has just vainly put his venture to cover up the incident dated 3-11-75 treating it as a part of the same transaction of 15-8-75. So, we hold that there is no law whatsoever to immune the killers in jail on 3-11-75. This Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 dated 26-9-75 only related to 15th August, 1975 incident and it was in no way connected with the incident which took place in jail on 8-11-75.

81. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has given explanation to the words approval, ratification and confirmation showing Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, Volume I and Volume 3 By adding paragraph 3A of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution the "other law" made in between the period from 15-8-75 and 9-4-79 were deemed to have been validly made. By adding paragraph 18, Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits, "other laws" were ratified and confirmed by the two-third majority of the members of the Parliament and as such this Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, being in the category of "other laws" was made part of the Constitution which can be amended or repealed only by two-third majority in the Parliament. We have already made our discussions above and expressed our view on this point. Further discussion on it is not necessary at all.

82. Considering the submissions of the learned Advocates of both sides and the view expressed by the learned Amicus Curiae, it appears to us that both in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution ouster of jurisdiction of Court was incorporated in the manner that whatever was done or made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79 cannot be called in question in any Court or Tribunal. But we are happy to record that the learned counsels of both sides and all the Amicus Curiae unanimously expressed their valuable views that in spite of barring clause in paragraphs No. 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution this Court has got inherent jurisdiction to look into and consider the Constitutional validity of any law passed during the above period if the same is found to be made without jurisdiction, coram non judice or malafide.

<u>83. In this connection mention has already been made of the decisions reported in 33 DLR (AD) 154, 45 DLR (AD) 1 and 34 DLR (AD) 222 and 125. We are proud to see that by several celebrated judgments our Appellate Division has already settled the principle that in spite of ouster clause in law, this Court has got authority to make judicial scrutiny and review under its constitutional jurisdiction, if the law is passed or the thing is done without jurisdiction, coram-non-judice or malafide. If any Act is passed or any amendment of the Constitution is made even by two-third majority, even then this Court can interfere with it, if it is found that the Act or amendment affects the very fundamental structure of the Constitution. This point has been elaborately considered by the Appellate Division in the celebrated decision popularly known as Constitution (8th Amendment) Case, BLD (AD) 1989, Special Issue.</u>

<u>84. In the instant two cases the main point for consideration is as to whether the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, repealing Indemnity Ordinance (No. 50) of 1975, is repugnant to the Constitution. According to the petitioners, the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is a part of the Constitution being saved and protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and the repealing Act viz, Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 offended paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Schedule and Article 142 of the Constitution inasmuch as the said Act No. 21 of 1996 was passed by simple majority in the Parliament. It is difficult to accept the above contention of the petitioners. It appears to us that this Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was an ordinary legislation promulgated by the then President Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed under Article 93(1) of the Constitution. This was protected and saved in the category of "other laws" referred to in both paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. So, we hold that this Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 is not a part of the Constitution, rather it is an Ordinary Law protected and saved in the category of "other laws" in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule. Further, in pursuance of paragraphs 3A(7) of the 4th Schedule and Article 149 of the Constitution, we hold, this Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 has been legally repealed by simple majority members of the Parliament, as such the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, does not offend either paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule or Article 142 or any other provisions of the Constitution.</u>

85. With regard to the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, the Respondents advanced two-fold arguments. Firstly, Constitution was in force with the proclamation of Martial Law on 20th August, 1975, and when Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was promulgated on 26-9-75, it offended Articles 46, 27, 31, 32, 62 and 93(1)(i) of the Constitution and, as such, it was void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. Secondly, it was not brought to judicial scrutiny at any time before and with the withdrawal of Martial Law the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 was saved and protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule as existing law within the category of "Other Laws". So, this Ordinance No.50 of 1975, is repugnant to the Constitution offending its Articles 46, 27, 31, 32, 62 and 93(1)(i) and, as such, it is void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. Considering the above we hold that the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is ultra vires the Constitution and as such it is void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. As we are declaring this Ordinance No.50 of 1975 void, it had and has no legal existence in the eye of the Constitution on the very day when it was promulgated that is on 26-9-75 and now.

<u>86. As the Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 is declared void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution, it will not create any benefit, consequence, result or legal or vested right in favour of the persons for whom it was made and, as such, we hold that the benefit of section 6 of the General Clauses Act is not applicable to those persons who claim any benefit or legal right out of the said Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975.</u>

87. As the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 repealed the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, and as the petitioners, relying upon the provisions of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, have made prayers for declaring the institution of the two criminal cases viz, Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10) of 1996 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11) of 1975 void, illegal and without jurisdiction, we had to see the constitutional validity of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975. After due consideration of the provisions of the Constitution and Law, we hold that the prayers of the petitioners for declaring the above two criminal proceedings illegal, void and without jurisdiction cannot be accepted, because the very Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 itself is void being repugnant to the Constitution.

88. In this connection we like to refer to the famous sayings of MD Bidwas, a renowned Jurist, made in his book "Philosophy of Law" that "jurisprudence is said to be the daughter of philosophy. Every law must have its own philosophy. But a legal philosophy devoid of moral quality, if based purely on legal relations, may ultimately reduce the terms to be related to a cipher. This skeleton of legal relations may so dominate over the members of the social order that they vanish altogether. So the social order must be "good" one and one in which both the individual and the community are properly balanced and harmonised.

"It must not be forgotten that life of law is logic though law cannot stand divorced from life either. The end of law is justice which is twofold: natural and conventional. Natural justice is law because it is right, while conventional justice is law because it is law."

89. For this point of view the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, attained a technical status of law because of ratification by the Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979, but being against nature and natural justice cannot be law in the true sense of the term. Besides, this being repugnant to our Constitution cannot be a law and is void.

90. The purpose behind Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was to save or indemnify some killers, a purpose which is against fundamental human rights adopted by UN Charter and different International Conventions. In this connection it is worth-while to quote William Shakespeare, from his drama-"The life and death of King John,"

"There is no sure foundation set on blood,

No certain life achieved by others' death."

91. Allah Rabbul Al-Alamin disliked and disapproved of killing a man by another man and declared punishment for such killing in his Holy Quran as under (English Translation):

"If a man kills a Believer

Intentionally, his recompense

Is Hell, to abide therein

(For ever): and the wrath

And the curse of God

Are upon him, and

A dreadful penalty

Is prepared for him."

Sura No. IV (Nissa), verse-93

(The meaning of the Glorious Quran by Abdullah Yusuf Ali, Vol-1, page 210)

92. Thus the Idemntity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 offends the very spirit of the preamble of our Constitution which proclaimed "pledging that the high ideals of absolute trust and faith in the Almighty Allah."

93. Mr. Muhammad Korban Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, being assisted by his learned Junior Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam Khan, has put real efforts to do justice to his clients. In spite of ill health he rendered his valuable assistance to the Court in such an important constitutional case. His efforts and assistance are praiseworthy.

94. Learned Attorney-General Mr. KS Nabi being assisted by Senior Law Officers ably assisted the Court in a magnificent way and he left no stone unturned to do justice to his clients, namely, the respondents. His elaborate, thorough and lengthy arguments on constitutional points helped the Court to arrive a. a decision in such a constitutional matter of great public importance. His efforts to assist the Court are really commendable.

95. We are thankful to the six eminent and renowned jurists viz, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Dr. Kamal Hossain, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, Mr. M Nurullah and Mr. M Amir-ul Islam who, in spite of their own heavy pre-occupations, had spent their valuable time to assist us taking so such pains. The valuable views expressed by the aforesaid learned Senior Members of the Bar and renowned jurists of our country, in fact, helped the Court to arrive at a decision in this matter inasmuch as the result of this case has great public importance having far-reaching effect upon the nation. The sincere, valuable and honest views expressed by them before us are really praiseworthy and commendable. We, therefore, record their valuable assistance in this judgment with deep appreciation.

96. One learned Advocate Mr. Bazlur Rahman sought permission to speak a few words before the Court. He stated that Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 is a correct and valid legislation. No law can be made protecting and immuning the killers of man which is an offence against humanity. Our Constitution does not also approve of making such a law in order to give protection to a person who commits offence against humanity.

97. We have heard the lengthy submissions of both the parties and considered the views expressed by the learned Amicus Curiae. We have also put our thoughts on the legal and Constitutional provisions as referred to by them. In our opinion, the submissions of Mr. Attorney-General and the views of the five learned Amicus Curiae out of six on the points of validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 and the repugnancy of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 appear to be legally and constitutionally correct and, as such, the same are accepted by us.

98. The upshots of our lengthy discussions and the findings made above may be summarised as follows:

(1) It is held that both the Writ Petitions are maintainable in their present form.

(2) It is held that Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, (Act No. 21 of 1996) is a valid piece of legislation and it is not ultra vires of the Constitution.

(3) It is held that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance No. 50 of 1975) is void since it is repugnant to the Constitution.

(4) It is held that since the Indemnity.

Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 is ultra vires the Constitution and Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 does not offend and infringe any provision of the Constitution, the prayers for declaring the institution of Dhanmondi PS Case No.10(10)/1996 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11)/1975 without lawful authority and illegal are hereby refused.

(5) It is found that five out of six learned Jurists of the country (excepting Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed) who assisted the Court as Amicus Curiae, expressed their views that the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 is a valid piece of legislation and the Indemnity Ordinance, No. 50 of 1975 is void being ultra vires the Constitution. Submissions of the learned Attorney-General and the views of the majority Amicus Curiae on the points of validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 and the repugnancy of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 appear to be constitutionally and legally correct and, as such, the same are accepted.

99. In the result, both the Rules issued in these two Writ Petitions are hereby discharged with the above findings without any order as to costs.

Mr. Korban Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, prays for a certificate under Article 102 of the Constitution for preferring appeal before the Appellate Division against this Judgment. Since several substantial questions of law as to the interpretation of several provisions of the Constitution are involved in the instant cases, the certificate prayed for is granted.

End.
