<u>35. At this stage, we think it is time that we quote from the High Court Division judgment where this subject has been dealt with. This part, in our opinion, is the most relevant and soundest in an otherwise prolix judgment. The views expressed by us above are confirmations of what is now quoted below:</u>

<u>According to Mr. Korban Ali and M Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, this Ordinance was made a part of the Constitution by paragraph 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. But it appears that neither the 4th Schedule nor any other provision of the Constitution provides that this Indemnity Ordinance, No. 50 of 1975 should, be treated as a part of the Constitution. Rather by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution it was protected and continued as existing law in the category of "Other Laws" which were promulgated in between the period from 15th August, 1975 and 9th April, 1979. Since it was an ordinary piece of legislation being saved, protected and continued under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, it can be amended or repealed by simple majority members of the Parliament. In paragraph 3a (7) of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution a clear provision has been laid down to the effect that all laws made during the period from 15-8-75 to 9-4-79 were protected, but the same can be amended, altered and repealed by the authority. It means, the Parliament is the actual authority for repealing of law. Nowhere in the 4th schedule or in any other provision of the Constitution it was stipulated that the laws which were continued and saved under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution would require two-third majority members of the Parliament for necessary amendment or alteration or repeal. Since there was no provision like that, we cannot import such a provision and, as such, we hold that the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 can be amended or altered or repealed by simple majority members of the Parliament and two-third majority of the members of the Parliament was not at all required for the same. The learned Attorney-General as well as other five learned Amid Curiae expressed their views that this Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 has been legally passed by a simple majority members of the Parliament and to pass such all law, two-third majority of the members of the Parliament was not at all necessary.</u>

<u>36. The next important submission of Mr. Korban Ali is that even if it is conceded for argument's sake that the Indemnity Ordinance was validly repealed, the starting of the criminal cases against the appellants for the occurrences of the 15th August, 1975 was unlawful because notwithstanding the repeal of the Ordinance, the rights and privileges which had accrued to them under the said Ordinance would remain unaffected. Evidently, this argument is based upon section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. It is true that a repealing Act does not affect any right, privilege which is acquired under the repealed enactment but there is an overriding condition and that is as provided in section 6 itself, that "unless a different intention appears". The different intention in the present case has been made abundantly clear in section 2 of the Act. Therefore, although it was a question of fact whether the appellants could at all claim protection of the Ordinance for the alleged acts attributed to them, the legislature has completely sealed that chapter by expressly nullifying everything under the repealed Ordinance.</u>

37. The other submissions made by Mr. Korban Ali, he has himself realised, have neither much force nor carry any conviction. For example, he has submitted that the Act is an ex post facto legislation which offends Article 35(1) of the Constitution. The question does not arise because the Act has not made anything punishable which was not so punishable when the alleged acts were committed. Then he has argued that the Act was passed mala fide because the party in power now never raised question in previous Parliaments for repealing the Indemnity Ordinance but with the recent change of Government immediate step was taken maliciously to nullify the protection so Lang enjoyed by the appellants under the Ordinances.

<u>38. It is not permissible for the Court to impute malice to the legislature in making laws which is its plenary power. As long as the laws passed by it do not offend any provision of the Constitution, the Court cannot strike them down on any other ground. On the subject of Inquiry into legislative motives, Cooley in his A Treatise on the Constitutional Limitations at page 186 says:</u>

From what examination has been given to this subject, it appears that whether a statute is constitutional or not is always a question of power, that is, whether the legislature in the particular case, in respect to the subject-matter of the act, the manner in which its object is to be accomplished, and the mode of enacting it, has kept within the constitutional limits and observed the constitutional conditions. If so, the courts are not at liberty to inquire into the proper exercise of the power in any case. They must assume that legislative discretion has been properly exercised. If evidence was required, it must be supposed that it was before the legislature when the Act was passed, and if any special finding was required to warrant the passage of the particular Act, it would seem that the passage of the Act itself might be held equivalent to such finding. And although it has sometimes been urged at the bar, that the courts ought to inquire into the motives of the legislature where fraud and corruption were alleged, and annul their action if the allegation were established, the argument has in no case been acceded to by the judiciary, and they have never allowed the inquiry to be entered upon.

39. Mr. Korban Ali raised the question of malafide also because the criminal cases were started even before the repeal of the Indemnity Ordinance. It has been noticed that in such matters what is of importance is the authority to act and not with -What motive the action is taken. It could not be said that the alleged bar under the Indemnity Ordinance was attracted automatically as soon as the FIR was lodged. It has/had to be pleaded at some stage. Since the Ordinance has already been repealed, the bar does no longer operate and no question of malafide can be raised in opposition to the proceedings.

40. In view of the discussion above, these appeals cannot succeed and are accordingly dismissed without any order as to costs.

Mustafa Kamal J: Little or nothing is left to be said after perusal of the judgments delivered by my Lord, the learned Chief Justice and by my learned brother Latifur Rahman J, with both of whom I fully concur, but even then there remains a few observations which I venture to express in view of the constitutional importance of these appeals.

42. The lopsided pre-occupation of the learned Judges of the High Court Division with the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 being void ab initio, leaves me with a finding that the following matters remain completely unanswered by them and also by the learned Attorney-General while defending the impugned judgment before us.

<u>43. First, it was open to any citizen to ask for a declaration from the High Court Division in the writ jurisdiction that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was void ab initio No person has ever done it at any point of time during the 21 years that the said Ordinance was in operation. The said Ordinance was repealed on the 14th November, 1996 by the Parliament passing by a simple majority the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996. The writ petitioner-appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the Repeal Act of 1996 in their respective writ petitions. The Government-respondents put up as defence that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was void ab initio. They did not and indeed could not have sought for a declaration as respondents in the two writ petitions that the said Ordinance was void ab initio. Yet the High Court Division gave in favour of the respondents an unsolicited and uncalled for declaration that the said Ordinance was void ab initio. It is as if a plaintiff in a suit had asked for a declaration of title to the suit land, but obtained instead a declaration that he is the illegitimate son of his father. The High Court Division may or may not have accepted the soundness of the respondents' defence but it could not have given a declaration to that effect in the writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the validity of another Act. It is not permissible in a writ petition to give a declaration in favour of the respondents because it is the writ petitioners who are seekers of a declaration, not the respondents. No one had the boldness to challenge the said Ordinance frontally in a writ petition for such a declaration. If the High Court Division can take such an unusual step it will set up a dangerous precedent.</u>

44. Secondly, Parliament has already acted earlier on November 14, 1996 repealing the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. The High Court Division could not have declared the same Ordinance as void ab initio at a later date on 28-1-97. This is like killing a mocking bird twice. To declare a statute as void when it is already repealed is to kill a dead horsetwice. Also it means in effect that the exercise of the Parliament was an exercise in futility and that the Repeal Act, 1996 was absolutely unnecessary. Can the High Court Division ascribe futility to the legislative activities of the Parliament and give a parallel and competing decision of its own when the issues involved could be decided on other points conclusively? For it is a cardinal principle of interpretation of statutes that no statute or part of it will be declared unconstitutional or void if the issues involved in a case can be decided otherwise.

45. Thirdly, the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 has suffered two different fates in the hands of two organs of the State—Parliament has repealed it and the High Court Division has declared it void ab initio. A statute cannot be repealed and void declared a b initio at the same time, because the effect of repeal and the effect of such a declaration are different. The learned Chief Justice has quoted Crazies on Statute Law (Seventh Edition) at p.351 as to the effect of a repeal. When an Act of Parliament is repealed it must be considered (except as to transactions past and closed) as if it had never existed. But repeal is always relatable to an existing law and a valid law. In Black's Law Dictionary (Fifth Edition) at p.1167 "Repeal" is defined as follows:

<u>"The abrogation or annulling of a previously existing law by the enactment of a subsequent statute which declares that the former law shall be revoked and abrogated (which is called "express" repeal), or which contains provisions so contrary to or irreconcilable with those of the earlier law that only one of the two statutes can stand in force (called "implied" repeal) to revoke, to rescind or abrogate by authority."</u>

46. Therefore only an existing law can be repealed but if a Court declares a statute void ab initio then the effect is that the statute did not exist at all in the statute-book. It was never an existing law at any point of time. There can be no transaction under a void statute. The question of past and closed transactions does not arise in the case of void statutes. When a statute is repealed by Parliament section 6 of the General Clauses Act comes in aid in preserving and continuing vested rights, privileges, obligations or liabilities acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment, unless a different intention appears in the repealing statute. In the Repeal Act, 1996 this different intention has been expressed in section 2 of the Act by doing away with past actions, measures taken, certificates or orders or instructions given, etc. under the repealed Ordinance. If section 2 was not there, which it was the option of the Parliament not to incorporate, all the actions, certificates granted, advantages gained, if any, under the repealed Ordinance would have had a continuing force. Further, a statute is repealed prospectively or retrospectively according as the tenor of the repealing statute is. In the present case the Repeal Act, 1996 repealed the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 prospectively (এতদ্বারা রহিত করা হইল). It means it was an existing law till the 13th November, 1996. When a statute is repealed by the Parliament its disappearance from the statute-book takes place from the date of repeal, either prospectively or retrospectively according as the legislature prescribes. But if a statute is declared void ab initio by the Court its disappearance from the statute-book takes place retrospectively from the date of enactment of the repealed statute, never prospectively. If a statute is declared void ab initio by a Court no rights accrue at all. No obligation or liability generates from the void law. But a repealed statute retains accrued rights and obligations, unless avoided specifically or by necessary implication. The High Court Division did not keep in mind this vital distinction between a repeal of a statute and declaration of a statute as void ab initio and therefore put itself into the pitfall of committing a constitutional fallacy, expressing unnecessarily, a separate intention of its own than that of the Parliament which had already repealed the statute.

47. Fourthly, a void statute may be avoided in two ways, as rightly argued by one of the Amicus Curiae before the High Court Division, namely, by approaching the Court for a declaration that the statute is void ab initio or by the Parliament itself passing a declaratory statute. As already noticed no one has ever approached the Court for a declaration of that kind. The Parliament did not pass a declaratory statute either. The High Court Division wrongly held "a void law though not declared void so long by any Court was legally repealed by the Parliament". Again the High Court Division made a confusion between repeal and enactment of a declaratory statue.

48. Cooley in his A Treatise on the Constitutional Limitations (Eighth Edition), Volume 1 at p.188 quotes inter alia Austin on Jurisprudence and says, "A declaratory statute is one which is passed in order to put an end to a doubt as to what is the common law, or the meaning of another statute, and which declares what it is and ever has been." He also quotes some US decisions at page 191 and says, "To declare what the law is, or has been is a judicial power, to declare what the law shall be, is legislative. One of the fundamental principles of all our Governments is that the legislative power shall be separate from the judicial". Again, "If the legislature would prescribe a different rule for the future from that which the courts enforce, it must be done by statute, and cannot be done by a mandate to the courts, which leaves the law unchanged, but seeks to compel the courts to construe and apply it, not according to the judicial, but according to the legislative judgment. But in any case the substance of the legislative action should be regarded rather than the form, and if it appears to be the intention to establish by declaratory statute a rule of conduct for the future, the courts should accept and act upon it, without too nicely inquiring whether the mode by which the new rule is established is or is not the best, most decorous, and suitable that could have been adopted."

49. In the present case no Court of law has earlier pronounced that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 is void ab initio. The Parliament was therefore free to pass a declaratory statute declaring that the said Ordinance was void from the very beginning, but it did not do so. It preferred to treat the said Ordinance as an existing law and repealed it. The High Court Division made a basic mistake in holding that the Parliament has legally repealed a void law, little giving thought that a void law has to be declared void by a declaratory statute and a repeal can only be made of an existing law.

50. Fifthly, in case of repeal the Repeal Act is itself liable to be repealed by the same Parliament or subsequent Parliament, reviving the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, but when a Court declares the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 void ab initio the Parliament cannot re-enact the same legislation afresh. It will be struck down as unconstitutional. It is buried forever. This distinction was lost sight of by the High Court Division.

51. Next comes the question as to the competence of the Parliament to repeal the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 by a simple majority and not by amending the Constitution as urged by the appellants. The High Court Division has ultimately given a correct answer to this question but has unfortunately not been precise in the formulation of its reasons.

52. It is well-known that Martial Law is not a part of the constitutional scheme of our country. It is an extra-constitutional dispensation. When the Martial Law authorities abrogate an existing Constitution, as did Ayub Khan in Pakistan in 1958, and frame a new Constitution, as he did in 1962, it still became necessary for them to make provision for a law relating to indemnity by inserting Article 223A to the Constitution of 1962 by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1963; but Article 223A left it to the then Central Legislature to make any law relating to indemnity in future. No indemnity clause was incorporated in the Constitution of 1962, because the old Constitution of 1956 was buried, thereby getting rid of the liability of violating it. But when Martial Law is imposed keeping the existing Constitution either in suspension or in operation (subject to the Proclamation and Martial Law Regulations), the Martial Law authorities are continuously at work to ensure that the imposition of Martial Law and all actions taken under it are incorporated, ratified and confirmed in the Constitution itself when Martial Law is withdrawn and the Constitution is revived in order to constitutionalize and legalese the extra-constitutional steps taken by them. If the existing Constitution is revived without this protection the Martial Law authorities will face trial for their extra-constitutional interference with the working of the Constitution. In the two Martial Laws that we had in Bangladesh there was a hierarchy of legislations taken recourse to, namely, Proclamations. Proclamation Orders Martial Law Regulations Martial Law Orders, Martial Law Instructions etc. These legislations are part and parcel of Martial Law activities proper which are undertaken when Martial Law is in force. But there is a second kind of legislation which any Government for the time being in power, be it a democratic Government elected by the votes of the people or a Martial Law Government or even a Caretaker Government under the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996, has to make which has nothing to do with the running of Martial Law or holding of General Elections. Ordinances dealing with various matters of on-going administration have to be promulgated. Rules Regulations, Bye-laws, Orders Notifications and other instruments having the force of law have to be framed and published under different existing statutes to keep the wheels of Government and statutory bodies running. During Martial Law period the Martial Law authorities lack the constitutional authority even to promulgate Ordinances and make Rules, Regulations, etc. because the source of their power is not the Constitution but an extra-constitutional interference with the Constitution. That is why they have to ensure ratification and confirmation in the Constitution itself all those Ordinances, Rules, Regulations, etc. promulgated and framed by them during the Martial Law period. But one common feature in both the two Martial Laws in Bangladesh is that while Proclamations, Martial Regulations, etc. which are Martial Law activities proper, were allowed to die a natural death upon the withdrawal of both the Martial Laws, the "other laws", namely. Ordinances, Rules, Regulations, etc. were allowed "to continue in force until altered amended or repealed by the competent authority". Zia-ul-Haque of Pakistan went a degree further. He made the Martial Law Regulations an integral part of the heavily amended Constitution. By substituting Article 270A of the Constitution of Pakistan by the Constitution (Eighth Amendment) Act, 1985 all the President's Orders. Ordinances, Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law Orders, enactments, Notifications, Rules, Orders or Bye-laws in force were "to continue in force until altered, repealed or amended by the competent authority" "Competent authority" was defined by an Explanation. The appropriate legislature was named the competent authority "in respect of President's Orders, Ordinances, Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law Orders and enactments. In respect of Notifications, Rules, Orders and Bye-laws, the authority in which the power to make, alter, repeal or amend the same vests under the law was made the "competent authority" A Seventh Schedule was added to the Constitution and some President's Orders and Ordinances were specified therein the amendment of which can only be made in the manner provided for amendment of the Constitution and all other laws may be amended by the appropriate legislature in the manner provided for amendment of such laws.

53. In paragraph 3A(7) of the Fourth Schedule to our Constitution the words "competent authority" have not been defined or explained, as in the case of Zia-ul-Haque's Constitution of Pakistan described above. But inspite of lack of such definition or explanation it is not difficult to see who can alter, amend or repeal an Ordinance and who can do so in respect of Rules, Regulations, etc. Under our Constitution an Ordinance cannot be amended by a statutory body. It can only be amended by the Parliament. Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws, etc. can only be altered, amended or repealed by the authority in which the power to make, alter, amend or repeal vests under the relevant laws. If these Ordinances, Rules, Regulations, etc. were meant to be unalterable laws of the country then paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution ought to have been specific like the substituted Article 270A of the Constitution of Pakistan. It should have been provided that to amend "any other laws" the procedure followed for amendment of the Constitution needs to be followed. In the absence of any such provision these ordinary laws made by the Martial law authorities will be altered, amended or repealed by following the ordinary process of alteration, amendment or repeal as is followed by the competent authority in their respective fields. Parliament has competently passed the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 by a simple majority.

54. Now coming to the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 the word "indemnity" has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary (Fifth Edition) at p.262 as follows:

"A legislative act, assuring a general dispensation from punishment or exemption from prosecution to persons involved in offences, omissions of official duty, or acts in excess of authority, is called an indemnity strictly it is an act of indemnity"

55. The learned Chief Justice has fully quoted the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. This Ordinance has not assured anybody a general dispensation from punishment but has only granted exemption from prosecution to persons involved in possible offences. This legislation was made not by way of Proclamation, Martial Law Regulation, Martial Law Order, etc. It was done in the shape of an Ordinance, i.e., in the shape of an ordinary law, Mr. Korban Ali, learned Counsel for the appellants, was keenly aware of the constitutional and legal status of this legislation and therefore it was the main burden of his submission that although an Ordinance in form, it was in substances a rehearse of the Proclamation of the 20th August, 1975 so as to be a part of the Proclamation itself. It therefore needs a two-third majority in the Parliament for its repeal, he urged. The learned Chief Justice has dealt elaborately with the factual and contextual difference between the Proclamations and the Ordinance and I need not dwell upon it further. It stares us in the face that an Ordinance, of whatever importance it may be to the appellants, remains an Ordinance, i.e. an ordinary law and an ordinary law can never beirrepealably. It is a cardinal principle of constitutional law that legislature cannot pass an irrepealably law. As Cooley says in his book "A Treatise on the Constitutional Limitations" (Eighth Edition), Volume 1 p.247, "To say that the legislature may pass irrepealably laws, is to say that it may alter the very constitution from which it derives its authority, since, in so far as one legislature could bind a subsequent one by its enactments, it could in the same degree reduce the legislative power of its successors, and the process might be repeated, until, one by one, the subjects of legislation would be excluded altogether from their control, and the constitutional provision that the legislative power shall be vested in two houses (in our Constitution, in the House of the Nation) would be to a greater or less degree rendered ineffectual. "That is why I have stated earlier that the Repeal Act, 1996 can also be repealed by the same or a subsequent Parliament. This is an inherent power of the legislature.

56. With the aforesaid observations, I again concur with the judgment delivered by my Lord, the learned Chief Justice.

Latifur Rahman J: I have had the advantage of perusing the judgment of My Lord, the Chief Justice. Though I am in respectful agreement with him having regard to the importance of the Constitutional issues, involved in this case, I would like to add few words.

57. In the main judgment, the learned Chief Justice has already narrated the facts of the writ petitions and has quoted the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 and Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution. Hence I do not feel it necessary to repeat the same in this supporting judgment.

58. These two Certificated Appeals, being Civil Appeal Nos.18 and 19 of 1997 arise out of Writ Petition Nos.5021 and 5313 of 1996 filed by Shahariar Rashid Khan and Mahmuda Rahman, mother of Colonel (Retd) Sayeed Faruque Rahman on his behalf. Both the Rules issued in those writ petitions were discharged by a common judgment of the High Court Division.

59. In the writ petitions the appellants prayed for two reliefs, namely;

(1) Why Indemnity (Repeal Act, 1996 should not be declared as void, illegal, ultra vires of the Constitution and of no legal effect.

(2) Declare the Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)96 dated 2-10-96 and Lalbagh PS Case No.11(11)75 dated 4-11-75 as unlawful and void.

60. A little back ground would be necessary as to why and how the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 came into being.

61. In the morning of the 15th August, 1975 the President Shakih Mujibur Rahman, all his family members who were in his Dhanmondi house and some other persons were killed by a group of army personnel who also declared Martial Law through Radio Bangladesh. Subsequent thereto, Khandaker Mostaq Ahmed, a Senior Cabinet Member of Shaikh Mujibur Rahman proclaimed Martial Law all over the country by his proclamation dated the 20th August, 1975. In this Proclamation order he assumed and entered upon the Office of the President of Bangladesh with effect from the 15th August, 1975. In this proclamation, he declared that the constitution shall remain in force subject to this proclamation and the Martial Law Regulations and orders and other orders made by him in pursuance thereof. Thereafter the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 was promulgated on the 26th September, 1975 by Khandaker Mostaque Ahmed in pursuance of the proclamation of the 20th August, 1975 and in exercise of the powers conferred by Clause (1) of Article (1) of Article 93 of the Constitution. The Indemnity Ordinance was promulgated putting restrictions on taking of any legal or other proceedings against persons in respect of certain acts, things committed by those persons in connection with, or in preparation or execution of any plan for, or as necessary steps towards, the change of the Government of Bangladesh and the proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of the 15th August, 1975.

62. This Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, briefly, the Ordinance was repealed by the Indemnity (Repeal) Act (Act 2 of 1996), briefly the Repealing Act. The material question for consideration before the High Court Division as well as before us was whether the Repealing Act was validly made by the Parliament in its plenary legislative power. It has been found that through proclamation of the 20th August 1975 Khandaker Mostaque Ahmed assumed and entered upon the Office of the President of Bangladesh by declaring Martial Law throughout the country. The Indemnity Ordinance was promulgated by him under purported exercise of legislative power under Article 93 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as if, it is an ordinary law made by the President as the Parliament was not in session.

63. After withdrawal of First Martial Law and coming into force of the Constitution the Fourth Schedule was amended. Paragraph 3A was added to the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution by the proclamation Order No. 1 of 1977 and amended by the Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978. Thereafter paragraph 18 was added to the Fourth Schedule by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act, 1979 (Act I of 1979) By this Constitutional amendment paragraph 18 was inserted in the Fourth Schedule giving validity to the acts and things including constitutional amendments done during the Martial Law period and ousted the jurisdiction of the courts in respect of these acts and things of Martial Law period.

<u>64. In the judgment of the High Court Division, the main thrust was with regard to the constitutionality of the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. It appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that the learned Advocates of the appellants and the respondent as well as the Amicus Curiae appearing in this case mainly argued with regard to the constitutionality of the Ordinance itself. After consideration of the submissions of the learned Advocates the learned Judges held that the Ordinance is ultra vires of the Constitution and consequently declared the same as void as if, it had no legal existence in the eye of Constitution on the very day when it was promulgated and thereafter. Consequently, the learned Judges in the ordering portion in Item No. 3 held as follows:</u>

<u>"It is held that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance No. 50 of 1975) is void since it is repugnant to the Constitution."</u>

<u>It may be stated that in both the writ petitions no challenge was made in respect of the Ordinance itself rather it was the case of the writ petitioners that the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 is void, illegal, ultra vires of the Constitution and is of no legal effect. The Repealing Act was under challenge and not the original Ordinance. In that view of the matter, on the averments in the writ petitions the declaration with regard to the Ordinance itself was un-called for within the frame of the writ petitions when the Ordinance itself was not the subject matter of challenge before the High Court Division. The Repealing Act being under challenge the learned Judges of the High Court Division was under an obligation to decide the validity of the Repealing Act itself, but unfortunately the learned Judges travelled beyond their lawful limits and unnecessarily decided that issue which was not necessary to decide in this case at all. The whole exercise should have been in a narrow compass as to the constitutionality of the repealing Act.</u>

65. Mr. Korban Ali learned Advocate appearing for the appellants in both these appeals mainly urged one ground and he very candidly submitted that if this ground does not find favour with the court then all his other ancillary grounds are of no material consequences. His main argument is, that Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 is protected and saved by Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution and, as such, the Ordinance has become a part of the Constitution, and, as such, the Indemnity Ordinance cannot be repealed without amending Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution by 2/3rd majority of the Members of Parliament as provided under Article 142 of the Constitution. He thereby argues that paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule have given such a status to the Ordinance that it has acquired the status of a constitutional law and has became a part of the Constitution which cannot be repealed like an ordinary law by Parliament without following the procedure of constitutional amendment. His objection is more of procedure than of power of the Parliament to repeal. His other two ancillary grounds are.

(1) After the recent change of the Government, repeal of the Ordinance itself by the Repealing Act and starting of two criminal cases against the accused-appellants is a clear indication that the Repealing Act is passed with a malafide intention of the Government to harass and victimize the appellants by repealing the Ordinance in hot haste.

(2) The Repealing Act (Act 21 of 1996) is nothing but a colourable legislation inasmuch as paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule was amended indirectly by this repealing Act which cannot be done directly under the ordinary Legislative power of Parliament.

66. I will deal with the main argument of Mr. Korban Ali as the whole issue in reality revolves around the main argument.

67. Article 142 of our Constitution provides for both the power and procedure to amend any provision of the Constitution. Article 142 provides for a special procedure wherein it requires that any constitutional amendment must be passed by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of members of Parliament. By paragraphs 3A and 18 in the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution validity, ratification and confirmation of some Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations, Orders and other "laws" were given and incorporated in the Constitution. We are to find out whether by adding Paragraphs 3A and 18 in the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution the Indemnity Ordinance has acquired a qualitative status of a Constitutional law and has become a part of the Constitution.

68. The whole exercise depends upon a critical examination of the Sub-paragraphs of paragraphs 3A and 18 which have given validity to 'The laws in force' during that period including the Ordinance itself. In paragraph 3A(1) of the Fourth Scehdule, the Proclamations, Martial Law Regulations, etc. and "all other laws" made during the subsistence of Martial Law shall be deemed to have been validily made and shall not be called in question in or before any court or tribunal on any ground whatsoever.

69. I will try to give a reasonable interpretation of Paragraphs 3A and 18 as it would carry out the intentions of the law makers and also which is in accord with the constitutional practice in adopting such transitional and temporary provision in the Constitution under Article 150 of the Constitution, which is preferable to Pre-constitutional Laws and Martial Law Regulations and Orders, etc. and laws made during the period of Martial Law in Bangladesh.

70. The concept of Martial Law is foreign to our Constitution. Our Constitution does not at all contemplate imposition of Martial Law. Yet it is true that Martial Law visited Bangladesh several times wherein many Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations, and laws were made. During that period many acts and things were done in pursuance of those Martial Law Regulations, etc. and laws. Hence it was necessary to give a constitutional validity, ratification and confirmation to ensure constitutional continuity of those acts and things done. By imposition of Martial Law existing legal order was changed and a new legal order was promulgated outside the Constitutional mandate and, as such, constitutional coverage was given by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule only. As a matter of fact, Constitution (Fifth Amendment) has given a post facto validation of all acts and things of that period. These paragraphs are like Indemnity Act which is passed after every declaration of Martial Law, ratifying and validating all acts and things done during that period.

71. I will quote Sub-paragraph (7) of Paragrph 3A which reads as follows:

"All laws in force immediately before the revocation of the said Proclamations and withdrawal of Martial Law shall, subject to the Proclamation revoking the said Proclamations and withdrawing the Martial Law, continue in force until altered, amended or repealed by the competent authority."

"Subject to the proclamation revoking the said proclamations and withdrawing the Martial Law", this expression means that if there is any conflict between "all laws in force" during the period of Martial Law with the proclamation, revoking and withdrawing of the Martial Law, then latter will prevail As a matter of fact there is no conflict between 'laws' and the Martial Law proclamations. These laws were saved and continued until altered or repealed by the competent authority. Sub-Para(8) of paragraph 3A speaks of application of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to the said proclamations, Martial Law Regulations and Martial Law Orders made during that period. But General Clauses Act was not made applicable to 'law' which clearly indicated that the effect of law will continue until altered, amended or repealed by the competent authority. Sub-paragraph (10) of Paragraph 3A defines law which includes Ordinance, rules, regulations, bye-laws, orders, notifications and other instruments having the force of law. This Sub-paragraph includes subordinate laws not constitutional law. The object of Paragraphs 3A and 18 is to maintain the constitutional continuity of those laws after the revival of the Constitution till they are repealed, altered or amended by the competent authority. If paragraphs 3A and 18 were not incorporated in the Constitution then there would be utter confusion in the field of Constitutional dispensation and law. There would be discontinuity of constitutional dispensation and the period in issue would be outside the Constitution. How the Martial Law Regulations, etc. laws and all actions, deeds and imposition of punishment by Martial Law Courts during that period could be condoned without giving a constitutional coverage to maintain continuity of laws and actions? I also find that there is no conflict with the proclamation revoking and withdrawing Martial Law with the Ordinance, Martial Law having ceased, the operation of ordinary civil law continued.

<u>72. Thus under the constitutional dispensation addition of paragraphs 3A and 18 were indispensable to maintain the constitutional continuity. One cannot seek in Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule more than what was in reality saved and validated. The real under-line meaning of this inclusion in Fourth Schedule is that according to the Constitution the Martial Law Regulations, etc. and law was valid and legal by application of legal fiction theory. Thus, by this validation and ratification clauses in the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution the Ordinance was not made part of` the Constitution other than giving a constitutional validity and immunity, Sub-paragraph (5) of Paragraph 3A also contemplates the intention of continuous operation of the Constitution after withdrawal of Martial Law with amendments and modifications.</u>

<u>73. This Act of indemnity was promulgated not only to justify unlawful acts ex post facto, but to stop any legal or other proceedings against persons involved in the charge of Government of Bangladesh and the proclamation of Martial Law on the morning of 15th August, 1975. AV Dicey in his book 'The Law of the Constitution, 10th Edition page 233 defines an act of indemnity as, "though it is the legislation of illegality, it itself a law". Thus it appears that by this Indemnity Ordinance coverage was given to certain illegal acts committed on the morning of 15th August, 1975. It is to be presumed that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was a valid Ordinance which was recognized in the Constitution. I must say that there is a fundamental distinction between a "constitutional law" and an "ordinary law". Constitutional provision conceptually has a distinct and qualitative feature separate from ordinary law which is in reality, the Ordinance itself.</u>

74. The legislature in its wisdom thought that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 which is just an ordinary law should be repealed and consequently the same was repealed by the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 on the 14th November, 1996. The Ordinance is like many Ordinances which were passed during the period of Martial Law and it is subject to the plenary power of Parliament of amending, altering or repealing such laws. For such amendment the procedure of Article 142 of the Constitution is not necessary. Simple majority is enough to repeal the Ordinance as it is an ordinary existing law.

<u>75. The argument of malafides advanced by Mr. Korban Ali is without any foundation. These two writ petitions are conspicuously absent with any averments of malafides. There being no pleading as such as to mala-fide, the argument of the learned Advocate is without any basis. Malafides are to be established by assertion of facts. Besides that, the ordinance making power being a legislation power the argument of mala fide is misconceived. In the case of K Nagraj vs. State of AP AIR 1985 Supreme Court 551, it has been held as such.</u>

<u>"The legislature as a body cannot be accused of having passed a law for an extraneous purpose. Its reasons for passing a law are those that are stated in the Objects and Reasons and if, none are so stated, as appear from the provisions enacted by it. Even assuming that the executive, in a given case has an ulterior motive in moving legislation, that motive cannot render the passing of the law malafide. This kind of 'transferred malice' is unknown in the field of legislation."</u>

<u>In the case of GG Kanungo vs. State of Orissa, AIR 1995 SC 1655 it has been held that the malafides or ulterior motives attributed to the legislature in making a law within its competence can never make such law unconstitutional.</u>

76. The doctrine of colourable legislation means that legislature cannot make a law indirectly which it cannot make directly. Since I hold that the Parliament has plenary power to repeal the Ordinance the question of colourable exercise of legislative power does not at all arise in this case. The Parliament had rightly repealed the Ordinance as an ordinary law. After what I have said above the question of either amending paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule does not also arise.

Mohammad Abdur Rouf J: I have had the privilege of going through the main judgment written by my Lord the Chief Justice as well as the supplements thereto written by my learned brothers Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman JJ.

78. The points raised for consideration before us having been dealt with very lucidly in the main judgment I do not propose to add anything more but to concur fully with the views expressed by my Lord the Chief Justice and Mustafa Kamal, J in dismissing both the appeals.

BB Roy Choudhury J : I have had the advantage of going through the judgments which my Lord the Chief justice and my learned brethren Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman JJ have prepared in draft.

The constitutional issues posed before us were two: (1) whether the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was made a part of the Constitution by virtue of paragraph 18 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, and (2) whether the repeal of the Ordinance by the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 passed by less than two thirds majority was violative of Article 142 of the Constitution.

My Lord the Chief Justice has exhaustively dealt with the material questions involved in these appeals. I concur with his judgment without consideration of the validity of paragraph 18 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution which was not agitated before us.

End.
