full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: As common questions of law and facts are involved in all the writ petitions these are taken up together for hearing analogously and are disposed of by this judgment which shall govern all. 

2. The case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3233 of 2000, in brief, is that the Village Murarikati within Kalaroa Police Station District Satkhira is a very remote rural area and 85% lands are agricultural and 95% people earn their livelihood from agriculture. The authority without following the relevant rule has included the same within Kalaroa Pourashava. The local Member of Parliament has submitted representation to the Government for exclusion of Murarikati Mouza from Kalaroa Pourashava. The local Thana Settlement Officer on 27-8-98 issued a report showing that in the said Murarikati Mouza total land is 1403.53 acres out of which 1366.10 acres are agricultural. After inquiry the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Kalaroa submitted a report for exclusion of Murarikati Mouza from the Kalaroa Pourashava. Under section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 it has been provided than the Government shall not declare a rural area as urban area unless it is satisfied that three-fourth of the adult male population of the area to which it relates are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture and such area contains not less than 15,000 population and an average number of not less than 2000 inhabitants per square mile. 

3. One Kazi Ashraf Ali filed Writ Petition No. 3051 of 1991 and obtained a Rule but on 20-3-1997 the Rule was discharged as not maintainable. The respondent No. 1 also moved for exclusion of Murarikati Mouza from Kalaroa Pourashava and to exclude the said Mouza from the urban area and the respondent No. 1 stopped the functioning of Kalaroa Pourashava with regard to this area but the petitioner learnt that the inclusion of the mouza in Pourashava has been completed without information to these petitioners. The petitioner then sent a demand of justice notice to the respondents to exclude the said area from Kalaroa Paurashava. The petitioner having no other alternative remedy filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule. 

4. The respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition but the learned Additional Attorney-General made his submissions. 

5. The petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3073 of 2000 filed the same on the self same facts and allegations for exclusion of Murarikati Mouza from Kalaroa Pourashava, District Satkhira. The added respondent No. 5 filed affidavit-in-opposition but at the time of hearing of the Rule none appeared to oppose the Rule. 

6. In Writ Petition No. 313 of 2002 the facts, in short, are that the respondent No. 2 by notification being SRO No. 173/Law /1999 dated 28-6-1999 purportedly under Rule 4(2) of the Declaration and Alteration of the Municipalities Rules, 1978 declared a new Paurashava namely, Zanjira Pourashava and included Zanjira and Mulna Union Parishads of Zanjira Upazila in the said Paurashava. According to Bangladesh Population Census, 1991, in Zanjira Thana 83.74% people depend on agriculture as the source of income. The mouzas included in the proposed pourashava do not have any feature by which they could be termed as Urban Area save the small area within Thana Sadar of Zanjira Police Station. In the impugned notification dated 28-6-1999 it has been indicated that a public notice was issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Shariatpur calling for proposal or objections with regard to declaration of proposed Pourashava and that the report has been submitted by the Deputy Commissioner, Shariatpur. The Chairman of Zanjira Union Parishad and the petitioners are not aware of such public notice. The local inhabitants filed a representation to the respondent No. 3, Deputy Commissioner, Shariatpur, by way of objection on 28-7-1999 against declaration of urban area from Rural Area but till date the aforesaid respondents neither informed the objectors nor made any steps in the matter. The petitioner very recently came to learn that the respondents have declared a schedule for holding of election in the said newly created Zanjira Pourashava without disposing of the objections filed by the local inhabitants and in violation of the provisions of section 3(2) of the Ordinance. The inhabitants of the area proposed to be included in the Pourashava depend mainly on agricultural activities and the impugned order has been issued without any lawful authority inasmuch as the respondents do not have any authority to declare a Paurashava in respect of an area in which the overwhelming majority of population are engaged in the activities relating to agriculture. 

7. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

8. Respondents did not yet file any affidavit-in-opposition. 

9. The case of the petitioner in Writ Petition 6680 of 2001, in brief, is that the respondent No. 3 by SRO No. 677 / Ain/2001 dated 22-3-2000 has declared the area of Bauphal Pourashava including the areas of Mouza Bauphal JL No. 87 plot Nos. 10-44, 47-230, 234-382, 730-909, 911-916, 918-952, 954-1027, 1029-1430, 1436, 1448, 1808-1950, 2006 and Mouza Bilbilash JL No. 89 Plot Nos. 1258-1285, 1288-1484, 1548-1550, 1562, 1564 within the area of No. 12 Bauphal Union Parishad, Bauphal, Patuakhali. The Government by SRO No. 177-Ain/2001 dated 2-7-2001 has declared the area of Bauphal Pourashava under section 4(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 with effect from 10-7-2001 which was communicated to respondent No. 4 vide Memo No. Poura-3/Ba-Bi/Gathan-13/99/811 dated 8-7-2001. The Government also appointed one Jiban Krishana Saha of village-Upazila Bauphal District Patuakhali as the Administrator of Bauphal Pourashava, Patuakhali. The respondent No. 4 vide Memo No. Sha-Ga-3- 17/2001-441 dated 3-9-2001 has divided the Bauphal Poura area and invited objection under rules 19, 21 and 21-A of the Pourashava Ordinance 1977. Subsequently, by notification dated 22-10-2001 the Government appointed Upazila Nirbahi Officer Bauphal as the Administrator of the Bauphal Pourashava. It is submitted that the total population in 9 wards of Bauphal Pourashava is 11,199 male and 5070 female which is not sufficient for formation of Pourashava and declaration of Bauphal Pourashava is contrary to the rules framed under the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. It is further submitted that under section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 the Government shall not declare any rural area to be an urban area unless it is satisfied that three-fourth of the adult male population of the area to which it relates are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture and such area contains not less than 15,000 population and an average of not less than 2,000 inhabitants per square mile. In the circumstances the formation and declaration of the Pourashava is illegal. 

10. The respondent No. 1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition and denied the material allegations made in the writ petition. It is stated that the Government has not declared Bauphal Pourashava by SRO 677-Ain dated 22-3-2000 but by SRO 67- Ain /2001 dated 22-3-2001 has declared Urban Area. Some portion of ward Nos. 4 and 5 and major part of ward No. 6 Bauphal Union have been included within Bauphal Pourashava. The formation of Bauphal Pourashava and appointment of Administrator are lawful and within jurisdiction. 

11. The case of the petitioner is Writ Petition No. 1667 of 2001, in brief, is that the Government intended to form a new Pourashava at Kaliakoir Police Station and selected Sreefaltali Union Parishad, Atabaha Union Parishad and Mouchak Union Parishad to be declared as Pourashava and accordingly published notification by SRO No. 84-Ain/2001 dated 9-4-2001 under section 3 of the Pourashava Ordinance 1977 (XXVI of 1977) declaring some plots of mouzas Kochakuri, Vannara, Panchlaxmi, Baraba, Kalampur, Kulua, Sina Baha, Majukhar, Shatipur, Harira, Utpalkar, Habibpur, Ulushara, Chandara, West Chandara, Ma tikata, Karab Swrichda within Mauchak Union, some plots of and mouzas Goalbathan, Pirer Teki, Latifpur, Tengla Bari, Jarerchala, Sreefattali, Kaliakoir, Shimultali within Sreefaltali Union and some plots of Mouzas Dainkina, Hartakitala, Uttar Baktupur within Union Atabaha. The Government accordingly, declared a new Pourashava including the above mentioned mouzas as Urban Area. The Government declared the above mentioned mouzas from rural to urban areas as stated above. It is stated that the Sreefaltali Union within Kaliakoir Police Station is entirely surrounded by water based low lands. The other mouzas are under developed and the people of that area depend for their livelihood upon agriculture. 

12. Being aggrieved by the SRO the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

The respondent No. 1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition and denied the material allegations made in the writ petition. It is stated that the area included in Pourashava is already developed and there are offices of several organizations and educational institutions in the area. It is also stated that as per provisions of Rule 3(1) of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules 1978 and section 3 of the Pourashava Ordinance, the Municipality has been formed lawfully and the people of the area welcomed the declaration of the Government. It is also stated that considering the importance of the area people oriented institutions, hat-bazar, mills and factories, density of population the pourashava was declared after observing all formalities of law. It is further stated that on 6-1-2001, Chairman of Mouchak Union Parishad arranged a public meeting and in that meeting the participants agreed on 5 conditions to form the pourashava and one of the conditions was to set up a pourashava at Safipur and the office of the said pourashava was opened at Safipur on 15-6-2001. 

13. The case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2388 of 2001, in brief, is that the Deputy Commissioner, Panchagarh (respondent No. 2) issued notification vide Memo No. LG-Sat-29/2000/276(7) dated 3-7-2002 inviting objections from the inhabitants of villages Ayabgonj, Muslempur, Hossainpur, Liakatpur, Hajipur, Jaigirsharam and Satkhamar, against declaring these villages as urban areas. In response to the above notification the people of Satkhamar gave an objection in writing to the Deputy Commissioner, Panchagarh with copies to the Prime Minister and Minister for Local Government, and others not to include Satkhamar in the proposed Boda Municipality stating, inter alia, that 75% of the total population of the Sathkamar village are agriculturists. It is further stated that the Chairman, Balarampur Union Parishad came to know that village Kurulia was also included in the Municipal area of Boda Municipality and the Chairman convened a meeting of the members of the Union Parishad on 4-9-2000 and passed a resolution not to include the villages Satkhamar and Kurulia in the newly created Boda Municipality on the ground that 80% of the village people are farmers. The local parliament member also wrote a DO letter to the Ministry of Local Government stating that 75% of the population of the said two villages viz, Satkhamar and Kurulia under Balarampur Union Parishad, are agriculturists and requested the Hon'ble Minister for Local Government not to include these two villages in the newly created Boda Municipal Area. The respondent No. 1 without making due consideration of the objection and representation and the relevant provisions of law, issued notifications vide SRO No. 113-Ain/2001 dated 7-5-2001 wherein the villages Satkhamar and Kurulia have been included in the area of newly created Boda Municipality. The petitioner then served notice demanding justice on the respondents but no reply was given and, as such, justice has been denied. 

Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

14. The respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition. 

15. The short facts in Writ Petition No. 6074 of 2002 is that the Deputy Commissioner, Jessore vide  memo No. Zeproka/Sasosha/ 4pa-8/02 /541(7) dated 15-08-2002 invited objections under rules 3 and 4 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 for declaration of some areas of Bagharpara Upazila as Urban area. The local inhabitants raised objection on the ground that 95% of the population of the area are agriculturists. The Deputy Commissioner, Jessore did not give any reply to the local inhabitants and thereafter by notification No. pa ura-3 /khubi-Ga-1 /2002/1365 dated 29-10-2002 declared Bagharpara Pourashava within District Jessore. This declaration has been done in violation of section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 as the government must be satisfied that three-fourth of the adult male population of Bagharpara are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture and, as such, the impugned order was made without any lawful authority and hence of no legal effect. 

16. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

The respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition. 

17. The case of the petitioner in Writ Petition 3009 of 1996, in a nutshell, is that the respondent No. 1 by SRO No. 315-Ain/94 Poura-2/Gos-3/94 dated 2-11-1994 declared some areas of 17 villages, situated within the territorial jurisdiction of Gognagar, Enayetnagar, Fatulla, Godnail Union Parishad of Narayangonj District to be urban areas. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 have not complied with any of the provisions of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules of 1978 in directing the respondent No. 3 to issue public notice inviting objections under Rule 3 of the said Rules. It is stated that 90% of the people of the above mentioned villages are cultivators and three-fourth of the adult male population of those areas are chiefly employed in agriculture. It is also stated that the respondents did not invite any objection under Rule 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules 1978. As a result the said impugned notification is illegal and without any lawful authority. The petitioners have sent demand of justice notice through their Advocate to cancel the order but the respondents did not comply with the demand. 

18. Being aggrieved the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

19. The respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition. 

20. The case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3215 of 1998, in a nutshell, is that Sujanagar Union is situated in the remotest corner of the District of Pabna and it is a very undeveloped Union. The people of the said Union are very poor and three-fourth of the people earn their livelihood from agriculture. The Government decided to declare the Union as Pourashava. The respondent No. 2 issued notice under Rule 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 showing that certain mouzas of Sujanagar Union need to be declared as urban area. The notice by respondent No. 4 was issued on 5-9-1998. As per notice of the respondent No. 4 dated 5-9-1998 the respondent received suggestions/objections from the local people and on 15-9-1998 he addressed a letter to the Deputy Commissioner, Pabna suggesting that the concerned Union may be declared as Municipality. The Deputy Commissioner having received the suggestions/objections from the Thana Nirbahi Officer addressed a letter to the Government stating that the people of the locality were notified and suggestions and objections were taken from them for declaration of Sujanagar Union as a Pourashava. Thereafter, the respondent No. 2 published a notification on 25-8-1998 declaring Sujanagar Union as Urban Area. Thereafter, the respondent No. 2 has declared the Sujanagar Union as a Municipality by the Gazette dated 5-10-1998. It is submitted that the relevant rules have not been followed in this case as stated above as more than three-fourth of the adult male population of the area are chiefly employed in agriculture. 

21. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

22. The respondent Nos. 1, 3 and 4 contested the Rule by filing joint affidavit-in-opposition and denied the material allegations made in the writ petition. It is stated that Sujanagar Thana Head Quarter is only 20 Km from the Pabna District Head Quarter. Sujanagar Union is the Sadar Union of Sujanagar Thana. All the Thana level offices namely, office of Thana Nirbahi Officer, Police Station, Hospital and other departmental offices are situated at Sujanagar Union Head Quarter which is also Sujanagar Thana Head Quarter. According to 1981 census report, more than three-fourth of its population earn their livelihood from the sources other than agriculture and during last 19 years the percentage of population living on non-agricultural means has greatly increased. The schedule of Pourashava election was not declared at any point of the time after creation of Sujanagar Pourashava. It is further stated that it is true that Sujanagar Union is an undeveloped area. It is a declared Government policy that all the Thana Head Quarters will go under Pourashava phase-wise and as a part of this policy Sujanagar Union has been declared as a Pourashava. It is stated that a notice under rule 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 was issued by the respondent No. 4 on 5-9-98 inviting suggestions and objections fixing 10-9-98 for hearing at Thana Parishad auditorium. Subsequently, another notice to the same effect was issued on 10-9-98 refixing the date on 13-9-98. Both the notices were circulated through different Government offices at Thana level, Police Station, Union Parishad, etc and by having the same in many prominent places. Moreover, the said notices were circulated amongst the members of the public by beating of drums on 7-9-98 and 11-9-98 at Sujanagar hat. A large number of people Were present at the hearing of objections/suggestions held on 13-9-98 and respondent No. 4 received suggestion /objections in open hearing on 13-9-98. On the basis of the objections/suggestions as received on 13-9-98 respondent No. 4 sent a letter to the Deputy Commissioner, Pabna on 15-9-98 proposing Sujanagar as a Pourashava. The Deputy Commissioner, Pabna on receipt of the suggestion made enquiry of his own and sent a report with his comments to respondent No. 1 on 17-9-98 stating therein that the local people were notified and suggestions were received. It is stated that the Thana Nirbahi Officer did not declare Sujanagar Union as Pourashava. The Government of Bangladesh through Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives under notification being SRO No. 186-Law/98 dated 23-8-1998 published in the Bangladesh Gazette on August 25 of 1999 declared certain areas of Sujanagar Thana as urban areas. Thereafter complying with and observing all the provisions and formalities as are required under the relevant Ordinance and Rules, the Government by notification being SRO No. 214 Law/98 dated 30-10-1998 published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 5-10-98 declared the constitution of Sujanagar Municipality. It is stated that three-fourth of the adult population of the concerned area are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture and, as such, there is no contravention of section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. It is also stated that it is the long cherished desire and aspirations of the local people that Sujanagar Union may be upgraded into a Municipality. To achieve this aspiration the local people have been taking different steps to press home their demand for declaration of the locality as a Municipality and pursuing the matter at different levels for years together. Late Ahmed Tafizuddin, a Freedom Fighter and the local Member of the Parliament from the constituency, made repeated endeavours to meet the said demand of the local people. As a result the Government is response to the just demand of the local people after complying with all the legal requirements has declared Sujanagar Union as a Municipality and the long time dream of the local people ultimately was fulfilled. 

23. In Writ Petition No. 1232 of 1996 the case of the petitioner, in short, is that the respondent No. 2 published a notification being SRO No. 244-Ain/94 Sa-Pro-2/Ga Sa-13/93 dated 17-6-1994 in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) purportedly pursuant to section 3(1) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 declaring certain areas of Atharokhada, Kosundi, Chaulia, Jagadal and Moghi Unions of Magura Sadar Thana as urban areas without fulfilling the required conditions of section 3(2) thereof. The respondent No. 2 failed to comply with the requirements of section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance. Therefore the inhabitants of those areas could not make any effective representations opposing declaration of urban areas prior to publication of the said SRO No. 244. The respondent No. 2 thereafter issued a letter bearing Memo No. 401(5) dated 2-8-1994 addressed to the Chairman of Jagadal Union Parishad enclosing a notice issued purportedly pursuant to section 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 directing the Chairman to publish the same in the localities to notify the inhabitants. Similar notices were served on each of the Chairmen of the aforesaid Union Parishads. The Chairmen of Atharokhada, Kasundi, Chaulia, Jagadal and Moghi Union Parishads in compliance with the direction of the respondents circulated the said notice issued under section 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 in the locality. The inhabitants of their respective unions against the aforesaid notice raised serious objections and made a series of written objections opposing the proposed inclusion of their areas within the Magura Pourashava on the grounds, inter alia, that about 90% of the inhabitants of the said mouzas/unions are dependent on agriculture. The respondents received the aforesaid objections from the inhabitants of the concerned unions but by disregarding the facts and without considering the objections and/or affording any personal hearing, published a notification being SRO No. 306-Ain/94/Poura-2/Ga Sa-13/93 dated 20-10-1994 in the Bangladesh Gazette purportedly pursuant to section 4(b) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 read with Rule 5 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 including Mouzas Atharokhada, Kanda Bashkotha, and Nanduali of Atharokhada Union; Mouzas Parnanduali, Baruntuil and Laskmikandar of Kasundi Union, Parla, Bui Chitoal and Ghoramara of Chaulia Union; Mouzas Raigram, Shimulia and Bhitasair of Jagadal Union and Seetarampur of Moghi Union within the Magura Pourashava without complying with the required formalities as provided in section 3 of the Pourashava Ordinance and Rule 3 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municiplities Rules, 1978. 

24. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

25. The respondent No. 1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition and denied the material allegations made in the writ petition. 

26. It is submitted that under section 4(b) of the Pourashava Ordinance the Government is empowered to extend the limits of a municipality under this section, declare any rural area to be an urban area, if it is satisfied that three-fourth of the adult male population of such area are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture. The male adult population of extended area of Magura Paurashava is about 12,472 and out of this 9825 are employed in pursuits other than agriculture. So the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

27. We have heard the learned Advocates for the petitioners in all the writ petitions and the learned Additional Attorney-General with the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondents. 

28. In Writ Petition 3233 of 2000 and Writ Petition No. 3073 of 2000 the inclusion of Mouza Murarikati by SRO No. 120/Ain /90- Sha /pu/20-44 /88 dated 11-3-90 into Kalaroa Paurashava and also declaration of Urban Area to Rural Area by SRO No. 112/L/85/S-10/A-2/82 dated 4-3-85 were called in question. The learned Advocate for the petitioners of both the writ petitions submitted that the inclusion of villages Murarikati and Mirzapur was made in the Kalaroa Pourashava without observing the provisions of section 3 of Pourashava Ordinance 1997 and Rule 3 of the Rules. Moreover, three-fourth of the adult male population of the area are employed in agricultural activities. Hence the declaration of rural area to urban area and the declaration of urban area to Municipality are without any lawful authority. The learned Additional Attorney-General in this connection has produced copies of judgment dated 20-3-1997 passed in Writ Petition No. 3051 of 1991 (unreported) and judgment dated 2-11-1997 in CPLA No. 457 of 1997 and further submitted that in that case it was observed that whether three-fourth of the adult male population are dependent on agriculture or not is a disputed question of fact which cannot be decided in a writ petition without evidence. It was further held that since the Government has duly declared rural area into urban area and urban area to Municipality it will be deemed that these have been done after complying with the necessary legal formalities. He further submits that in Writ Petition No. 3051 of 1991 the same SRO No. 112-L/85/S-10/A-2/82 dated 4-3-1988 and SRO No. 120-Ain/90-Sha-Pou-2 /2C-44/88 dated 11-3-1990 were called in question so far as these relate to Murarikati mouza but the Rule issued in the above mentioned writ petition was discharged on the ground that all the requirements to constitute an urban area as Municipal area have been fulfilled and also that the Pourashava was not made a party in the writ petition. This finding of this court was approved in CPLA No. 457 of 1997 by the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division further observed that, the Pourashava in question was constituted and it has been functioning since 1990 and accordingly, refused to interfere with the judgment passed by the High Court Division. In the circumstances we find no substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the petitioners in these two writ petitions namely, Writ Petition Nos. 3233 of 2000 and 3073 of 2000 as the matter has already been decided upto the Appellate Division. 

29. Accordingly, the Rules issued in Writ Petition Nos. 3233 and 3073 of 2000 are discharged without any order as to cost. 

30. In all other writ petitions the learned Advocates for the petitioners submit that 75% of the adult male population of the area earn their livelihood from agriculture and the area does not contain 15000 population and an average number of 2000 inhabitants per square mile. They further submit that the provision of sections 3 & 4 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 and Rules 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978 were not complied with. 

31. The Government filed affidavit-in-opposition in some writ petitions and the learned Additional Attorney-General also produced the relevant Government files before us. He submits that the allegations made in the writ petitions are not correct. He further submits that all the ingredients as required under section 3(2) of the Pourashava Ordinance 1977 were present and all the legal requirements in declaring rural area as urban area and urban area as Municipality were duly complied with and all actions taken in this regard must be presumed to have been correctly and duly done and no cogent evidence in the instant cases could be nroduced before this court to show that the acts done by the Government were not done in accordance with the relevant law and rules. He further submits that these are all highly disputed questions of fact which cannot be decided in the writ petition without evidence. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submits that in the affidavit-in-opposition filed in Writ Petition No. 3215 of 1998 the respondent had clearly asserted that it is the declared Government policy that all the Thana headquarters will go under Pourashava phase-wise and as part of this policy the areas in the above writ petitions were declared as Pourashava or included in the existing Pourashava. He further submits that in the affidavit-in-opposition in some of the writ petitions it has been clearly stated that suggestions/objections were invited and those were duly considered before declaration of urban area as Municipality and it was also the desire of the local people to declare their areas as Pourashava and to fulfil the long cherished desire of the local people the rural areas were declared as urban areas and urban areas as Municipalities. 

32. To appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates for the writ petitioners and the learned Additional Attorney-General, let us quote below sections 3 and 4 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 and Rules 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rules, 1978. 

Section 3 of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977: 

3(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare any rural area to be an urban area; 

Provided that notwithstanding the declaration of a rural area to be an urban area, the Union Parishad which immediately before such declaration exercised any function in relation to that area shall, until the area is declared to be, or to be included in, a municipality continue to exercise those functions. 

(2) The Government shall not declare any rural area to be an urban area unless it is satisfied that three-fourths of the adult male population of the area to which it refers are chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture, and such area contains not less than fifteen thousand population and an average number of not less than two thousand inhabitants per square mile. (Provided that the Government may, for the purpose of extension of the limits of a municipality under section 4(b), declare any Rural Area to be an Urban Area, if it is satisfied that three fourths of the adult male population of such area is chiefly employed in pursuits other than agriculture.)

4. The Government may, in the prescribed manner,

(a) declare any urban area other than a cantonment, to be a municipality; 

(b) extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any municipality; and 

(c) declare that any urban area shall, from a date to be specified, cease to be a municipality. 

Rules 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the Declaration and Alterations of Municipalities Rules, 1978: 

3. Notice inviting suggestion or objection - (1) When the Government proposes to declare any urban area to be, or to cease to be, a municipality, or if it intends to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any municipality under section 4 of the Ordinance, it shall direct the Deputy Commissioner concerned to issue a public notice inviting suggestions and objections to be filed to him within thirty days from the date of service of the notice in relation to the proposed declaration or, as the case may be, alteration. 

(2) The notice under sub-rule (1) shall clearly state the particulars of the area showing the JL No. proposed to be declared to be a municipality or by which the limits of a municipality shall be extended, curtailed or otherwise altered. 

(3) Hanging of notice in some prominent places in the area specified in it and announcement to this effect by beat of drums in the said area shall be deemed to be issue of notice for the purposes of this rule. 

4. Deputy Commissioner to enquire - 

(1) On receipt of suggestion or objection, if any, under rule 3, or if there is none, the Deputy Commissioner shall make such enquiry as he deems fit and forward a report with his own comments to the proposed declaration, extension, curtailment or otherwise alteration of a municipality or, as the case may be, the limits of a municipality. 

(2) On receipt of the report under sub-rule (1) with comments of the Divisional Commissioner, the Government shall take a decision in respect of the proposed declaration, extension, curtailment or otherwise alteration of a Municipality or, as the case may be, the limits of a Municipality. 

5. Notification to be issued - (1) If the Government finally decides under rule 4 for declaration or, as the case may be, alteration with or without modification in the particulars of the area specified in the notice under sub-rule (2) of rule 3, it shall issue a notification in the official Gazette specifying the date on or from which the urban area shall be or shall cease to be a Municipality, or the limits of a municipality shall be extended, curtailed or otherwise altered. 

6. Consequences of Notification - If the Notification under rule 5 results in the reconstitution of any municipality or union, the Prescribed Authority, as defined in the Ordinance, shall make such order relating to the distribution of staff, assets and liabilities of the municipality or union concerned as he deems fit. 

33. In the case of Khalilur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 53 DLR (AD) 25 = 5 MLR (AD) 80 it was held that the dispute regarding variation of population cannot be resolved invoking writ jurisdiction as it requires adjudication of facts on evidence. It is true that in that case delimitation of wards of the Pourashava was called in question but the principle of law that disputed question of fact cannot be decided in Writ Jurisdiction equally applies in the present cases. In Writ Petition No. 2388 of 2001, Mr Idris Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited the case of Mr Abdul Hye Bhuiyan vs Secretary reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 196 regarding formation of opinion by the Government. The facts of that case are distinguishable from the facts of the present case. He also cited the case of Government of Bangladesh & others vs Md Tajul Islam reported in 49 DLR (AD) 177 on point of principle of natural justice. In our view, the principle of law enunciated in that case is not applicable in the present case. 

34. In Writ Petition No. 1232 of 1996 the learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited the case of Baladev Raj Chadha vs Union of India and others reported in AIR 1981 SC 70. In our view, the facts of this case are distinguishable from the facts of the present case as that case was regarding service matter.

35. Moreover, the learned Advocates for the petitioners in the writ petitions could not produce any undisputed document regarding their contentions that in the areas which have been included in the Municipality/ Pourashava three-fourth of the adult male population are chiefly employed in agricultural activities and the area does not contain 15000 population and an average number of 2000 inhabitants per square mile. On the other hand, the submissions of the learned Additional Attorney-General is that all actions taken and all other acts done by the Government in this regard and publication of official gazette notification must be presumed to have been properly and correctly done/ taken after complying with the official formalities and the requirements of law. In our view, there is substance in the submissions of the learned Additional Attorney-General. 

36. In view of the discussion above we are of the view that the allegations on which the writ petitions were brought could not be substantiated by producing undisputed documents. Moreover, in our view, these are all disputed questions of fact which cannot be resolved in writ petitions. Furthermore, since the Government by filing affidavit in opposition and by producing relevant Government files have been able to show that all the legal formalities required for the purpose were duly complied with, so, in our view, there is no merit in the above writ petitions. 

Accordingly, the Rules issued in all the above mentioned writ petitions are discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This appeal at the instance of petitioner, Nani Gopal Hazra, under section 229 of the Succession Act of 1925 is directed against the judgment and order dated 29-9-1988 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi, in Miscellaneous Case No. 188 of 1982 dismissing the same on contest under section 263 of the Succession Act for revocation of the grant of Probate by Mokshada Bala Dasaya (deceased) as granted by the District Judge, Rajshahi on 24-2-1974 in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 in favour of respondent No. 1 Nagendra Nath Roy.

2. The petitioner, Nani Gopal Hazra, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 in the court of District Judge, Rajshahi, for revocation of Probate granted on 12-4-1974 arising out of will dated 13-2-1972.

3. The case of the petitioner, in short, is that principal opposite party No. 1, Negendra Nath Roy, obtained Probate of last will and testament of Mokshada Bala Dasaya (deceased), wife of Fakuram Hazra from the Court of the District Judge, Rajshahi, on the 2nd February, 1974 as per proceeding in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 without serving any notice to the petitioner and other interested persons; that the proceedings of the Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 were defective in substance inasmuch as the petitioner and other interested persons as referred were not made parties in that proceedings and that there was no notice upon the petitioner and other interested persons were served; that the said grant was obtained by the principal opposite party No. 1 by exercise of fraud upon the Court by showing so-called service of general and special citations and that notice of the said proceedings was fraudulently suppressed in collusion with the process server of the Court.

4. It is further stated that the will alleged to have been executed by Mokshada Bala Dasaya is a forged document which was created antedated by forgery after death of Mokshada Bala Dasaya by the principal opposite party No. 1 in collusion with others; that the property purported to have been given by the will belonged to Fakuram Hazra; that Fakuram Hazra had two brothers namely, Dhaneswar Hazra and Laba Krishna Hazra; that Dhaneswar Hazra died leaving behind son Nonigopal Hazra, the present appellant and daughter Shishubala Roy the constituted attorney of the appellant; that Laba Krishna Hazra died leaving two sons namely, Titul Hazra and Balai Hazra, preformed opposite parties Nos. 3 and 4 respectively and that Fakuram Hazra died without any issue leaving his widow, Mokshoda Bala Dasaya; that the appellant and the opposite parties Nos. 3 and 4 became the owners of the estate left by Fakuram Hazra according to Hindu Law of Dayabhaga and for that matter they became and are owners of the property purported to have been bequeathed by the said will. It is further stated that principal opposite party No. 1 subsequently, after the obtaining the said probate, created a sale deed in respect of the property contained in the will in the name of Gulu Hemron, principal respondent No. 2, that subsequently, the principal respondent No. 2 made a petition for mutation of jama in his name on the basis of his purchase from the principal opposite party No. 1 in the Tahsil office at Barakuthi; that the notice of mutation issued from the office of the Co. (Rev.) Paba Boalia upon the name of Fakuram Hazra was not served which was collusively suppressed and that subsequently Shihubala Roy informed about that proceedings to her brother petitioner. Thereafter, the petitioner making contact with the Barakuti Tahsil office got full particulars regarding the said probate from the papers submitted by the principal opposite party No. 1 in the mutation proceeding.

5. It is further stated that the petitioner is a service holder and, as such, it is not possible for him to manage the property as contained in the will and furthermore, Shishubala Roy resides upon the land as contained in the will and in this view of the matter, the petitioner gave a general power of attorney in favour of Shishubala Roy vide registered Khas Moktarnama executed and registered by petitioner appellant on 23-9-1982. As per that khas Moktarnama, this petitioner has conferred Shishubala Roy all powers including powers of conducting all legal proceedings regarding the property contained in the will. As such, the petition for revocation is filed by him by his lawful constituted attorney, Shishubala Roy. It is further stated that the probate being obtained from the Court by exercising fraud upon the Court, the petitioner has suffered irreparable loss for which he prays for revocation of granting of probate in respect of the will.

6. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 Nagendra Nath Roy and Gulu Hemron contested the case denying all material allegations contained in the petition contending, inter ail, that the property as contained in the will belonged to Fakuram Hazra ; that Fakuram Hazara died leaving a widow, namely Mokshoda Bala, as his only legal heir; that Mokshada being satisfied with the service of the opposite party No. 1, Nagendra, executed a will in respect of the estate and property left by her husband Fakuram Hazra in favour of the opposite party No. 1 who happens to be the nephew by distant relation of Mokshada Bala Dasaya; that this will was voluntarily executed on 13-2-1972 by the said Mokshada Bala Dasaya.

7. It is further stated that since before the date of execution of the will, the opposite party No. 1 being nephew by distant relation used to reside upon the land contained in the will with the said Mokshada Bala Dasaya in the same family and mess; that opposite party No. 1 used to maintain Mokshada Bala Dasaya in all respects and also used to look after the property and person of Mokshada Bala Dasaya till her death and for that matter she became satisfied and voluntarily executed a will on 13-2-1972 in favour of opposite party No. 1; that Mokshada Bala Dasaya died in the house upon the land contained in the will and that the opposite party No. 1 graveside and entertainment for the death of the said Mokshada Bala Dasaya and performed all religious functions for her death memory; that the will executed by Mokshada Bala Dasaya is a genuine will; that the opposite party No. 1 has got the probate of the will on 12-4-1974 in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972; that the notice of the probate proceeding was duly served and that the notice upon the general people was also duly served by a 'Beggapti' published in Rajshahi Barta dated 27-8-1973; that after due service of notice and after exhausting all procedure, the Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 was allowed and probate was granted according to .law and that the opposite party No.1 has been in possession of the property living in his house in his own right and interest.

8. The further case of the opposite party is that the opposite party No. 1 for his necessity has sold out .0330 acres of land in SA plot Nos. 670 and 671 by a registered sale deed to the opposite party No. 2 who is a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration; that after purchase the opposite party No. 2 filed a petition for mutation and mutated his name. It is also asserted by these opposite parties that the petitioner had or has no possession in the property contained in the will and probated in favour of the opposite party No.1; that the petitioner and his so-called attorney, Shishubala Roy, were in the knowledge and was fully aware of the matter of execution of the will since its inception and also of the matter of granting probate since before 1975; that Shishubala Roy being baffled in her illegal attempt in the mutation case has filed this case in the name of Nani Gopal as his so-called attorney with a motive to grab the property and to harass these opposite parties unnecessarily which is liable to be rejected.

9. At the trial, the petitioner examined 4 witnesses in support of his case. PW 1 is constituted Attorney Shishubala Roy PW 2, Nonigopal Hazra, is petitioner himself PW 3, Upendra Mondal, is neighbour of the petitioner, PW 4 is Labi Ghose who knows the parties and PW 5 Shebendra Nath is the local member of union parishad.

10. The petitioner submitted the certified copy of the Death Register of Sree Mati Mokshada Bala Dasaya marked Exhibit 1 and the will dated 13-2-1974 executed by Mokshada Bala Dasaya marked exhibit 2 in favour of his contention.

11. While the opposite parties examined 3 witnesses. DW 1, Nagendra Nath, is the opposite party No. 1. DW 2 is Jalaluddin Mollah who knows the parties and DW 3 is Dinobandhu who is a local Chowkider. The opposite parties submitted registered deed dated 9-5-1978 marked Exhibit Ka, in support of their contention.

12. The following two issues were framed by the learned District Judge:

1. was the probate obtained collusively and illegally?

2. Is the petitioner entitled to get any relief?

13. The learned District Judge considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record found that the petitioner was not subsequent heir of Fakuram Hazra, husband of Mokshada Bala, who is the executants of will and, as such, the petitioner has no locus stand to challenge the will. Thus the learned District Judge took the view that the probate was not obtained collusively and, as such, the petitioner is not entitled to get any relief and thus he dismissed the petition by the judgment and order dated 29-9-1988.

14. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 29-9-1988, the petitioner, Nani Gopal Hazra, has preferred the present appeal.

15. Mr. HN Nondy, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the principal respondent No. 1 obtained probate of the alleged last will of testament of Mokshada Bala Dasaya, wife of Fakuram, on 2-2-1974 as per proceedings in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 without any knowledge of and serving any notice on the appellant and other interested persons; that the grant of alleged probate in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 as obtained by the respondent No. 1 by practicing fraud upon the Court and by misrepresentation of facts and suppression of notice upon the appellant and other interested persons, in collusion with the process server and, as such, the judgment is liable to be set aside.

16. Mr Nondy also submits that the alleged will was not executed by Mokshada Bala Dasaya, widow of late Fakuram Hazra, in favour of respondent No. 1 which is a forged, antedated and a manufactured one by the respondent No. 1 after the death of the executrix. He further submits that Fakuram Hazra who died leaving behind two brothers namely Dhaneshwar Hazra and Laba Krishna Hazra and that Dhaneshwar Hazra died leaving behind son, Nani Gopal Hazra, the appellant and daughter Shishubala, the constituted Attorney of the appellant and that Laba Krishna Hazra died leaving behind Titul Hazra, proforma respondent No. 3, and Balai Hazra, proforma respondent No. 4. He further submits that the learned District Judge without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record passed the impugned judgment and order dated 29-9-1988 which is liable to be set aside.

17. In support of his case Mr Nondy referred to a Case of Brajabala vs Tarapada Saha Minor and others reported in 11 DLR 40 and also refers to section 113 of Successions Act, in support of his contention.

18. Mr Khondaker Saiful Hoque, the learned Advocate for the respondent, opposes the appeal and submits that Mokshada Bala Dasaya being satisfied with the service of opposite party No. 1, Nagendra Nath Roy, executed the will in respect of estate and property left by her husband Fakuram Hazra in favour of opposite party No. 1 who happens to be the nephew by distant relation of Mokshada Bala Dasaya; that opposite party No. 1 has got the probate of will dated 13-2-1972 and the notice of the probate proceedings was duly served and that the opposite party No. 1 for his legal necessity has sold out .0330 acres of land by registered sale deed to the opposite party No. 2 who is a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration. He further submits that the opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the land contained in the will. Mr Khondaker Saiful Hoque further submits that the learned District Judge considering the facts and circumstances of the case passed the impugned judgment and order dated 29-9-1988 and the learned District Judge is justified in passing the impugned judgment assigning sound and good reasons and there is no reasons for setting aside the impugned judgment of the learned District Judge which shall be upheld.

19. The point for determination is whether the judgment and order dated 29-9-1988 passed by the learned District Judge in Miscellaneous Case No. 188 of 1982 is justified.

20. Mr HN Nondy, the learned Advocate for the appellant,, has placed before us the impugned judgment and order, petition of the case and the objection thereof and the deposition of the witnesses.

21. It is admitted that the estate in question belonged to Fakuram Hazra who died childless leaving widow, Mokshada Bala Dasaya.

22. The case of the opposite party is that Mokshada Bala Dasaya being satisfied with the service of the opposite party No. 1, Nagendra Nath Roy, executed a will in respect of the estate and property left by her husband, Fakuram Hazra in favour of opposite party No. 1 who happens to be the nephew by distant relation of Mokshada Bala Dasaya; that the opposite party No. 1 has got the probate of the will on 12-4-1974 and that the opposite party No. 1 for his necessity sold out .0330 acres of land by registered sale deed to the opposite party No. 2 Gula Hamron.

23. The petitioner's case, on the other hand, is that the will alleged to have been executed by Mokshada Bala Dasaya is a forged document which was created antedated by forgery after the death of Mokshada Bala Dasaya by the opposite party No. 1, Nagendra Nath Roy, in collusion with others and that moreover, since the opposite party No. Nagendra Nath Roy, is the distant nephew of Mokshada Bala Dasaya, execution of will in his favour is not legal as per Succession Act and Dayabhaga school of law. The further claim of the petitioner-appellant is that Fakuram Hazra had two brothers namely, Dhaneswar Hazra and Labu Krishna Hazra; that Dhaneshwar died leaving behind son Nani Gopal Hazra , the present petitioner and a daughter Shishubala Roy, the attorney of the petitioner and Laba Krishna Hazra died leaving behind two sons namely, Titul Hazra and Balai Hazra, proforma opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 respectively.

24. Scanning the evidence, we find that the learned District Judge, Rajshahi, came to the conclusion that execution of will of Mokshada Bala Dasaya in favour of his nephew, Nagendra, is genuine and that Dhameswar Hazra and Laba Krishna Hazra are not the brothers of Fakuram Hazra and, as such, the petitioner and others are not entitled to challenge the will and probate.

25. Now the pertinent question for determination is that whether Fakuram Hazra had two brothers namely Dhameswar Hazra and Laba Krishna Hazra and whether a Hindu widow can will the estate left by her husband by way of will to her distant nephew.

26. The law relating to the burden of proof is stated in section 101 of the Evidence Act which runs thus:

"101. whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist.

When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person."

27. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it. Moreover, it is but reasonable and just that the suitor who relies upon the existence of a fact, shoula be called upon to prove his own case. The party on whom the onus of proof lies must in order to succeed, establish a prima facie case. He cannot, on failure to do so, take advantage of the weakness of his adversary's case. He must succeed by the strength of his own right and the clearness of his own proof. The burden of proving his case is upon the claimant. Here in this case both sides have two different cases and they have to prove their respective case.

28. Now let us see how far the parties have succeeded in their respective part by adducing oral and documentary evidence.

29. The first allegation of the petitioner is that the alleged will was created antedated by forgery after the death of Mokshada Bala Dasaya. PW 1 Shishubala Roy deposed that Mokshada Bala Dasaya did not execute the will and the same is forged one. When this allegation is supported by oral evidence, then the burden of proof shifts to the opposite party vide rulings reported in the case of Pannu Geegania vs Devi Proshad AIR 1963 MP 15. But the opposite party has totally failed to adduce any evidence in this respect.

30. Next we see how far the petitioner has succeeded to prove that Fakuram Hazra had two brothers namely, Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna Hazra. It is not disputed that petitioner, Nonigopal, opposite party No. 3, Tatul Hazra, and opposite party No. 4, Balai Hazra, are the subsequent heirs of Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna Hazra.

31. To prove this aspect of the case, petitioner has examined 5 PWs. PW 1, Shishu Bala Roy, and PW 2, Nani Gopal, are the descendants of Dhaseswar and Laba Krishna who stoutly deposed that Fakuram Hazra had two brothers. PW 3 Upen Mondal and PW 4 Labi Ghose are the close neighbors who, supporting PW 1 and 2, testified that Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna were the brothers of Fekuram Hazra. PW 5 Shebendra Nath Sarker is the local member of Union Parishad who deposed supporting other witnesses. We do not find any reasons to disbelieve PW 5, member of Union Parishad, and PW 3 and 4 neighbours of the petitioner who are the disinterested and competent witnesses who consistently deposed that Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna are the brothers of Fekuram Hazra.

<u>32. Moreover, OPW 1, Nagendra Nath Roy, admitted that Sree Krishna Hazra was the father of Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna; that Shishu Bala called Fakuram as Mama; that Fakuram allowed Shishu Bala and her husband in his house to live. This assertion of DW 1 also helps to prove the petitioner's case. Thus, it is crystal clear from the evidence that Fakuram Hazra had two brothers namely, Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna Hazra. But the learned District Judge misread this aspect of the evidence which led him to arrive at a erroneous conclusion.</u>

33. Now the point for determination is whether Mokshada can execute the will in respect of property left by her husband to her distant nephew.

34. In this respect, it will be profitable to mention some paragraph of Hindu law in the following lines.

"176. Widow's estate-A widow or other limited heir is not tenant for life, but is owner of the property inherited by her, subject to certain restrictions on alienation and subject to its devolving upon the next heir of the last full owner upon her death. (i) The whole estate is for the limited time vested in her and she represents it completely (j) as state in a Privy Council (k)," her right is of the nature of a right of property; her position is that of owner, her powers in that character are, however limited but...so long as she is alive no one has any vested interest in the succession. The principles relating to the nature of a widow's estate were reiterated by the Supreme Court in the under mentioned cases."

<u>35. A widow under the Hindu Law takes a special and qualified estate, and she has limited power of disposition of her husband's property. The restrictions on her power of alienation are inseparable from her estate, and their existence does not depend on that of heirs capable of taking on her death. If, for want of heirs, the right to the property passes to the government, the government has the same power that an heir would have for protecting its interest by impeaching any unauthorised alienation by the widow.</u>

<u>36. The estate taken by a Hindu widow in property inherited by her from her husband may best be described by saying that she is the owner thereof, except that she cannot sell the corpus of the property or mortgage it, or make a gift of it, or grant lease thereof for a long term, or otherwise alienate it, unless it be for a legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate or with the consent of the next reversionary. Where an alienation is made by her for a legal necessity or with the consent of the next reversionary, it passes an absolute estate to the aliened to the same extent as an alienation made by a full owner.</u>

37. It is also stated at page 196 of Mullah's Principles of Hindu Law which run as follows:

"181. Alienation by widow. A widow or other limited heir has no power to alienate the estate inherited by her from the deceased owner except for the following purposes, namely:

(i) Religious or charitable purpose,

(ii) other purpose amounting to legal necessity,

For the purpose of the first class she has a larger power of deposition than for purpose of the second class."

A surrender by a Hindu widow in favour of the next reversionary is not an alienation of her husband's estate. A widow or other limited heir cannot in any case dispose of by will property inherited by her or any portion thereof, whether the property be moveable or immoveable.

<u>38. In the instant case, Mokshada Bala Dasaya only could alienate the property left by her husband during her lifetime for religious purpose, welfare of the estate or to meet legal necessity. She could not dispose of the property during her life time excepting the above purposes. On a plain reading of the will, it appears that the intention of the testator was that after her death, her distant nephew Nagendra Nath Roy would become owner of the estate and enjoy and possess the same. This will creates an estate which is inconsistent with the general law of inheritance under the Hindu Law.</u>

39. Their Lordships of the Privy Council, in the case of Juttendromohun Tagore and another vs Ganendromohun Tagore reported in 18 WR, 350 have laid down that a private individual attempting by a gift or will to make property inheritable otherwise than the law directs is assuming to legislate and that the gift must fail and the inheritance take place as the law directs and also that all estates of inheritance created by gift or will so far as they are inconsistent with the general law of inheritance are void.

40. It has also been held in that case that by Hindu Law as a general principle, a person capable of taking under gift or will must either in fact or in contemplation of law be in existence at the time when the gift takes effect, i.e., in the case of a will, at the time of death of the testator.

<u>41. Keeping this principle of Hindu Law in view, Mokshada Bala Dasaya cannot legally execute the will in respect of the property left by her husband which will be effective after her death. Will in the present case purports to alter the law of inheritance according to Hindu Law and that if the will offends against the Hindu law of inheritance and succession, no probate can be granted as it will be repugnant and void.</u>

42. This view also finds support from a decision of the privy council in the case of Sapher and another vs Administrator General of Bengal and another reported in AIR 1944 (PC) 67.

<u>43. It is an elementary principle that a Court of law cannot be a party to a grant or disposition of that character. There is no authority for the proposition that even where a question as to the construction of the will is raised and the bequest provided therein appears to be a void one by reason of its being contrary to law or morality or opposed to public policy, the probate Court should shut its eyes and feel helpless and not construe the will and pronounce whether it is void or otherwise according to the provisions of the Succession Act No. XXXIX of 1925 which consolidates the law applicable to intestate and testamentary succession as previously provided in the Indian Succession Act (X of 1965), The Hindu Wills Act (XXI of 1870), The Probate and Administration Act (V of 1881) and other Acts. If, therefore, upon an application of the relevant provisions and tests laid down in the Succession Act a particular bequest as in the present case, appears to be a void one, it can have no effect in the eye of law. A void bequest means no bequest and in that case there is nothing to be administered on the authority of a probate. The fulfilment of the bequest in the instant case after the death of Mokshada Bala Dasaya, if at all, will be contrary to the terms of section 113 of the Succession Act and also will be repugnant to the law of inheritance and succession recognised under the Hindu law. In our view, there is no reason as to why the Testamentary Court should not decide the question as to whether a probate can at all be granted in respect of a bequest which offends against the provisions of the Succession Act or other laws of the land. In the present case, the bequest, subsequent to the death of Mokshada Bala Dasaya, is void and the will is no longer effective.</u>

<u>44. Scanning both the oral and documentary evidence, we find that the learned District Judge erred both in law and fact in ignoring the documentary evidence, Exhibit 1 and the oral evidence of PWs. 1 to 4 and relying only on Exhibit Ka a registered deed dated 9-5-78 produced by the respondent No. 1 showing that the name of the father Fakuram Hazra is Gopal Ram Hazra, which is not a conclusive proof in itself, and it having been rebutted by the oral evidence of PWs 1 to 4 and documentary evidence Exhibit 1. PWs 1, 2 and 3 and 4 proved the fact that Dhaneshwar, Fakuram and Laba Krishna are full brothers and their evidence having been fortified by, the Power of Attorney Exhibit 1 executed by PW 2 Nani Gopal Hazra in favour of his sister PW 1 Shishubala who are son and daughter of late Dhaneshwar nevertheless, the learned District Judge erred both in law and fact in not holding that the appellant has proved the proceedings both by oral and documentary evidence.</u>

45. The learned District Judge ignoring the oral evidence, of PWs 1 to 4 and the documentary evidence Registered Power of Attorney dated 23-9-1982 (Exhibit 1) on record and on misreading and misconstructing those illegally held that appellant is not entitled to challenge the alleged will as he is not the exclusive heirs of Fakuram.

<u>46. The petitioner appellant has completely succeeded in proving that Fakuram Hazra had two bothers namely, Dhaneswar and Laba Krishna and thus the petitioner as the heir of Dhaneswar Hazra has every right to challenge illegality of will and the probate arising out of it.</u>

47. The learned District Judge also erred both in law and fact in not holding that the widow of Fakuram, who died childless, was under legal disability and incompetent to dispose of the property by way of executing a will of her husband to a stranger. The proceedings for revocation of the grant of probate under section 263 of the Succession Act, 1925 having been produced on the specific grounds of substantial defect in the proceedings to obtain the grant and forgery, the learned Judge erred in law and fact in not holding that the onus is not in the petitioner appellant for revocation to prove that the will is a forgery but on the grantee respondent No.1 to prove that the will is a valid will of the testatrix and the respondent having not such facts the judgment is liable to be set aside. In view of the pleadings of parties and non framing of the issues of forgery which also created a substantial defect in the proceedings.

48. It is admitted that a Hindu widow has lifetime interest in estate left by her husband. She can only dispose of the estate for some limited purpose like legal necessity and religious and charitable purpose. She cannot execute a will which will be ineffective after her death. Moreover, the property left by the husband cannot go into the line of his wife and his property will legally devolve upon his own descendants. Here, in this case, the heirs of the brothers of Fakuram Hazra will be entitled to the property left by Fakuram Hazra.

<u>49. The learned District Judge erred both in law and fact in not discussing and weighing the evidence on record both of the PWs and that of the opposite party respondent in arriving in his decision. The learned District Judge has misconstrued and misapplied the provisions of Hindu Law and the provision of section 263 of the Succession Act in arriving at his decision and in holding that the grant of probate has become useless and inoperative and the sale arising out of such illegal probate has become also illegal and inoperative.</u>

50. Weighing the entire facts, circumstances and materials produced before this Court and in the light of the proposition of law emerging from the authorities referred above, we are of the opinion that the learned District Judge did not rightly apply his judicial mind, in view of the fact and circumstances of the case and law bearing to it, in passing his judgment and order dated 29-9-1988. His judgment is not well reasoned which suffers from legal infirmity. The learned District Judge on an erroneous view of the fact and law allowed the petition and thus his judgment and order is not justifiable which calls for our interference. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 29-9-1988 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi in Miscellaneous Case No. 188 of 1982 dismissing the same is set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1972 is allowed.

Send down the Lower Court's Record at once.

End.
