case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12-4-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7242 of 2009).
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: Delay condoned. These petitions arose out of the same Judgment of the High Court Division and accordingly they are disposed of analogously. Respondent Nos.1-4 instituted Writ Petition No. 7242 of 2009 seeking a direction upon the petitioners to mutate the record-of-rights "upon incorporating change of the ownership/possession of lands pursuant to the registered sale deed No.1997 dated 11-2-2009 (Annexure-A) executed by respondent No.5 (writ respondent No.5)".

<u>2. Writ-Petitioners averred in the writ petition that pursuant to an agreement for sale of the disputed property, they got a decree for Specific Performance of Contract in Other Class Suit No.40 of 1981 which decree was affirmed by this Division. Thereafter, they got a sale deed duly executed and registered through Court on 11th February 2009. The petitioners, who were the writ-respondents, were under obligation to correct the record-of-rights in their favour but they were delaying the procedure for collateral purpose. Petitioner No.1 contested the petition stating that the original owners of the disputed property surrendered the same as excess land under PO 98 of 1972 and accordingly, the property vested in the government free from all encumbrances and thus, the vendor of the writ petitioners had no saleable interest in the disputed property and therefore, the petitioners were under no obligation to mutate their names in the record-of-rights.</u>

3. The High Court Division by the impugned Judgment made the Rule absolute directing the petitioners to "mutate the names of the petitioners (writ-petitioners) in respect of the land in record-of-right upon changing ownership/possession of the land" within three months observing that in view of the judgments of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 5380 of 1991 and writ petition No.4997 of 2008, the petitioners are under obligation to mutate the disputed property in favour of the writ-petitioners under sections 143 and 143(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Against the said judgment and order, the writ-respondent Nos. 1-4 preferred Civil Petition No. 1718 of 2010. One Samar Chakrabartee and 4 others who are not parties in the writ petition preferred Civil Petition No. 869 of 2011 against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that they instituted Other Class Suit No. 197 of 2011 in the 3rd Court of Joint District Judge, Chittagong seeking declaration that the deed dated 11th February, 2009 is forged, collusive and not binding upon them, that the writ-petitioners' predecessors AKM Bashir Ahmed and others executed a collusive agreement with the writ-petitioners and that the writ-respondents obtained a collusive decree. They claimed title and ownership of the disputed property by way of amicable partition; the BS Khatian was prepared behind their back, and the High Court Division without affording them any opportunity passed the impugned judgment which is not binding upon them.

4. Lieutenant Colonel (Retd) Zillur Rahman and 19 others preferred Civil Petition No. 2686 of 2010 challenging the same judgment of the High Court Division stating that the owner Saifuddin Ahmed Siddiqui sold the disputed property in favour of AKM Bashir Ahmed and 3 others by registered deed dated 19th December, 1962. The said purchasers sold the same lands to Lieutenant Colonel (Retd) Zillur Rahman and after the death of AKM Bashir Ahmed, the petitioner Nos. 3-8 and 17 inherited the remaining land. During the last survey operation the disputed property was recorded in the name of the Government but on appeal by AKM Bashir Ahmed and others, the settlement officers directed for correction of the record-of-rights and a separate Khatian was prepared in their names. The writ petitioners in collusion with Saifuddin Ahmed Siddiqui instituted the suit for Specific Performance of Contract. The decree passed in the suit is not binding upon them as they were not made parties. They had no knowledge about the decree passed in the civil suit and the Judgment in Writ Petition No. 4997 of 2008. Those suit and writ petition were instituted upon untrue allegations of fact. 5. Mr. Rajik-al-Jalil, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the petitioners in Civil Petition No. 1718 of 2010 argued that the disputed property is the khas land of the Government as the vendor of the writ-petitioners surrendered the same as excess land under PO 98 of 1972 and in that view of the matter, the High Court Division erred in law in directing for correcting the record-of-right in favour of the writ-petitioners. It is further contended that the High Court Division acted in excess of power in directing the petitioners to mutate the names of the writ-petitioners in the record-of-rights in failing to consider that their .application for mutation has not been disposed of in accordance with law and pending determination of the matter, the High Court Division cannot give such direction.

6. Mr. AFM Mesbahuddin, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners in Civil Petition No.869 of 2011 contended that there are disputed questions of facts involved in this matter and the High Court Division acted illegally in directing for correction of the record-of-rights during the pendency of other suit No.197 of 2011 which was instituted for setting aside the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 40 of 1981, the Judgment in Writ Petition No. 7242 of 2009 and for declaring the deed in favour of the writ petitioners nullity, and if the disputed property is mutated in the name of the writ petitioners during the pendency of the suit, the suit will be rendered in fructuous.

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners in Civil Petition No. 2686 of 2010 contended that whatever interest Saifuddin Ahmed Siddiqui had in the disputed property had been extinguished after he had transferred the same in favour of the petitioners by deed dated 19th December, 1962 and, therefore, the writ petitioners could not acquire any title pursuant to the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 40 of 1981 and, therefore, the High Court Division erred in law in directing for correction of the record-of-rights in respect of the disputed property in favour of the writ-petitioners. It is further contended that the petitioners having not been made parties in Other Class Suit No.40 of 1981 and the subsequent writ petition, they are not bound by the judgments passed in those proceedings, thus the direction of changing the ownership pursuant to the deed dated 11th February, 2009 is unlawful.

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel appearing for the writ-petitioners while supporting the judgment of the High Court Division frankly conceded that there is technical error in the direction of the High Court Division upon the petitioners in Civil Petition No. 1718 of 2010 to correct the record-of-rights, which direction may be modified to the extent that the petition filed by the writ-petitioners for mutating their names be disposed of by the Revenue Officer in accordance with law.

9. We have perused the judgments in Civil Revision No. 5380 of 1991 which arose out of the Other Class Suit No. 40 of 1981, Writ Petition. No.4997 of 2008, plaint in Other Class Suit No. 197 of 2011, the writ petition and other connected papers. We have heard the learned Counsel at length. The High Court Division is of the opinion that since the writ petitioners have got a decree for Specific Performance of Contract in respect of the disputed property, the writ-respondents have no option other than to correct the record-of-rights in their favour and gave the direction relying upon the case of Qazi Kamal vs Rasdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha, 44 DLR (AD) 29.

10. The case considered by the High Court Division is quite distinguishable. In that case, Qazi Kamal with the prior permission of RAJUK purchased a plot of land with building at Gulshan from the original allotted after performing formalities and on payment of required fees as demanded by the RAJUK. Thereupon, the purchaser Qazi Kamal applied to the RAJUK for mutation of the plot with building by enclosing a copy of the deed. In the mean time, some inimical persons of the original lessee made a complaint to RAJUK alleging that he got allotment of the plot by filing a false affidavit. Pursuant to such complaint, RAJUK took a resolution not to mutate the said plot in favour of Qazi Kamal. In the context of the matter, Qazi Kamal filed a writ petition. This Division noticed that RAJUK had not taken any step to cancel the allotment of the original lessee, the vendor of Qazi Kamal or determined the lease of the vendor as per lease deed. In view of the above admitted position, this Division held that Qazi Kamal was not in any way connected with the filing of the alleged false affidavit by this vendor and that Qazi Kamal being a bonafide purchaser for value without notice to the act of this vendor, RAJUK acted illegally in denying the mutation. So, the High Court Division failed to appreciate the statement of law argued by this Division in the above case which has no manner of application in this case.

<u>11. Writ petitioners did not enclose any paper or order of the Revenue Officer pursuant to the filing of their application for mutation other than an application said to have been made on 12th May, 2009 to the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong. They stated that they prayed to the Assistant Commissioner (Lands, Sadar), Chittagong for mutation of their names who expressed his inability to mutate their names. They did not state when they applied for mutation and when the Assistant Commissioner (Lands) refused their prayer.</u>

<u>12. Since they claimed mutation of their names on the basis of the sale deed, section 143(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act will hold the field. The procedure for mutation of record-of-rights by way of transfer of a plot of land has been provided in chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules, 1954. Rule 23(3) of the said Rules provides that the Revenue Officer either on application or on receipt of a report of the Tahsildar shall make correction in the record-of-rights, after consulting with previous settlement records, Collector's copy of record-of-rights and Register II and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary. The Revenue Officer is required to see whether any entry has been procured by fraud while making any order for correction of an entry and his decision should be based on the report of the Tahsildar. The Revenue Officer shall carefully examine the report and unless he is satisfied with the correctness of the previous record-of-rights, he shall not make any order and in doing so, he is required to follow such procedures as may be directed by the Land Administration Board/the Board of Revenue.</u>

<u>13. Rule 24(4) provides that when the land vests in or comes to the possession of the Government, it shall be recorded in the khas khatian. Thus, there is no gainsaying fact that the mutation of record-of-rights requires enquiry, perusal of previous settlement records, collector's record and the annexed Register. These Rules show that the mutation of the record-of-rights is not mere routine work rather such mutation requires examination of the records which may take time. The writ-petitioners without awaiting the decision of the Revenue Officer moved the High Court Division by making a mere statement that the Revenue Officer refused their prayer.</u>

<u>14. The High Court Division without examining the relevant laws made the directions upon the petitioners to mutate the names of the respondents. The High Court Division, as it appears, seized the functions of the Revenue Officer for correcting the record-of-rights as if it were sitting on appeal from the order of the Revenue Officer. The High Court Division substituted its own wisdom for the discretion vested by law in the Revenue Officer. Admittedly no action or order contrary to law has yet been taken by the Revenue Officer and thus the writ petition in the nature of mandamus is prematured one.</u>

<u>15. As the petition for mutation is awaiting decision before the Revenue Officer, writ of mandamus may be issued upon such Revenue Officer to hear and dispose of the matter within a reasonable time after issuance of notice upon all the persons interested in the property and affording them an opportunity of being heard.</u>

16. What' s more, the writ-petitioners have also alternative remedy against the inaction of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), if there be any, for mutating their names. Where an alternative remedy is available, the remedy under Article 102(2) being discretionary High Court Division should refuse to grant relief to the aggrieved person. Where the alternative remedy could not be equally efficacious the exercise of discretionary power by the High Court Division is called for. The writ petitioners failed to make out any case that the alternative remedy available to them is not efficacious.

<u>17. In that view of the matter, the High Court Division acted in excess of power in directing the petitioners to mutate the names of the writ-petitioners in respect of the disputed property. Since the Revenue Officer has not given any decision pursuant to the application of the writ petitioners, we are of the view that the High Court Division should not have exercised its direction before a decision is given by the Revenue Officer. In other Leave petitions, the petitioners have raised disputed facts which can not be decided by this Division at this stage, the determination of which would require assessment of evidence. They may contest the mutation proceeding, if so advised. It is, accordingly, directed that the concerned Revenue Officer shall dispose of the petition of the writ-petitioners within a reasonable time not later than six months from the date of receipt of this judgment. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside.</u>

<u>These petitions are disposed of with the above observations.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Hassan MS Azim with Mohammad Abdus Salam, Riaz Uddin and Shakila Farzana, Advocates, in person--For the Petitioners. 
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney-General with Md Motaher Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General with Samarendra Nath Biswas, Assistant Attorney-General with Md Jahangir Alam, Assistant Attorney-General--For the Respondents.
parties:
Hassan MS Azim and three others ------Petitioners 
VS
Bangladesh ------Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J: This is an application filed under Article 102(1) and (2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

2. The petitioners are learned Advocates of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and filed the instant application as a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) with the view to uphold the "Supremacy of the Constitution "and "Rule of Law" for ensuring independence of the judiciary from other organs of the State. They are concerned about the deviations made by the government on four occasions in the recent past from the recognized well established Constitutional Convention to appoint the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. It is stated in the petition that it is a fundamental right of every citizen to have access to impartial and independent Court's Tribunals and the exercise of that right is dependent on the independence of judiciary which can be secured only through appointment of persons of high integrity, repute and competence, strictly in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Constitution, to the high office of Judges of superior Courts. The selection of a person to the high office of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh is a pivotal appointment for maintaining the independence of the judiciary and for providing a free and unobstructed access to impartial and independent Courts/Tribunals to the ordinary citizens. Any deviation from the method prescribed under the Constitution for appointment to the high office of Chief Justice of Bangladesh would give rise to infringement of the right of a citizen to have free, fair and equal access to independent and impartial Courts/Tribunals. It is further contended that if the appointments of Judges are not made in the manner prescribed in the Constitution then the same will be detrimental to the independence of the judiciary which will lead to lack of confidence among the people.

3. Mr Hassan MS Azim, learned advocate appearing in person as petitioner No. 1 submits that the Rule of seniority, i.e. the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court to be appointed as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh, is an established convention and the same exists in India and Pakistan. By reference to the decisions of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and another vs Union of India with SP Gupta vs Union of India, AIR 1994 Supreme Court 268 and the cases of Malik Asad Ali and others vs Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Islamabad and others, PLD 1998 Supreme Court 161 and in the case of Al-Jehad Trust through Raeesul Mujahideen Habibul-Wahabb-ul-Khairi vs Federation of Pakistan and others, PLD 1996 Supreme Court 324, he submits that the Supreme Courts of India and Pakistan -have upheld the Constitutional Convention that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court would be appointed as Chief Justice of India and Pakistan respectively. He further submits that the appointment of the senior-most Judge leads to certainly in the process of appointment and avoids any bias for ulterior motives or extraneous reasons. He also submits that the system of appointing the Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge leads to an independent judiciary, inasmuch as the Judges will work towards achieving the ultimate goal of reaching the pinnacle and will work without any fear or favour. He points out from the decision in the Al-Jehad case that if the system of appointing the senior-most judge is not adhered to then those who are not so senior will strive to please the party in power in order to be appointed the Chief Justice in super session of their senior colleagues. Echoing the dictum of his Lordship Manzoor Hussain Sial, J he submits that the senior-most Judge entertains a legitimate expectancy to be considered for appointment as Chief Justice.

4. Mr Azim further submits that our Constitution itself indicates in Article 97 that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is given priority in the absence of the Chief Justice from his office. He further submits that this Article is indicative of the fact that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is accepted as the most appropriate person to take the place of the Chief Justice. He submits that supersession of the senior Judges of the Supreme Court in appointing the Chief Justice undermines morale of the Judges of the Supreme Court and as such also the Rule of Law. He points out that in the past, where supersession has taken place in this country, political motives have always played a big role and as a result the independence of the judiciary has been adversely affected. He submits that, therefore, certainly in the process and for the sake of transparency the system of appointing the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of the country should be adhered to. He further submits that should there arise any particular reason for not appointing the senior-most Judge as the Chief Justice of the country, then there must be reasons given and those reasons must be apparent and must be notified in the official gazette. The learned advocate points out that apart from the few recent occasions of supersession, there has always been conformity with the age-old convention of appointing the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. By reference to supersession of Mr Justice Md Ruhul Amin and Mr Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim and the subsequent appointment of both of them as Chief Justice shows that there could not have been any valid reason for not appointing them to the position of Chief Justice at the first instance since it could not be said that they were lacking in merit. He submits that the failure to appoint Mr Justice Md Ruhul Amin and Mr Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim in their turn as the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court and their subsequent appointment as Chief Justice indicates that their super-session initially was an arbitrary exercise of power by the appointing authority.

5. In view of the importance of the matter Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General appeared and made submissions opposing the petition.

6. The learned Attorney General submitted that there is no such rule as a rule of seniority and the suggestion by the petitioners that the reasons for not appointing the senior-most Judge as Chief Justice must be published in the official gazette is not an acceptable proposition, since that would expose the Humble Judges of the Supreme Court, who are superseded, to ridicule. On the other hand, he submitted that the appointment of the Chief Justice of any country should be based on merit. He pointed out that the position of Chief Justice is not simply to provide the service of a judicial officer, but also involves many other administrative functions for which expertise is necessary and those matters are required to be considered when appointing the Chief Justice of the country. He pointed out from the provisions of the Constitution that there is no mandate for the appointment of the Chief Justice to be made from the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court. He further pointed out that there is no constitutional convention to appoint on the basis of the seniority. By way of explanation he pointed out that all Judges of the Supreme Court, once appointed, carry the same weight and the judgments pronounced by them also carries equal weight. There is no question of any Judge being junior or less important than any other who is senior. Each Judge, including those who are not yet confirmed, i.e. within the two year period as Additional Judge, have the same power of pronouncing judgment and have the power also to deliver a dissenting judgment. Equally, the judgment of any puisne Judge is equal to the judgment of the Chief Justice of this country. This status and tenure of all judges of the Supreme Court including that of the Chief Justice are the same and each of them will retire upon reaching the age of 67 years and none can be removed other than by way of reference to the Supreme judicial Council.

7. The learned Attorney General further pointed out that any appointment on the basis of seniority alone would detract from the efficiency in the judiciary, particularly if any Judge is of the view that he will reach the top no matter what his merit and acumen might be. The knowledge of his automatic accession would not enhance his performance, whereas if the appointment is made on the basis of merit, then the judges will work towards achieving better efficiency in order to reach the top. He submitted that the criteria should be based on merit at the first instance and then, amongst equally meritorious candidates, the senior-most would be taken. The selection on the basis of merit will give rise to intellectual competition which should be kept alive for the betterment of the judiciary. Referring to the Constitution, the learned Attorney General pointed out that the appointment of the Chief Justice is solely the prerogative of the President. By way of contrast, he pointed out that Article 48(3) of the Constitution requires that the President should take advice from the Prime Minister in the case of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court other than the Chief Justice. In the case of the appointment of the Chief Justice, the prerogative lies alone with the President. He further pointed out that it is entirely up to the President whom he will consult with regard to the appointment in order to find out who, among the Judges of the Supreme Court, is capable of doing the administrative as well as the judicial functions of the Chief Justice. The learned Attorney General further pointed out that the reference by the petitioner to a Constitutional Convention is not established; since admittedly the convention has been broken on 4/5 occasions and none challenged the breach of the convention of appointing from the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court. He submitted, therefore, that the present petition was not filed bona fide.

8. With regard to the submissions of the petitioner that Article 97 indicates that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is fit to take the place of the Chief Justice, the learned Attorney General pointed out that the same Article of the Constitution refers to the performing of the function by the senior-most Judge in the place of Chief Justice until some other person has entered upon that office. He submits, therefore, that precisely excludes the concept of seniority. He further pointed out that the wording of the Article refers to 'performing the functions of the Chief Justice' and not becoming the 'acting Chief Justice' which indicates that it is merely a stop-gap measure. The learned Attorney General categorically stated that the appointment of the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice is not a convention and there is no such concept of rule of seniority. He pointed out that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Justice and Parliamentary Affairs vs Md Idrisur Rahman, Advocate, 29 BLD (AD) 79 quite clearly established that there exists a positive convention of consultation with the Chief Justice before the President appoints anyone as a Judge of the Supreme Court, but there is no such consultative procedure laid down in the Constitution for the appointment of the Chief Justice.

9. In view of the importance of the matter, we allowed the learned Attorney General to place submissions before us and since we have heard both the learned Attorney General and the petitioners at length we are in a position to pass an order on merit.

10. Since the instant petition relates to the appointment of the Chief Justice, we will not consider any matters relating to appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Suffice it to say that it appears from the petition that the language used by the petitioners is a reflection of the language used in the case of SN Goswami, Advocate vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 55 DLR 332. That case had been related to supersession of Judges when being appointed to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

11. So far as it relates to the appointment of the Chief Justice, clauses (1) and (2) of Article 95 of the Constitution are relevant which provide as follows:

"95 (1) The Chief Justice and other Judges shall be appointed by the President,

(2) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge unless he is a citizen of Bangladesh and—

(a) has, for not less than ten years been an advocate of the Supreme Court; or

(b) has, for not less than ten years, held judicial office in the territory of Bangladesh; or

(c) has such other qualifications as may be prescribed by law for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court."

12. We may also refer to Article 48(3) of the Constitution which provides as follows:

"48(3) In the exercise of all his functions, save only that of appointing Prime Minister pursuant to clause (3) of Article 56 and the Chief Justice pursuant to clause (1) of Article 95, the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister."

<u>13. It thus appears that in the case of appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court, the President is obliged to act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister, but in the case of appointment of the Chief Justice there is no such obligation and the President alone has the authority to appoint the Chief Justice. So far as Article 97 is concerned, the petitioner has sought to impress upon us that the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division is mandated to perform the function of the Chief Justice in his absence and therefore, he is the one best suited to be appointed as the next Chief Justice. However, we find that as such the provision is simply an expedient method of filling up the gap in the temporary absence of the Chief Justice which may be caused by illness or any other cause mentioned in the article. We also find from Article 97 that even the placing of the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division to perform the function of the Chief Justice in his absence is itself a temporary measure until some other person has entered upon the office. We agree with the submissions of the learned Attorney General that this phrase "until some other person has entered upon that office" excludes the concept of seniority. In this regard it was the contention of the learned Attorney General that some other person does not necessarily mean either the senior-most Judge or indeed any other Judge. The position could be filled by any person, who qualifies to be appointed as a Judge under Article 95(2).</u>

<u>14. On careful scrutiny, we do not find any basis for the contention of the petitioner that the appointment of Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division is a rule of seniority or a Constitutional Convention.</u>

15. It seems to us that both Mr Azim and the learned Attorney General are in favour of appointment on the basis of merit, but Mr Azim had reservations due to the fact that the near past has shown appointments being made by way of supersession for purposes other than for the benefit of the judiciary, namely for political and other purposes and motives. Mr Azim did not deny the fact that the he would prefer to see appointment on merit, but he was apprehensive that the current system is not good because merit is not being taken as a criterion, rather political and other reasons are being used as criteria for the appointment.

<u>16. It seems to us, therefore, that there is some common ground, inasmuch as merit is accepted to be a good basis for appointment of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. As to who will decide on the merit, we believe the answer can be simply stated that the Constitution specifically gives the prerogative right to the President to decide as to who will be appointed as Chief Justice. In contrast to the provision of appointment of other Judges where the need is there for taking advice of the Prime Minister, there is no such provision with regard to taking any advice from any quarter in the case of appointment of the Chief Justice. No doubt the President will consider the merit of the person whom he chooses to become the Chief Justice of the country. The President is at liberty to take opinion from any quarter that he chooses in order to ascertain the merit of the candidate.</u>

17. We also feel that there is a need to consider the merit of any person, who may otherwise qualify to be appointed as a Judge as the Chief Justice of the country within the requirement of Article 95 (2) of the constitution. There is no authority or body of persons who may be identified as being in a position to comment on the merit of any candidate.

18. We may mention that the mode of appointing Chief Justices and Judges in the subcontinent have been inherited from the age old conventions followed in England, but the centuries-old convention of the appointment of Judges being made by the Lord Chancellor was done away within the year, 2006 with the promulgation of the Constitutional Reform Act, 2005. When the matter of appointment of Judges was discussed from the year 2003, Lord Faulkner, the then Secretary of State for Constitutional Affairs, asserted that it was no longer acceptable for judicial appointments to be entirely in the hands of a Government Minister (namely the Lord Chancellor). Accordingly, the British Government announced its intention to establish an independent Judicial Appointment Commission (JAC) to recommend candidates for judicial appointment on a more transparent basis. The judicial Appointment Commission comprises 15 members, including a Chairman, who come from various vocations and professions. A Committee is selected for the purpose of selecting the Chief Justice and other Judge, and within that Committee there will always be two senior members of the judiciary and two members of the Judicial Appointment Commission.

19. It is interesting to note that India has a system of appointing judges, other than the Chief Justice, by a collegiums of judges. In Pakistan judges, other than the Chief Justice, are chosen by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan, which was set up by incorporating an amendment in their Constitution. Article 175 and 176A provide as follows:

Amended Article 175A and 176

67. Insertion of Article 175A in the Constitution—In the Constitution after Article 175, the following new Article shall be inserted, namely:—

"175A. Appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court, High Courts and the Federal Shariat Court.—(1) There shall be a Judicial Commission of Pakistan, hereinafter in this Article referred to as the Commission, for appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court, High Courts and the Federal Shariar Court, as hereinafter provided.

(2) For appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court, the Commission shall consist of—

(i) Chief Justice of Pakistan Chairman

(ii) two most senior Judges of the Supreme Court: Members

(iii) a former Chief Justice or a former Judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan to be nominated by the Chief Justice of Pakistan, in consultation with the two member Judge, for a period two years: Member

(iv) Federal Minister for Law and Justice: Member

(v) Attorney-General for Pakistan: Member

(vi) a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Pakistan nominated by the Pakistan Bar Council for a term of two years: Member

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (1) or clause (2), the President shall appoint the most senior Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of Pakistan.

(4) The Commission may make rules regulating its procedure.

(5) For appointment of Judges of a High Court, the Commission in clause (2) shall also include the following, namely:—

(i) Chief Justice of the High Court to which the Member appointment is being made;

(ii) the most senior Judge of that High Court; Member

(iii) Provincial Minister for Law; and Member

(iv) a senior advocate to be nominated Member by the Provincial Bar Council for a term of two years:

Provided that for appointment of the Chief Justice of a High Court, the most senior Judge of the Court shall be substituted by a former Chief Justice or former Judge of that Court, to be nominated by the Chief Justice of Pakistan in consultation with the two member Judges of the Commission mentioned in clause (2):

Provided further that if for any reason the Chief Justice of High Court is not available, he shall also be substituted in the manner as provided in the foregoing proviso.

(6) For appointment of Judges of the Islamabad High Court, the Commission in clause (2) shall also include the following, namely:

(i) Chief Justice of the Islamabad High Court: and Member

(ii) the most senior Judge of that High Court: Member

Provided that for initial appointment of the Judges of the Islamabad High Court, the Chief Justice of the four Provincial High Courts shall also be members of the Commission:

Provided further that subject to the forgoing proviso, in case of appointment of Chief Justice of Islamabad High Court, the proviso to clause (5) shall, mutatis mutandis, apply.

(7) For appointment of Judges of the Federal Shariat Court, the Commission in clause (2) shall also include the Chief Justice of the Federal Shariat Court and the most senior Judge of that Court as its members:

Provided that for appointment of Chief Justice of Federal Shariat Court, the proviso to clause (5) shall, mutatis mutandis, apply.

(8) The Commission by majority of its total-membership shall nominate to the Parliamentary Committee one person, for each vacancy of a Judge in the Supreme Court, a High Court or the Federal Shariat Court, a the case may be;

(9) The Parliamentary Committee, hereinafter in this Article referred to the Committee, shall consist of the following eight members, namely:—

(i) four members from the Senate; and

(ii) four members from the National Assembly.

(10) Out of the eight members of the Committee, four shall be from the Treasury Benches, two from each House and four from the Opposition Benches, two from each House. The nomination of members from the Treasury Benches shall be made by the Leader of the House and from the Opposition Benches by the Leader of the Opposition.

(11) Secretary, Senate shall act as the Secretary of the Committee.

(12) The Committee on receipt of a nomination from the Commission may confirm the nominee by majority of its total membership within fourteen days, failing which the nomination shall be deemed to have been confirmed:

Provided that the Committee may not confirm the nomination by three-fourth majority of its total membership within the said period, in which case the Commission shall send another nomination.

(13) The Committee shall forward the name of the nominee confirmed by it or deemed to have been confirmed to the President for appointment.

(14) No action or decision taken by the Commission or a Committee shall be invalid or called in question only on the ground of the existence of a vacancy therein or of the absence of any member from any meeting thereof.

(15) The Committee may make rules for regulating its procedure.

68. Amendment of Article 177 of the Constitution—In the Constitution, in Article 177, for clause (1) the following shall be substituted, namely:—

"(1) The Chief Justice of Pakistan and each of the other Judges of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President in accordance with Article 175A."

20. Both India and Pakistan choose their Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court. It is perhaps feasible due to the system of selection of Judges of the High Courts and Supreme Court of India and Pakistan by an independent body, which effectively results in meritorious Judges moving up the ladder, ready for appointment to the position of Chief Justice. We do not have such a system in place. Here the President exercises his prerogative. Hence, merit must be discovered by the President.

21. It is not for us to suggest that a Judicial Commission must be created, but we only suggest that the President may consider taking opinion, when appointing Judges or appointing the Chief Justice, from any persons whom he so chooses, including any Commission or Committee set up under the Constitution that he may choose for his case of reference. We believe that in appointing the Chief Justice of the country the President would refer to all and any quarters who would advise him or assist him in choosing the right person for the post of Chief Justice and we believe that reference to any Commission made for the purpose of scrutinizing the ability of Judges to be appointed as a Chief Justice would lead transparency in the system of appointment. Allegations of politicizing appointments are abundant, as can be seen from the judgment of the High Court Division in Md Idrisur Rahman vs Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, 29 BLD 32 = 61 DLR 523. This niggling complaint pervades through the different strata of our society. It is our view that possibilities of any appointments being made on political considerations would be minimized if the selection was to be made by an independent constitutional body and to be decided finally by the President.

22. With regard to the petitioners' claim that reasons must be assigned for supersession, since we do not accept that there is any rule of appointing from the senior-most Judges, no question of assigning reasons could arise. Moreover, we agree with the learned Attorney General that giving reasons would only stigmatize the Hon'ble Judges who are superseded.

23. With the above observations, we dispose of lite application without issuing any Rule.

The learned advocate makes an oral application that a certificate may be issued under Article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution since, according to his submission, the matter involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. However, we have already expressed our view that the provision of the Constitution with regard to the appointment of the Chief Justice is clear and does not call for any interpretation. Hence, the application is rejected.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 872 of 2005
lawyer:
Md. Waliul Islam, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner.
Not represented—The Respondents.
parties:
RAJUK ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Iqbal Ahmed and ors ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated April 19, 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1910 of 2003)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the judgment dated April 19, 2005 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1910 of 2003 making absolute the Rule which was obtained against the judgment and decree dated February 8, 2003 of the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 520 of 1999 dismissing the same and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated July 12, 1999 of the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 129 of 1999 dismissing the same.

2. The suit was filed seeking declaration of leasehold right in the land in suit and for cancellation of the lease deed made in favour of the defendant No. 1 by the defendant No. 2.

3. Facts, in short, are that land in suit was acquired by purchase by Md. Amanullah, predecessor of the plaintiffs, from the allottee of the RAJUK, that the transfer was made by the allottee upon obtaining permission from the RAJUK as back as on January 24, 1988, that the property in suit was allotted by the defendant No. 2 (RAJUK) to certain Khaleda Rahman and the allotment was completed by execution and registration of the lease deed between RAJUK and Khaleda Rahman, wife of Md Mojibur Rahman, that the full consideration money of the leased land was paid and possession was duly delivered to the allottee by the RAJUK, that allottee entered into an agreement for transfer of the land in suit with Md Amanullah, predecessor of the plaintiffs, and the RAJUK (defendant No. 2) upon obtaining requisite fee accorded permission for transfer and that the RAJUK by written order accorded permission to transfer the land to the predecessor of the plaintiffs, that after the transfer was made by the original allottee Khaleda Rahman to Md Amanullah the RAJUK illegally allotted the land in suit to the defendant No. 1 beyond the knowledge of Md Amanullah and his vendor Khaleda Rahman although when the allotment was made to the defendant No.1 Md Amanullah on the basis of the permission accorded by RAJUK purchased the property in suit from Khaleda Rahman and intimated the RAJUK about the acquiring of the property on the basis of permission accorded by RAJUK from Khaleda Rahman and requested the RAJUK to mutate his name i.e. Md Amanullah's name i.e. predecessor of the plaintiffs.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing separate sets of written statement, stating the facts more or less common.

5. It was the case of the defendants that the suit as framed is not maintainable since defendant No. 2 has allotted the land in suit to the defendant No. 1, that the allotment of land made to the original lessee Khaleda Rahman was cancelled on May 21, 1995 and thereafter the land in suit has been allotted to the defendant No.1 on February 12, 1996 and finally lease deed was executed and registered on March 23, 1996 in favour of the defendant No. 1 and he is in possession of the land. It was the case of the RAJUK that Md Amanullah, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, did not file agreement, affidavit and certified copy of the registered document within the stipulated period of 4 months as was in the letter according permission to transfer and, as such, the RAJUK cancelled the allotment on May 21, 1995 and upon such cancellation allotted the land in suit to the defendant No.2 on observation of the formalities.

6. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the lessor cancelled the lease legally and, as such, the plaintiffs' predecessor by purchase from the lessee Khaleda Rahman did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit, that RAJUK cancelled the permission for transfer and thereupon allotted the land to the defendant No. 1 and that after such allotment executed and registered lease deed in favour of the defendant No.1 and, as such, lease deed executed between defendant Nos.1 and 2 is not void.

7. The plaintiffs went on appeal. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal upon observing that since papers as per terms and conditions set by the RAJUK were not submitted and consequent thereupon cancellation of the lease by the RAJUK was quite legal, that plaintiffs failed to prove that they are in possession of the land in suit and that the papers submitted from the side of the defendant No. 1 show that he is in possession of the land, that plaintiffs being not in possession of the land the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

8. Plaintiffs moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. It was contended before the High Court Division that plaintiffs' predecessor acquired the land from the lessee Khaleda Rahman who transferred the land in suit upon obtaining permission from RAJUK and that plaintiffs' predecessor having purchased the property applied to the RAJUK for mutation on December 30, 1990 and thus RAJUK had the information about the transfer in favour of the plaintiffs' predecessor but illegally cancelled the allotment made to Khaleda Rahman on September 11, 1995, although at that time Khaleda Rahman was not the lessee and that plaintiffs' predecessor was the owner of the land and to that effect intimation was made to the RAJUK. It was also contended that cancellation of allotment was made illegally without serving any notice to either Khaleda Rahman or Md Amanullah. It was further contended that after purchase by Md Amanullah on the basis of permission granted by the RAJUK he submitted all the papers i.e. kabala, by which Md Amanullah acquired the property, affidavit and the other papers as well as mutation fees.

9. The learned Advocate submitted that lower appellate Court was in serious error in holding that the suit as framed was not maintainable in that plaintiffs sought for declaration of his leasehold right and also prayed for cancellation of the lease made by RAJUK in favour of the defendant No. 1.

10. The learned Counsel for the defendant opposite party No. 1 submitted that RAJUK after compliance of due procedure allotted the land to defendant No. 1 and that he got his name mutated and that allotment was made in lieu of his earlier allotment and that lease deed having been executed and registered between him and the RAJUK he has right, title and interest in the land in suit, that RAJUK cancelled the allotment since the condition of the letter granting permission to transfer was not complied with and, as such, permission to transfer was cancelled and the permission to transfer having been cancelled plaintiffs' predecessor by purchase from the original lessee Khaleda Rahman did not acquire any interest in the land in suit.

11. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 (defendant No. 2) submitted that plaintiffs' predecessor or the plaintiffs were not recognised by the RAJUK as the lessee of the land in suit and, as such, RAJUK was not required to serve any notice to plaintiffs or to their predecessor in terminating the lease which was earlier made to Khaleda Rahman from whom plaintiffs' predecessor said to have purchased the land in suit, that original lessee Khaleda Rahman was duly informed about the matter of cancellation of the lease as well as the cancellation of the permission accorded earlier, that it was the stipulation in the lease deed that if transfer is made before making any construction the lease shall stand cancelled and the land shall vest in the lessor and that transfer having been made without making any construction and that permission having been sought for transfer in that state and that finally, the lessee Khaleda Rahman has transferred the land without making construction and thus having had violated the condition in the lease deed, RAJUK was quite legal in cancelling the lease of Khaleda Rahman, that lessee Khaleda and her proposed transferee having not submitted the papers as were required to be submitted in terms of letter dated June 20, 1988 issued by the RAJUK, the RAJUK in cancelling the lease deed did not commit any illegality, that the plaintiffs' predecessor submitted the requisite papers beyond the period fixed in the letter according permission for transfer i.e. on December 30, 1990, and as such, lease was cancelled on November 9, 1995 and the letter according permission was also cancelled. It was also contended on behalf of the RAJUK that since transfer to the plaintiffs' predecessor was not in accordance to the terms and conditions set forth by RAJUK and consequently, the transfer being not legal, the RAJUK was not required to serve any notice on the predecessor of the plaintiffs, that plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the land in suit and that opposite party was successful in proving that he is in possession of the land in suit.

<u>12. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record held that transfer was made pursuant to the permission accorded by the RAJUK and the said transferee i.e. plaintiffs' predecessor, submitted the deed of transfer, deed of agreement and deed of undertaking with the RAJUK on December 30, 1990 along with a petition with the prayer for mutation. The High Court Division also has noticed that after lapse of almost 5 years i.e. on November 9, 1995, RAJUK without mutating the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor cancelled the lease and also cancelled the letter according permission to transfer.</u>

<u>13. It was the case of the RAJUK that it wrote a letter on 26-6-1988 directing the lessee and the plaintiffs' predecessor to submit the papers i.e. deed of agreement, deed of undertaking and deed of transfer, etc. within 4 months from the date of issuance of the said letter and that the papers as required to be submitted in the light of the letter dated 26-6-1988 having not been furnished, the RAJUK cancelled on September 26, 1995 the lease as well as the letter according permission to transfer. It was the case of the plaintiffs that their predecessor and the original lessee Khaleda Rahman did not receive any such letter. From the RAJUK's side no attempt was made to establish before the Court that the said letter was served on the plaintiffs' predecessor and the original lessee Khaleda Rahman and the said letter was also not produced in Court. The High Court Division in the afore state of the matter held that the lease was cancelled "Without hearing the original lessee or petitioners and without issuing any notice upon them, the transfer permission was cancelled, which cancellation order was not even communicated to Khaleda or to the plaintiff-petitioners". The High Court Division in the background of the materials on record held that whatever were in letter dated 26-6-1988 the same was complied with though at a point of time other than the time as claimed by RAJUK to have been fixed but RAJUK sat over the matter of mutation for 5 years although prayer was made upon furnishing the requisite documents by the plaintiffs' predecessor and then went for cancellation of the lease and the letter of permission. As it is seen that whatever action RAJUK took as regard the matter of cancellation of the lease and the letter of permission, the same were taken beyond the notice of the allottee and the valid transferee.</u>

<u>14. In that state of the matter we are of the view High Court Division was quite correct in holding that RAJUK's action was not legal. The High Court Division in the background of the materials on record has observed "that the original allottee did not violate any condition of the lease deed because she got time extension from RAJUK for construction and also permission to transfer the land without construction and subsequently transferred the property in favour of Amanullah. Amanullah also in compliance with the requirements of RAJUK, deposited transfer fees, service charges and the relevant documents with RAJUK for mutation but as he was not aware of the prescribed time limit of such submission directed by the letter dated 26-6-88, he submitted those at a belated stage. The opposite parties could not show anything before the courts below that the letter dated 26-6-88 was received by Amanullah or by the plaintiff-petitioners. The courts below failed to consider that before canceling of the transfer permission notice ought to have been issued to the prospective transferee who has filed the required documents before RAJUK and was awaiting mutation". The High Court Division reversed the finding of the lower appellate Court as to maintainability of the suit since plaintiff prayed for declaration of his leasehold right and also prayed for cancellation of the lease deed by RAJUK in favour of the defendant No. 1 and thereupon affirmed the finding of the trial Court that the suit is maintainable.</u>

<u>15. It is seen from the judgment of the appellate Court that the said Court held that the suit was not maintainable since the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the land in suit and that defendant No. 1 was able to prove his possession. The appellate Court was in serious error in that no material was brought; on record from the side of the RAJUK that after cancellation of the lease of Khaleda Rahman or, for that matter, letter according permission for transfer the RAJUK obtained the possession of the land in suit from Khaleda Rahman. It is not denied by the RAJUK that possession of the property in suit was made over to Khaleda Rahman. Nor it was the case of RAJUK that Khaleda Rahman had not gone into possession after execution and registration of the lease deed. Since no material was placed before the Court from the side of RAJUK that after cancellation of the lease of Khaleda or, for that matter, letter according permission for transfer to the plaintiffs' predecessor the RAJUK took over the possession. So, whatever materials produced before the Court from the side of the defendant No. 1 in assertion of his claim of possession were mere paper transactions and thus the appellate Court was in error in holding that the defendant No.1 has proved his possession in the land in suit and thereupon held that the suit was not maintainable since consequential relief in that regard was not prayed for.</u>

16. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we find no merit in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Md Salahuddin Dolon with Md Mansurul Haque and Md Kamal Hossain, Advocates-For the Petitioner. 
Karuna Moy Chakma, Deputy Attorney-General with Titus Hillol Rema, Assistant Attorney-General, Unnus Ali, Assistant Attorney-General and Nazibur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General — For the Respondents.
parties:
Shafiqur Rahman (Md) ------ Petitioner 
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order contained in Memo No. অম/অবি/(বাস্ত-৫)বিবিধ-৭/৯৬-২০০৯/৫৩ dated 12-3-1009 (Annexure-'L') issued under the signature of the respondent No. 2 refusing refixation of the pay sale of the petitioner to the scale of the Driver of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondent No. 1-2 should not be directed to refix the pay scale of the petitioner to the pay scale of the driver of this Court.

2. The petitioner after a competitive examination for the post of Member of Lower Subordinate Service (herein after called MLSS) was appointed and joined on 7-5-1984 as MLSS in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh with a pay scale of Taka 225-6-315. Thereafter, the petitioner was promoted to the post of Jamadar on 9-10-2005 at a pay scale of Taka 2850-130-3760 EB 150-5-410 vide office order dated 9-10-2005 and since then he has been discharging his duties to the full satisfaction of the authority. Subsequently, the Scale of pay of the petitioner of Jamadar was changed and it was refixed at a pay scale of Taka 2500-110 x 7-3270 EB-120 x 11-4590. Further case of the petitioner is that the Jamadar of the Supreme Court and the Driver of the Supreme Court are in the same class of the same grade according to Service Rules of the High Court Division (Employee) appointment Rule 1987 of the Supreme Court.

3. Further case of the petitioner is that under the National Pay Scale of 2005 the Jamadar of the Supreme Court was enhanced to the pay scale of Taka 2500-110 x 7-3270 and the pay scale of the Driver of the Supreme Court enhanced to the pay scale of Taka 3000-150 x 7-4050.

4. Being aggrieved by the said discrimination, the petitioner field an application on 20-7-2006 before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh with the prayer for refixation of the pay scale of the petitioner Jamadar as like as Driver of the Supreme Court through the Registrar of the Supreme Court. Thereafter, the matter was placed before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh for his opinion so that the file may be placed before the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for enhancement of pay scale of the petitioner as like as the pay scale of the Driver of the Supreme Court the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh on 28-2-2007 opined with the comment "yes" thereby approved the same and thus directed the concerned authority to implement the same.

5. After receiving of the said file, the Senior Assistant Secretary Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs sent a letter to the Registrar of Bangladesh Supreme Court vide Memo No. বিচার-২/১ই-১/২০০৭-২০১৭ dated 16-5-2007 requesting him to submit the papers and documents in respect of the application of the petitioner. Thereafter the Deputy Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh fulfilled the requirement of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs forwarded the summary to refix the pay scale of the petitioner according to pay scale of the Driver of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh vide Memo No.92324 dated 2-10-2007. Thereafter, the Ministry of Law sent the matter to the Ministry of Establishment vide Memo No. বিচার-২/১ই-১/২০০৭-৪৫৬ dated 3-12-2007. Thereafter, the Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Establishment forwarded the matter to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs vide Memo No. সম(বিধি)-পদোন্নতি-৭১/০৭/২১ dated 15-1-2008 with an observation to sent the matter to the Ministry of Finance as the matter relates to Finance Ministry.

6. Thereafter, the Deputy Secretary Ministry of Finance, Implementation cell 5 informed vide Memo No. অম/অবি/(বাস্ত-৫)বিবিধ-৭/৯৬-২০০৯/৫৩ dated 12-3-2009 to the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs without any reason stated that there is no scope of refix the pay scale of the Jamadar of the Appellate Division and High Court Division as like as Driver.

7. The said information was communicated to the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh by the Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs vide Memo dated 20-4-2009. (Annexure-'L' and 'L-1')

8. The petitioner finding no other alternative sent a notice for demand of justice on 26-5-2009. Though the respondents received the said notice but was of no effect. Consequently, the petitioner filed instant writ petition and obtained Rule.

9. Mr Md Salahuddin Dolon appearing with Mr Md Kamal Hossain and Mr Md Mansurul Haque, the learned Advocates for the petitioner submits that the petitioner and others were appointed as Member of Lower Subordinate Service (MLSS) and after getting three time scale on completion of 8,12,15 years of service they were upgraded to the scale of Taka 2850-130-3760 EB 150-5-410 i.e. in grade No. XVII of the National Pay Scale of 2005.

10. The Scale of Pay of Jamadar as was fixed at Taka 2500-110 x 7-3270 EB-120 x 11-4590 under the National Pay Scale of 2005. Though scale of pay of Jamader was fixed at Taka 2500 but under Rule 42 of Bangladesh Service Rules, Part-1, Salary drawn by the employee cannot be reduced. After his promotion to the post of Jamadar, the petitioner's salary was reduced from Taka 2850 to Taka 2500 to grade XIX which was illegal. He further submits that a newly appointed Jamadar may be allowed the new scale of pay but the promotees of the feeder post should be given their salary which they were getting before the promotion (Pay Protection).

11. He further submits that the recommendation as made by the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh (Annexure-G to the writ petition) was in the following manner:

এমতাবস্থায়, উপরোক্ত অবস্থাধীনে মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহোদয়গণের সাথে সার্বক্ষণিক কাজে নিয়োজিত জমাদারগণের অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমকে গাড়ী চালকদের পরিশ্রমের ন্যায় বিবেচনায় আনিয়া তাহাদের বেতন স্কেল ৩০০০-৫৯২০ টাকার স্কেলে উন্নীত করণ সহ তাহাদিগকে ভি,আই,পি, ভাতা প্রদানের প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করার জন্য বিশেষভাবে অনুরোধ করা হইল।

12. He further submits that under the provisions of Article 113 of the Constitution the Hon'ble Chief Justice has the constitutional authority to determine the terms and conditions of the service of the employees of the Supreme Court including their appointment. In pursuant to the said constitutional power the Hon'ble Chief Justice decided to upgrade the pay scale of the petitioner and other Jamadars to the pay scale of Driver who are getting the scale of Taka 3000-5920 i.e. in Grade-XVI under the National Pay Scale of 2005. The Hon'ble Chief Justice has also decided to pay them VIP allowances as they are entitled to. He further submits that the impugned memo under Annexure-'L and L(1)' of the writ petition have been issued by the Deputy Secretary who has turned down the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice taken by him in pursuant to the power and authority vested upon him under Article 113 of the Constitution. He further submits that the provisions of Article 113 of the Constitution other than the Recruitment Rules of 1987, no Rules have been framed determining in the terms and conditions of the Services of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court, the recommendation of the Hon'ble Chief Justice is a decision of the Supreme Court, which is final and binding upon all the authorities serving under the Republic according to Article 112 of the Constitution. He further submits that earlier similar dispute was raised in the case of drivers for whom the Hon'ble Chief Justice has taken a decision to allow them over time allowances for 250 hours per months at the rate of 2,670 22 + 8 x 250 totaling Taka 3,792.50 per month. The calculation was made on the basis of taking into consideration of the basis pay of a Driver.

13. The Ministry of Finance, respondent No. 1 did not accept the said decision. Being aggrieved by the said order, the Driver of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh filed Writ Petition No. 3599 of 2000. The said writ petition was heard by a Division Bench comprising their Lordships Mr Justice Mohammad Gholam Rabbani and Ms Justice Nazmun Ara Sultana and by a judgment and order dated 9-11-2000 the Rule of the said Writ Petition No. 3599 of 2000 was made absolute.

14. Against the said judgment and order; respondent filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2032 of 2001 and subsequently made Civil Review Petition No. 13 of 2003. After hearing the learned Advocate of the parties the said Civil Review Petition No. 13 of 2003 was rejected vide judgment and order dated 10-11-2003 and 19-5-2004 respectively. He further submits that the finding of the judgment of the said Writ Petition No.3599 of 2000 runs thus:

"Upon reading this article we find that the learned Chief Justice is authorized to determine the conditions of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court subject to the provisions of any Act of the Parliament. Thereafter, in the absence of any Act contrary thereto we find no difficulty in holding that the decision of the learned Chief Justice shall prevail over the decision of the Ministry of Finance with regard to the condition in question of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court and therefore the impugned memo is found to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect."

15. The above decision is a declared law of this land which is also final and binding upon all the authorities. He further submits that the present case of the Jamadars are also same and covered by the said decision of the Supreme Court and, as such, the petitioner as well as the other Jamadars of the Supreme Court are entitled to get the benefit of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the same manner as it has been allowed in the case of Drivers of the Supreme Court. He further submits that the power and authority of the Hon'ble Chief Justice as contemplated under Article 146 of the Indian Constitution, as like as Article 113 of our Constitution. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association vs Union of India reported in AIR 1990 (SC) 334 and also reported in 1989 SCC (L&S) 569 Specifically paragraph 56 and 57 of the said decision.

16. Mr Md Salahuddin Dolon, the learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that, under Article 113 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, it is the Chief Justice who is the Supreme authority to take decision with regard to terms and conditions of the service of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court and there is no scope on the part of the executive to change, alter or turn down any decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh. He further submits that in case of any disagreement with the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice with regard to the terms and conditions of service of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court, the President or the government may exchange thoughts and views but not a Deputy Secretary is empowered to turn down a decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. He further submits that to protect the Supreme Court from the arbitrary and illegal action of the executive, the Hon'ble Chief Justice has to frame rules with the assistance of his own Justices and Officers of the Supreme Court. He further submits that due to distinguish function, allocation, status of staff and officers of the Supreme Court, the Constitution has created there as separate entity apart from the other services. He further submits that the job of the Officers and Staffs of the Supreme Court are highly technical and high mental standing. For which the Hon'ble Chief Justice has been vested with a Constitutional power to make rules for the Officer and Employee of the Supreme Court. He further submits that Officers and Employees of the Supreme Court who get a special pay structure because of their Supremacy in the work-field, work load, skilled responsibility undertaken by the employees and duties of various categories. He further submits that the summary as has been placed before the Ministry by the Registrar of the Supreme' Court who has acted as an agent of the Hon'ble Chief Justice and the summary sent by him should be dealt to have been sent by the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh. He further submits that the claim of the petitioner to refix the salary by enhancing the salary with the salary of the drivers are legal and both the job of the Drivers and the Jamaders are similar and they have work load with the Justices of the Supreme Court and their claim is very legitimate. He further submits that if the petitioner and Jamaders had not been promoted as Jamader, they would have been more higher scale than the Drivers because of their scale; MLSS starts from 2850 and during the last 15-20 years all the Jamaders would have entitlement of 15-20 increments, which would have been increased the pay too much higher level than they are claiming now.

17. Mr Karuna Moy Chakma the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing with Mr Eunus Ali, Mr Titas Hillol Rema and Mr Nazibur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney Generals for the respondents submits that the petitioner and other Jamadars having been working with the Justices for whole time from 8 -OOAM to 9-00 PM they are obviously entitled to get VIP allowance and over time, as it has been decided in Writ Petition No.3599 of 2000. He further submits that under Rule 42 of the Bangladesh Service Rules, Part No.1, the pay (Scale) drawing by the petitioners cannot be reduced and they are also entitled to get protection of their pay. He further submits that even though the Drivers and Jamadars are working in the same grade and their service with the Justices is similar but their scales are different and since the Jamadars are working under the different scale then that of Driver they are not entitled to get the scale of Driver of the Justice of the Supreme Court. He further submits that the doctrine of equal work and equal pay does not apply as their job is not similar. But during his argument, he found it difficult to argue regarding turn down of the reference of the Hon'ble Chief Justice of the Supreme Court by the Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Finance. But he submits that before turn down of the reference of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, the President of the People's Republic or the government ought to have exchange thought and views between themselves as the summary was sent by the Supreme Court was placed before different Ministries including the Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Ministry of Establishment and lastly Ministry of Finance.

18. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties at length and perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit, and affidavit-in-opposition and the annexures thereof.

<u>19. In appears from the writ petition that the petitioner and other Jamadars were appointed as Member of Lower Subordinate Service (MLSS) and after entry in the service their three time scale was completed on their service at 8, 12 and 15 years and they were upgraded to the Scale of Taka 2850-130-3760 EB 150-5410 i.e. grade XVII under the new National Pay Scale of 2005. It further appears that scale of Jamadar is Taka 2,500 - 110 x 7 -3270 EB-120 x 11-4590 under grade XIX under the National Pay Scale of 2005. Under Rule 42 of, the Bangladesh Service Rules, Part-1 though the pay scale of the Jamadars started at Taka 2500-110 x 7-3270 EB-120 x 11- 4,590 but they crossed such scale and drawing their salary at the scale Taka 2850-130-3760 EB 150-5410 and, as such, the petitioner is entitled to pay protection of their pay as drawn by them before their promotion.</u>

<u>20. The petitioner and others Jamadar are working whole time with the Justices of the Supreme Court and their services are Highly Technical; Highly skilled and, as such, they are working with the VII' and they are entitled to get VIP allowances in accordance with law. The petitioner and other Jamadars of the Supreme Court since working with the Justices of the Supreme Court since from 8-00 AM to 9-00 PM or more for every day; they also entitled to get over time in accordance with law. The matter of VIP allowance and over time has already been settled in the case of Md Hanif Ullah vs Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Bangladesh in writ petition No. 3599 of 2000, the learned Deputy Attorney General also conceded to it.</u>

<u>21. Let us now consider the salary structure of the Jamadar along with the salary structure of the Drivers of the Supreme Court. It appears that from the Recruitment Rules, 1987 of the Supreme Court, the Drives and Jamadars are in the same grade within Class-III. The job description and work load of the Drivers and Jamadars are very identical. The Drivers drive their car carefully with the Justices but the job of the Jamadars are also very important, highly technical and high skilled for the movement of the files and the Justices of the Court .with more responsibility and confidence and, as such, the work load of the Drivers and the Jamadars working with the Justices are more or less similar.</u>

বাংলাদেশ সুপ্রীম কোর্ট, হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ (কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধি ১৯৮৭ এর তফসিল-১ এ্যাক্ট অনুযায়ী জমাদারগণকে ৩য় শ্রেণীর কর্মচারী হিসাবে অন্তর্ভুক্ত করা হইয়াছে ৷ জমাদারগণ মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহোদয়গণের সাথে নিযুক্ত থাকিয়া দায়িত্ব পালন করেন । সেই কারণে জমাদারগণকে নির্ধারিত অফিস সময়ের অনেক পূর্বে অফিসে আসিয়া অফিস ছুটির অনেক পরেও ভাহাদিগকে অফিসে অবস্থান করিতে হয় ৷ অর্থাৎ ৯-৪৫ মিনিট হইতে ৫-০০ মিনিট পর্যন্ত অফিস সময় হইলেও জমাদারগণকে সকাল ৮ ঘটিকা হইতে সন্ধ্য। অবধি কিৎবা কখনও কখনও তার অধিক সময় অফিসে থাকিতে হয় ৷ এই দিক বিবেচনায় জমদারগণ মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহাদয়গণের সাথে সম্পৃক্ত থাকিয়া অফিস সময়ের পরও অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রম করিয়া থাকেন ৷ অন্যদিকে অত্র কোর্টের ড্রাইভার পদটিও উক্ত নিয়োগ বিধি অনুসারে ৩য় শ্রেণীর পদ ৷ কিন্তু গাড়ী চালকগণ ৩য় শ্রেণী কর্মচারী হিসাবে ৩০০০-৫৯২০ টাকার স্কেলে চাকুরীতে যোগদান করিয়া হেভি লাইসেন্সের কারণে ৩ টি টাইম স্কেল পাইয়া ৩৭০০-৮০৬০ টাকার স্কেলে উন্নীত হইয়া বেতন আহরণ করেন৷ অতিরিক্ত খাটুনির কারণে তাহারা ওভার টাইম ভাতা প্রাপ্ত হন । জমাদারগণ ভারী লাইসেন্সধারী না হইলেও তাহারা গাড়ীচালকদের ন্যায় অফিস সময়ের পরও অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রম করিয়া থাকেন ৷ কিন্তু উক্তরুপ অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমের জন্য কোন প্রকার পারিশ্রমিক তাহারা প্রাপ্ত হন না ৷ এমনকি এম, এল, এস, এস, পদ হইতে কমপক্ষে ২ বৎসরের অভিজ্ঞতা অর্জন করার পর জমাদার হিসাবে, পদোন্নতি প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ৩য় শ্রেণীর পদমর্যাদার হইয়াও গাড়ীচালকদের অপেক্ষা কম বেতন পাইয়া থাকেন । আরও উল্লেখ্য যে, জমাদারগণ অর্জিত ছুটি ব্যতীত ৩য় শ্রেণীর কর্মচারী হিসাবে অন্য কোন সুযোগ সুবিধা পান না। ফলে জমাদারগণ মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহাদয়গণের সহিত সর্বক্ষণিক কাজে নিয়োজিত থাকিয়া অফিস সময়ের পরেও অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রম করিয়া আর্থিকভাবে কোন প্রকার সুযোগ-সুবিধা না পাওয়ায় তাহারা আর্থিক ও মানসিকভাবে ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হইতেছেন ৷

গাড়ী চালকগণ তাহাদের অতিরিক্ত খাটুনির বিনিময়ে ওভার টাইম ভাতা এবং হেভি লইিসেন্সধারী হিসাবে ৩টি টাইম ���্কেলের সৃবিধাদি ভোগ করিয়া থাকেন৷ জমাদারগণের উক্তরুপ কোন হেভী লাইসেন্স না থাকিলেও তাহারা পাড়ী চড়ালকদের ন্যায় অফিস সময়ের পরেও মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহাদয়গণের সহিত সার্বক্ষণিক কাজে নিয়োজিত থাকার কারণে পাড়ী চলেকদের ন্যায় ওভার টাইম ভাতার পরিবর্তে ভি,আই,পি ভাতা পাইতে পারেন। ওভার টাইম ভাতার পরিবর্তে ভি,আই,পি ভাতা পাইতে পারেন । অন্যদিকে অফিস সময়ের পরেও জমাদারগন অতিরিক্ত খাটুনিকে বিবেচনায় আনিয়া তাহাদের বেতন স্কেল পাড়ী চালকদের স্কেলে অর্থাৎ ৩০০০-৫৯২০ টাকার স্কেলে উন্নীত করা আবশ্যক । কেননা গাড়ী চালকগণের অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমকে বিবেচনা করিয়া ৩য় শ্রেণীর কর্মচারী হওয়া সত্বেও যেহেতু ৩০০০-৫৯২০ টাকার স্কেলের সুবিধাদি প্রদান করা হয় সেহেতু । জমাদারগণের অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমকে বিবেচনায় আনিয়া তাহাদেরকেও উক্ত একই স্কেলভুক্ত করা না হইলে তাহাদের অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমকে একদিকে অস্বীকার করা হয় এবং অন্যদিকে আর্থিক সৃৰিধাদি হইতেও তাহাদিগকে বঞ্চিত করা হয় কাজেই একই শ্রেণীর অর্থাৎ ৩য় শ্রেণীর ২ টি পৃথক ক্যাটাগরির কর্মচারীদের প্রকৃতি পৃথক হইলেও অতিরিক্ত পরিশ্রমের বিষয়টি সাধারণ বিবেচনায় আনিয়া জমাদারগণকে পাডী চালকদের স্কেল আনয়ন পূর্বক তাহাদিগকে ভি,অইি,পি ভাতা প্রদান করা যুক্তিযুক্ত হইবে। অন্যথায় জমাদারগণ যে সেবা মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহোদয়গণকে প্রদান করা হয় উহা অফিস সময়ের পরে অফিসে অবস্থান করিয়া প্রদান না করিলে মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহেদেয়গণের বিচারিক কাজের মত স্পর্শকাতর ও গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কাজের উপর উহার প্রভাব পড়িবে সেই দিক বিবেচনায় জমাদারগণ কর্তৃক যে সেবা প্রদান করা হয় তাহা নিঃসন্দেহে গাড়ী চালকদের সেবার চাইতে কোন অংশে কম গুরুতুপূর্ণ নয় ৷

<u>29. The memo itself shows that memo is not a speaking memo, no reason was assigned, which is not sustainable in law. It has been held in the case of Md Hanif Ullah vs Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Bangladesh passed in Writ Petition No. 3599 of 2000, that : "By the terms of our oath we are to do right to all manner of people according to law without fear and favour affection or ill-will. There should be no doubt about it. Article 113 of the Constitution reads as follows:</u>

<u>113.(।) Appointments to the staff of the Supreme Court shall be made by the Chief Justice, or such other judge or officer of that Court as he may direct, and shall be made in accordance with Rules made with the previous approval of the President by the Supreme Court. (2) Subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament the conditions of service of members of the staff of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by Rules made by that Court. Upon reading the above quoted article we find that the Hon'ble Chief Justice is authorized to determine the conditions of the service of the staffs of the Supreme Court subject to the provision of any act of the Parliament. Therefore, in the absence of any Act contrary thereto, we find to difficulty in holding that the decision of the learned Chief Justice shall prevail over the decision of the Ministry of Finance with regard to the conditions in question of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court and therefore, the impugned memo is found to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect."</u>

30. In the said case also the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh referred the matter to the Ministry vide Memo No. 504 dated 20-1-2000 for awarding over time to the Drivers of the Supreme Court, which has been turned down by the Ministry of Finance dated 7-6-2000 and the said refusal has been challenged in Writ Petition No.3599 of 2000.
