<u>31. In the present case also the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh referred the matter to the Ministry of Finance as he is authorized to do under Article 113 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>32. It appears that under Article 112 of the Constitution all Authorities, Executive and Judicial in the Republic shall act in aid of the Supreme Court and under Part 6 of the Constitution the Chief Justice is the Head of the Judicially, an organ amongst three of the State. Under Article 113, the appointment of the Staff of the Supreme Court shall be governed by the Chief Justice and conditions of service of the Staff and Employees of the Supreme Court shall be governed by the Supreme Court prescribed by the Rules, subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament. In the instant case Parliament has not yet promulgated any Act, Rules and Regulations or the Constitutions of the Service of the members and staffs of the Supreme Court. Nor the Supreme Court has yet formed any Rules for the terms and conditions of service of the Staff of the Supreme Court (terms and conditions of service has not been made by the Supreme Court). Since no Rules has yet been made by the Supreme Court, the recommendation made by the Chief Justice is binding upon the executive authorities according to Article 112 of the Constitution which has also been held in the case of Md Hanif Ullah vs Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Bangladesh passed in Writ Petition No. 3599 of 2000.</u>

33. Similarly the Supreme Court of India in the case of Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association vs Union of India reported in AIR ।990(SC) 334 held that—

"Under Article 146(2), the Constitutions of the Service of Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by the Rules made by the Chief Justice of India or by some other judge or officer of the Court authorized by the Chief Justice of India to make Rules for the purpose. This is however subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament. It is apparent from Article 146(2) that it is primarily the responsibility of the Parliament to lay down the conditions of service of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court but so long as Parliament does not lay down such conditions of service, the Chief Justice of India or some other judge or officer of the Court authorized by the Chief Justice of India is empowered to make rules for the purpose. The legislative function of Parliament has been delegated to the Chief Justice of India by Article 146(2). It is not disputed that the function of the Chief Justice of India or The judge or the officer of the Court authorized by him in framing rules laying down the conditions of service is legislative in nature the conditions of service that may be prescribed by the Rules framed by the Chief justice of India under Article 146(2) will also necessarily include salary, allowances, leave and pensions of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court. The provision to Article 146(2) puts a restriction on the power of the Chief Justice of India by providing that the rules made under Article 146(2) shall, so far as pensions, require the approval of the President of India. Prima facie, therefore the conditions of service of the employees of the Supreme Court that are laid down by the Chief Justice of India by framing the rules will be final and conclusive, except that with regard to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions the approval of the President of India is required. In other words if the President of India does not approve of the salaries allowances, leave or pensions it will not have any effect. The reason for requiring the approval of the President or the Government of India regarding salaries, allowances leave or pensions is the involvement of the financial liability of the Government. One important thing that is to be noticed is that under clause (3) of Article ।46 the administrative expenses of the Supreme Court including all salaries allowances, leave and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India. In view of the provision of clause (3), such administrative expenses shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, as provided in Article 113 of the Constitution. It is apparent that in order to maintain the independence of the judiciary, the framers of the Constitution thought it wise and expedient to make such a provision as contained in clause (3) of Article 146."

In paragraphs 56, 57, 58 and 62 of the said decision held—

"The real question is how and in what manner the President of India should act after the Chief Justice of India submits to him the Rules framed by him relating to the salaries, allowances, leave and pensions of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court. The President of India is the highest dignitary of the State and the Chief Justice of India also is a high dignitary of the State. Upon a comparative study of some other similar provisions of the Constitution, we find that under Article 98(3), the President of India has been empowered to make rules regulating the recruitments and the conditions of service of persons appointed to the secretarial staff of the House of the People or the Council of States, after consultation with the Speaker or the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be. Article 148(5) provides that the conditions of service of persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and the administrative powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the President of India after consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Similarly, the Governor has been empowered under Article 187(3) to make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed to the secretarial staff of the Assembly or the Council after consultation with the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly or the Chairman of the Legislative Council, as the cause may be, thus it appears that except in the cases of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court and those of the High Courts in other cases either the President of India or the Governor has been empowered to frame rules.

So far as the Supreme Court and the High Courts are concerned, the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court are empowered to frame rules subject to this that when the Rules are framed by the Chief Justice of India or by the Chief Justice of the High Court relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, the approval of the President of India or the Governor as the case may be required. It is apparent that the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the High Court have been placed at a higher level in regard to the framing of rules containing the conditions of service. It is true that the President of India cannot be compelled to grant approval to the rules framed by the Chief Justice of India relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, but it is equally true that when such rules has been framed by a very high dignitary of the State it should be looked upon with respect and unless there is very good reason not to grant approval, the approval should always be granted. If the President of India is of the view that the approval cannot be granted he cannot straightway refuse to grant such approval but before doing so there' must be exchange of thoughts between the President of India and the Chief Justice of India.

In Gurumoorthy's case (AIR 1971 SC 1850) this Court took the view that the unequivocal purpose and obvious intention of the framers of the Constitution in enacting Article 229 is that in the matter of appointments of officers and servants of a High Court, it is the Chief justice or his nominee who is to be the supreme authority and there can be no interference by the Executive except to the limited extent that is provided in that Article. The same observation will apply to the rules framed by the Chief Justice of India under Article 146(2) of the Constitution.

On the other hand, the Chief Justice of India has to apply his mind when he frames the rules under Article 146(2) with the assistance of his officers. In such circumstances, it would not be unreasonable to hold that the delegation of the legislative function on the Chief Justice of India and also on the President of India relating to the officers and servants of the Supreme Court involve, by necessary implication, the application of mind. So not only that the Chief Justice of India has to apply his mind to the framing of rules but also the Government has to apply its mind to the question of approval of the Rules framed by the Chief Justice of India relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions. This condition should be fulfilled  and should appear to have been so fulfilled from the records of both the Government and the Chief Justice of India. The application of mind will include exchange of thoughts and views between the Government and the Chief Justice of India and it is highly desirable that there should be a consensus between the two. The rules framed by the Chief Justice of India should normally be accepted by the Government and the question of exchange of thoughts and views will arise only when the Government is not in a position to accept the rules relating to salaries allowances, leave or pensions."

<u>34. Even if there be any disagreement with the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice regarding the terms and conditions of the service, pay scale of the officer and employees of the Supreme Court, the Hon'ble President or the government ought to have exchange thought and view if any disagreement with the Hon'ble Chief Justice. Executive of government like Deputy Secretary is not authorized nor have any power to turn down the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. The Hon'ble Chief Justice is not a person but an Institution of a country and protect the judiciary from the arbitrary and illegal action of the executive. The Hon'ble Chief Justice is to frame Rules with the assistance of his own Justices and officers of the Supreme Court to deferent function, allocation of status of staff and officers of the Supreme Court. Constitution created the separate entity apart from other services. The job of the officers and staffs of the Supreme Court highly technical and mental standing who are entitle to get special pay structure for their supremacy of the work field, work load, skill, responsibility, respectability undertaken by the employees and duties of various categories.</u>

<u>35. In determining the pay scale, the authority has to consider the work load, the degree of skill, mental development, strength of work, experience of a person, responsibility undertaken by the Jamader's mental and physical requirement, an act of attendance and attention in the work of the Jamader is to be considered. In the instant case, the petitioner as many as the Jamadars have to work more than ।2 hours a day. Under the doctrine of equal pay for equal work, the service of the Jamadars and the Drivers even if two designation of employees does their duties almost similar work under the same person and, as such, the doctrine of equal pay for equal work will apply and thus the Jamadars are entitled to the salary equivalent to the scale of Drivers.</u>

<u>36. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we find substances in the instant Rule and, as such, the impugned order contained in Memo No. অমি/অবি/(বাস্ত-৫) বিবিধ-৭/৯৬-২০০৯/৫৩ dated 12-3-2009 (Annexure-'L') issued under the signature of the respondent No. 2 is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and that the respondent No. 1 should be directed to refix the pay scale of the petitioner-Jamadars to the pay scale of the Driver of this Court.</u>

37. In the result, the Rule is made absolute however without any order as to costs.

38. The impugned Memo No. অম/অবি/(বাস্ত-৫) বিবিধ-৭/৯৬-২০০৯/৫৩ issued under the signature of the respondent No. 2 is declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondents are directed to refix the pay scale of the petitioner Jamadars with the pay scale of the Drivers of this Court and the respondents are further directed to give effect of the decision of the learned Chief Justice according to observation made earlier (regarding Pay fixation, VIP allowance, over time and pay scale) within three months from the date of receipt of this order.

I must thank Mr Md Salahuddin Dolon, the learned member of the Bar and also the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr Karuna Moy Chakma for their assistance rendered in this regard.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This rule, at the instance of added respondents-petitioners, directed against judgment and decree dated 12-7-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka allowing Title Appeal No. 612 of 2002 thereby dismissing Title Suit No. 134 of 1974 on reversing those dated 29-8-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Pa Court, Dhaka.

2. It is the case of plaintiffs that suit land was originally belongs to Chinta Haran Debnath, CS and SA khatians were correctly prepared in his name. Chinta Haran Debnath had no son but had 6 daughters. Before his death Chinta Haran Debnath on 23-12-1965 made a will in favour of plaintiff No. 5 which was probated on 21-9-1971 and according to that will plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 4, defendant Nos. 3 and 4 got 94 decimals of land out of 120 decimals of land and plaintiff No. 5 alone got 26 decimals of land. Plaintiff sold that 26 decimals of land and said money was spend for giving marriage of defendant No. 4. As per said will Chinta Haran Debnath give authority to his wife, Sukyyada Bala Debi to enjoy 94 decimals of land as life interest. Defendant No. 1 is an influential man of locality and also greedy and scrupulous local man and local administration is on his pocket and while war of liberation of Bangladesh was in progress and plaintiff live there, defendant No. 1 with the help of Pakistani army, got forceful possession of the suit land. After independent of Bangladesh, plaintiffs came back in their house and requested defendant No. 1 to give up possession of the suit land to which defendant No. 1 disclose that defendant No. 2, Sukyyada Bala Debi sold the properly to him. Sukyyada Bala Debi never delivered possession to defendant No. 1 as she had no authority to sell the suit property as Sukyyada Bala Debi had only life interest for the said land. Later on, proforma defendant No. 4 was added as defendant No.2. Cause of action of the suit having arisen on last part of 1978, plaintiff filed the suit.

3. The case of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 make out the case in their written statement, is that, Chinta Haran Debnath for maintaining of his family on 12-4-1969 give authority to his wife, Sukhyyada Bala Debi for selling the suit property and on 17-4-1969 Sukhyyada Bala Debi transferred the properly to defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 2 possessing the suit property peacefully. SA record was correctly prepared in the name of Sukhyyada Bala Debi. Defendant No. 5 did not purchase 26 decimals of land and spent for marriage of defendant No. 4. The will as demanded by the plaintiffs is product of forgery and defendant No. 4 never appointed anybody as power of attorney holder and plaintiff never requested defendant to deliver possession of the suit land and the suit having filed on false statement is liable to be dismissed.

4. Learned Judge of trial court decreed the suit holding that Sukhyyada Bala Debi transferred the suit land but defendant No. 2 on 12-4-1969 was made false "shangsharik karjya bashat" having not qualified to be requirement of legal necessity the said transfer is not legal.

5. In Title Appeal No. 612 of 2002 the learned. Judge of appellate court by (he impugned judgment dismissed the suit holding that the transfer in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was for "paribarik Bhoran poshoner jannya" as such covered the requirement of legal necessity as such transfer is legal.

6. Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that, the learned Judge of the appellate court totally misconceive the doctrine of legal necessity and was devoid of law and facts in dismissing the suit as maintaining day to day affairs of family does not come with definition of legal necessity.

7. Mr Aminul Haque, the learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant opposite party, on the other hand, submits that, maintaining day to day affairs of family is covered by doctrine of legal necessity as such the learned Judge of the appeal court committed no illegality in dismissing the suit while allowing the appeal.

8. On the submissions of the parties only question calls for determination as to whether maintaining day to day affairs of family is legal necessity.

9. Let us see how said transfer covered by doctrine of legal necessity. Legal necessity as per provision of Hindu Law is alienated by widow and that has been defined in section 181 A and B which speaks:

Sub-sections 1 and 2 of section 181A contained 4 clauses and of these clauses 1, 3 and 4 are relevant for findings what legal necessity is. On a reading of these two sections, widow having her life interest can transfer land subject to legal necessity as per Hindu Law.

10. In view of the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties it is necessary to quote the relevant provisions of the Hindu Law. "Besides the legal necessity of a widow having life interest can also alienate property for religious or charitable purposes as enumerated in Clauses (i)-(iv) of section 181A and 181B.

(i) "181 Alienations by widow—A widow or other limited heir has no power to alienate the estate inherited by her from the deceased owner except for the following purposes, namely,

(i) Religious or charitable purposes (SI81A)

(ii) Other purposes amounting to legal necessity of (181 B)

181 A. Alienation by widow for religious or charitable purposes (J) Extent of power of alienation A widow or other female heir may alienate the estate for certain religious or charitable purposes. These purposes may be divided into two classes, namely:

(a) The performance of the obsequie ceremonies of the deceased owner mentioned in CI(I) below, and the payment of his debts mentioned in C1(1) below,

(b) The performance of religious ceremonies of persons other than the deceased owner mentioned in CI(ii) below, and religious or charitable acts which are supposed to conduce to the spiritual welfare of the deceased owner mentioned in (iii) below,"

Section 181B (2) is as under:

Gift by a widow to her daughter on the occasion of her marriage or at hiragana ceremony; also a gift to her son-in-law on the occasion of the daughter's marriage or a gift by way of marriage customary present called Bhat on the occasion of the marriage of her niece (husband's sister's daughter) provided that in each case the gift is of a reasonable amount. But there is no rule that the daughter is entitled to no more than 1/4 share of her deceased father's estate on the occasion of her marriage"

In sub-section 2 of section 181A there are 4 clauses, (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). Of these clauses clause (ii) is not relevant for our case. Clauses (i). (iii) and (iv) speak of performance of the funeral and Shraddha Ceremonies of the deceased owner. Religious or charitable acts which conduce of the spiritual welfare of her husband, payment of debts of the deceased owner, even though barred by limitation whether during his life time or after his death.

11. In the case of Shib Nath Das alias Shib Nath Sarker vs Shasti Bala Sarker, 1993 BLD 415 it is held that "according to Dayabagha principles of Hindu Law which is prevalent in Bangladesh as propounded in section 181B of Hindu Law, wherein the kinds of legal necessities have been clearly enumerated. According to the provision of section 182 of the Hindu Law the onus, obviously (For sections of Hindu Fifteenth Edition), is upon the alienee to prove the transfer to have been made for legal necessity. In the instant case, we hold that onus is upon both the transferor and the transferee (defendants Nos. 1 and 2) as both of them contested the suit to prove the kinds of legal necessity that led to the transfer of the suit land. The trial Court as well as me appellate Court by their concurrent finding of facts have disbelieved the alleged legal necessities, tried to prove by the widow has been transferred for nominal price. The legal necessities as alleged by the defendants are to clear the old debt, to go to Nabodip in India on the part of the widow, to give a Bhoj (grand feast) for the benefit of the said departed souls and to meet expenses of the marriage ceremony of the last daughter of the widow. Courts below disbelieved, therefore, said statements of the defendants as to therefore, the kinds of legal necessities which the defendants tried to substantiate. These being finding of facts based on evidence on record, this court in its revisional jurisdiction has no scope to destroy those concurrent findings of the courts below. We, therefore, accept the findings of the courts below that the defendants failed to prove that the property, in question was transferred for legal necessity. Principles relating to widows' power to alienate property were reiterated by the Supreme Court in India in the case of joyesres vs Raj Dewan, 1962 (SC) 857. Reference also can be made to the decision passed by our High Court Division in the case of Promode Kumar Roy vs Bindini Haider, 21 DLR 673, wherein it has been held that legal necessity must be proved by the person who claims property on the basis of the same. Another reference can be made to the decision of joyanta Bijoy Chakkraborty vs Gopesh Chandra Chakroborty, 35 DLR 319, as in the instant case the transfer in question has been made beyond the knowledge of the reversioner and they gave no consent for the same and, as such, the transfer is not valid in law."

12. Our considered view is that the touch stone of the authority empowered a Hindu widow to transfer her property wherein she has limited interest is "necessity". The word "necessity' when used in this connection has somewhat special, almost technical meaning. It does not mean actual compulsion, but the kind of pressure which the law recognizes as serious and sufficient. The receipt even of full value for the property sold by a Hindu widow, where there is no pressure on the estate, will not justify the sale.

13. In the case of Hara Kumar Kapali alias Bepari vs Sreemati Sundari Kapali, 42 DLR (AD) 59, the Appellate Division of Hon'ble Supreme Court accepted legal necessity to dedication to a temple of worship is dedication for a religious purpose. Dedication for religious or charitable purposes, "we think, includes dedication to hospital, university and other educational institutions.' Since these are intended for the benefit and welfare of the Society, an educational institution is regarded as a temple of learning.

It has been pointed out that Shastric Hindu Law regards Woman as inherently incompetent to hold property. So the rule is that on the husband's dying issueless, the wife has merely the us fact of her husband's property till she could be get a son. If she did, the son becomes the heir. If she could not, the estate passed to the husband's younger brother or failing him, his nearest Sapinda who was her guardian.

14. Now, woman generally takes a limited estate. It is immaterial whether, she takes as widow, daughter, mother or grandmother it being immaterial whether the property is inherited from male or female or whether it is acquired by partition or inheritance. It was held that woman took only a restricted interest and that on her death the property devolved on the line of the last male owner.

But though a woman takes a limited estate it is a proprietary estate in no way limited in interest, though it is limited in use. She does not hold in trust for her reversionary. In 37 All 369 PC it is held "her right is of nature of a right of property, her position is that of owner; her powers in that character are, however, limited but so long as she is alive, no one has any vested interest in succession." In 39 Mad 634 PC: 43 LA 207 it is held "The interest which her reversionary possesses in her estate is contingent and mere Spes Successions."

15. A Hindu Widow takes only a limited estate in the property of her deceased husband, inherited by her. The estate taken by her in such property is called "widow's estate" or "woman's estate". The estate taken by every other limited heir e.g. by any other female in the property inherited by her or obtained by her on her partition, is similar in its incidents to a widow estate, it is neither being nor her Stridhan i.e. absolute estate.

So the he estate taken by a Hindu widow in the properly inherited by her from her husband is called the widow's estate. A widow's estate has been called loosely an estate for life. But Privy Council in case law reported in 23 al 777 PC: 29 CLJ 539 observed that widow's estate is neither a fee nor a estate for life, nor an estate tail." So a widow is not a tenant for life, but is the owner of the property inherited by her subject to certain restrictions on alienation and subject to its devolution upon the next heir of the last full owner upon her death. The whole estate is for the time being vested in her and she represents is completely.

It is pointed out that woman generally takes limited estates. But subject to the restriction on alienation, she holds the property absolutely and she completely represents it. So the widow has absolute power of disposal of the income of the property. She is not bound to save it.

16. In 1937 Cal 229: 55 Mad 216 it is held it is entitled to its beneficial enjoyment, its rent and profits and income which is her own and not liable for her husband's debt. So she is entitled to absolute possession of the estate which vests in her by right of inheritance.

17. In 1935 Cal 689 it is held is a general rule, a widow is not entitled to alienate the immoveable property inherited by her. She may transfer all or any portion of estate for her life or until her estate is determined earlier as for example, by Surrender or by her remarriage.'

18. So in the following cases alienation by her is upheld

(i) she can alienate whole or part of immoveable for legal necessity;

(ii) she can also alienate with the con-sent of the next reversioner. But the consent must be of such a nature as the raise presumption that the trans-action is a fair one and justified by Hindu law;

(iii) A surrender by a widow is also a case of alienation and such surrender is valid when it is made in favour of next reversionary or reversionary at the time of the alienation and it is of the whole estate.

If she alienates the immovable property it should be proved:

(a) that the alienation was for legal necessity, or

(b) that the alienation after reasonable inquiry as to the necessity acted honestly in the behalf that the necessity exerted, or

(c) that there such consent of the next reversioner to the alienation as would raise a presumption that the transaction was a proper one, or

(d) that it was a surrender by her whole interest in the whole estate in favour of the nearest reversioner or reversioners at the time of alienation.

(iv) A widow has not the right to dispose of by will, property inherited by her whether the property be moveable or immovable.

(v) The entire estate being vested in her, she is entitled to manage same. But she must manage it as a prudent owner would do. She must not commit waste or do any injurious to the reversioner.

(vi) She has the power to alienate the estate (a) for religious or charitable purposes and (ii) other purposes amounting to legal necessity.

(vii) She can sell her life interest in the property or mortgage it or make a gift to it to any one she likes.

(viii) If she is dispossessed of any portion of the property by a third person, she can sue to recover it, but if she fails to sue and allows the possession of such person to become adverse to her, the reversioners are not affected by such adverse possession for they succeed not as her heirs, but as her husband's heirs and they may, therefore, sue for possession within 12 years from the date of her death.

19. Now let us look what is the legal necessity.-The following have been held to be family necessities within the meaning of section 242 of Hindu law:

(a) payment of Government revenue and of debts which are payable out of the family property;

(b) maintenance of coparceners and of the members of their families;

(c) marriage expenses of male coparceners and of the daughters of coparceners ;

(d) performance of the necessary funeral or family ceremonies ;

(e) costs of necessary litigation in recovering or preserving the estate: costs of defending the head of the joint family

(f) or any other member against a serious criminal charge;

(g) payment or debts incurred for family business or other necessary purpose. In the case of a manager other than a father, it is not enough to show merely that the debt is a pre-existing debt.

20. In the case of Har Kumar Kapali vs Sremati Sundari Kapali, 1987 BLD 221, ratio decidendi was "Legal necessity alienation of property by Hindu widow for legal necessity-The mode of proof of the same when alienation challenged by the reversionary heir-Whether recital in the deed of transfer about legal necessity is sufficient to hold that alienation was for legal necessity or independent evidence necessary"-it is held as it is well established that recitals cannot themselves be relied upon to prove legal necessity as the recital are binding on the parties to the deed and persons claiming under them and not against others. But such recitals assumes greater importance and cannot lightly be set-aside after long lapse of time when the concerned persons have grown old or died-When the court has taken both oral and documentary evidence including recital in holding that there was legal necessity there is no illegality in such finding."

21. In the case of Saraju Bala vs Lal Behari Mitra, VI BLD 225 it is held that "The recitals in a conveyance with regard to the existence of necessity of the alienation have never been treated as evidence by themselves of that fact.

22. In the case of Lola Brij Lal vs Musammat Inda Kun war (1914) ER 36 Allahabad 187 PC and in the case of Banga Chandra Dhur Biswas vs Jagat Kishore Chowdhury (1916) LR 43 LA 249, it is held that "In general terms the facts recited would establish the necessity alleged, but it is well established they cannot by themselves be relied upon for the purpose of proving the assertions of fact which they contain. Indeed it is obvious that if such proof were permitted the rights of reversionary could always be defeated by the insertion of carefully proved recitals under ordinary circumstances and apart from statute, recitals in deeds can only be evidence as between the parties to the conveyance and those who claim under them. But in such a case as the present their lordships do not think that these recitals can be disregarded, nor, on the other hand, can any fixed and inflexible rule be laid down as to the proper weight which they are entitled to receive. If the deeds were challenged at the time or near the date of their execution, so that independent would be available, the recitals would deserve but slight consideration, and certainly should not be accepted as proof of the facts".

23. In this respect also the onus of establishing legal necessity is on the transferees. Again if the transactions are impeached the burden lies on the transferees to prove either that there was legal necessity in fact or that proper and bonafide enquiries were made by the transferees as to the existence of necessity and they did all that was reasonable to satisfy them-selves as to the existence of the necessity. Thus it is seen that the transferees must establish both, but that may always prove one of these two alternatives. So it cannot be argued that if the transferees failed to establish the first alter-native, had happened here, it was incumbent on the court to investigate into the other alternative. The two considerations being alternative, in my opinion, one excludes the other. Here the first alternative has been found not to have been established and that was quite sufficient, and so there was no necessity to enquire into the other alternative.

24. In the case of Satish Chandra Pal vs Mosammat Mazidan Begum, reported in 10 DLR (1958) it is held that "Legal necessity, transfer of the debottar property 'valid,' when it is for protection and preservation of the deity and for its proper shib-puja.'

It was contended that for the shebaits the debottar property behind and thereafter transferring the property alleging that it was for the reconstruction of the temple and the reinstallation of the deity in a foreign country where they have gone contrary to the intention of the founder cannot be treated as legal necessity, as it practically means not the protection and preservation of the deity and the debottar property but destruction of them both.

25. The circumstances under which the property was transferred was held by the Courts below to be legal necessity, namely, for protection and preservation of the deity in a safer place and for sheba-puja thereof. It is found and not disputed by the parties that the image of the deity "Appileswari Kali" was taken away during the communal disturbances and soon after the disturbances this transaction took place. It is not unnatural for the shebaits to consider that the re-installation of the deity and carrying on sheba-puja of the same was not possible her and it was safe to re-install the deity and to carry on sheba-puja in safer place. For this purpose, 1 think the transfer was for legal necessity in the sense that the transfer was necessitated for the protection and preservation of the deity from and the sheba-puja thereof in a place away from the place where the founder installed it

26. In the case of Nowsha Mia vs Mahammad Idris Ali, reported in 10 DLR 641 it is held that "Recitals in the kabala as regards legal necessity are not by themselves evidence of the fact of legal necessity. Exceptions have been made in respect of old documents containing such recitals when other evidence become non-avail-able."

27. In the case of Nurun Nabi Mondal vs Joynal Abedin Khondkar, reported in 29 DLR (SC) 137 it is held that "Hindu widows in genera! without exception are deprived of the right to inherit and retain the property of their previous husbands when they re-marry after their husbands death-Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in Bhola Umar case being contrary to the generality of views expressed by other High Court of India, is different from."

28. From the history of the gradual evolution of a widow's right of inheritance to the husband's property, as has been generally referred to above, it is clear that the foundation of her such right, as recognized by the Jurists, was her capacity to render spiritual benefits to her husband's soul by participating in various religious performances as the wife of her deceased husband. As has been clearly laid down by Jimuta Vahana, and quoted above, "the wealth devoling on her is for the benefit of the owner," and the right which a widow acquires to the property of her deceased husband is a peculiar one and is known in the modem legal parlance as a widow's which is to be contra distinguished from the right of stridhan.

29. Jimuta Vahana explained the peculiar character of this right in Dayabhaga, Ch. IX, 1, 56-59 after quoting the aphorism of Katyana., which has been cited above by us in following manner.

"She shall enjoy her husband's estate during her life; and not, as with her separate property, make a gift Mortgage or sale of it at her pleasure. When she dies, it goes to her husband's heirs and not to her own heirs. The heir of the woman's separate property shall not take the succession to the exclusion of her husband's heirs. The heirs of her husband, who would have succeeded I the widow's right had never taken effect, equally succeed to the residue of the estate remaining after her use of it upon the demise of the widow in whom the succession had vested.

<u>30. From the above text it appears that a widow shall have a right of enjoyment of her husband's property, during her life tune but shall have to right to transfer or encumber the property in any way, and after her death, the property shall go to the heirs of her husband, and not to her own heirs. The Injunctions contained in other Texts require the widow to enjoy with moderation and lead a life of austerity, and in that sense, she has not even a life interest. On the other hand, she is not a tenant for life, but the property is vested in her and she is the owner of the property, subject to certain restrictions. She has the right to alienate the property absolutely for what is known as "legal necessity', namely, for payment of husband's debts, for performance of acts which conduce to the spiritual welfare of the husband, for discharging obligations of her husband, for her own maintenance which is also an obligation of the husband and for the preservation of the estate.</u>

31. In the case of HR Kapali vs Sreemati Sundari Kapali 42 DLR (AD) 59 The Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh accepted the legal necessity in subject matter of legal necessity "Widow, alienation by-Religious or charitable purpose-Dedication to a temple of worship is a dedication for a religious purpose-Dedication for a religious purpose or charitable purpose includes dedication is a temple of learning."

32. Let us see the impugned deed itself. It is registered on 17-4-1969 wherein it is recited as "in need of my cash money"

On a reading of the entire deed we find that by the deed itself the land sold for maintaining day to day affairs of family. It is settled by court that the recipient of deed is to prove legal necessity. DWI who in his depositions stated as:

"I am opposite party No. 5. I am deposing for opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 as well.

Not a fact that on 24-4-78 a talk of compromise between the petitioner and the opposite party was held in presence of Abdur Rahman and others.

Not a fact that the petitioner has sustained loss due unexpected order.

The petitioner did not take step in the original suit. He has filed this case for harassing me. The PWs are men of same group and that for that reason they deposed falsely.

I know PW Abdur Rahman. Even he was known to me when he was Hindu. His home is 1/8 miles off from mine.

Not a fact that I on and often go to him. Not a fact that A. Rahman settled his family dispute. Not a fact that I went to A Rahman in Baishakh before last for talk of compromise of the suit with the petitioner.

Not a fact that A Rahman advised to take adjournment on the next date of hearing of the suit and then steps would be taken for compromise.

Not a fact that there was a talk that both the parties would file petition on the next date.

I do not know if the petitioner filed written statement in the original suit.

Not a fact that I am deposing today for grabbing the suit property."

33. It appears from the depositions of the recipient of the deed that it was not a deed covered with minimum legal necessity as defendant sold for maintaining of her day to day affairs of family. It appears that Chinta Haran Debnath died on 30th Magh, 1372 BS and the impugned deed of sale was registered on 17-4-1969 i.e. in early part of 1374 BS. It is also on evidence that out of 5 of the daughters of Chinta Haran Debnath, 4 has already been given marriage and for the remaining daughter, Chinta Haran Debnath has made sufficient arrangement. It appears from the depositions of defendant's witnesses that none speaks for selling of the property to defendant No.1 for legal necessity. The woman necessity means a kind of pressure which the law describe as serious and sufficient.

As such on an overall consideration of the Hindu Law it appears that defendant failed to prove the requirement of legal necessity for transferring the suit land as such, we find sub-stance in the rule.

34. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

35. The judgment and decree dated 12-7-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka allowing Title Appeal No. 612 of 2002 is set-aside and those of Title Suit No. 134 of 1974 dated 29-8-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka is restored.

36. Send down the lower court records.

Communicate this order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mostafa Niaz Mohammad with Muntasir Uddin Ahmed, Advocates-----For the Petitioner 
Majumder Saiful Islam, Advocate-----For the Respondent No.4
parties:
Idris Chowdhury (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs
Waqfs Administrator Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order of appointment of Md Shah Alam alias Md Shah Alam Chowdhury as Official Mutawalli of Md Taqui Chowdhury Waqf Estate under section 44 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 issued by the Waqfs Administrator, Bangladesh under Memo No. O. Pro./Cha./ Uo./170/09 dated 10-8-2009 (Annexure-'D') should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The case of the petitioner, as set out in the Writ Petition, in short, is as follows:

On 22-11-1901 the grandfather of the petitioner late Sheikh Ahmad Ali Chowdhury dedicated some of his properties for creation of Md Taqui Chowdhury Mosque Estate (EC No. 1155) by a Waqf-al-Awlad deed. According to the terms of the Waqf deed, the descendants of the wakif's family became the Mutawallis of the Waqf Estate one by one. In this way, the Waqf Estate was successfully managed and administered by the heirs of the wakif. The last Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate was Md Ali Chowdhury of the same family. While he was managing the affairs of the Waqf Estate as Mutawalli, he died on 17-4-2007. After the death of Md Ali Chowdhury, the petitioner, being the proper descendant in order as per the deed of Waqf, started performing the functions of the Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate unofficially. While the petitioner was managing and administering the Waqf Estate as its Mutawalli unofficially and contemplating to make an application to the Waqf Administrator of Bangladesh to become Mutawalli as per terms of the Waqf deed, one Md Shah Alam (respondent No.4) made an application to the Waqf Administrator to become Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate on 12-4-2009. However, the petitioner made an application to the Waqf Administrator for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate on 30-7-2009. But curiously enough, the Waqf Administrator did not respond to his application dated 30-7-2009 and appointed the respondent No.4 Md Shah Alam as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate by the impugned order dated 10-8-2009 on the basis of a report of the Waqf Inspector of Chittagong. Anyway, the respondent No. 4 Md Shah Alam is a stranger to the Waqf Estate. He has no interest whatsoever therein. According to the deed of Waqf, the Waqf is for the benefit of the local mosque and the descendants of the wakif. Besides, the mode of appointment of Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate is stated in the deed of Waqf. As a lineal descendant of the wakif, the petitioner is eminently suitable for the office of Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate. Against this backdrop, the application by a third party (respondent No. 4) for appointment of Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in the name of alleged mismanagement thereof cannot be entertained. So the appointment of the respondent No. 4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate cannot be sustained in law. Although the application of the petitioner dated 30-7-2009 was pending for disposal before the Waqf Administrator, the petitioner was not given any opportunity of being heard and behind his back, the impugned order dated 10-8-2009 was passed.

3. The respondent No. 4 has contested the Rule by filling an Affidavit-in-Opposition. His case, as set out in the Affidavit-in-opposition, briefly runs as follows:

As per desire of the local people and to save the Waqf Estate from extinction, the respondent No. 4 made an application to the Waqf Administrator to appoint him as Mutawalli of the same. On receipt of the application filed by the respondent No. 4, the Waqf Administrator caused an inquiry into the affairs of the Waqf Estate by a Waqf Inspector of Chittagong. According to the report of the Waqf Inspector, the allegations leveled against the descendants of the wakif were prima facie proved and accordingly the Waqf Inspector recommended to appoint the respondent no.4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate. On the basis of the recommendation made by the Waqf Inspector, the respondent No.4 was appointed as Official Mutawalli.

4. Be that as it may, the petitioner himself, amongst others was present at the time of holding of the inquiry by the Waqf Inspector. In reality, the inquiry was carried out in his very presence. Although the respondent No. 4 is not a descendant of the wakif but he is very devout Muslim. Out of his concern for protection of the Waqf Estate from extinction, he made .an application to the Waqf Administrator for his appointment as Official Mutawalli. It is a fact that the petitioner is a descendant of the wakif, but he is not a competent person to be appointed as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate. The petitioner and other descendants of the wakif executed a bainapatra for selling of a portion of the Waqf property in favour of a third party. So in the hands of the petitioner and other descendants of the wakif, the Waqf Estate is not safe.

5. In the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition dated 19-5-2010, it has been averred that the petitioner was away from the country for many years and on his return from abroad, he took over as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate unofficially but he did not make any application for appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in accordance with the terms and conditions of the deed of Waqf. Due to chaos, mismanagement and irregularity in the affairs of the Waqf Estate, the Waqf Administrator appointed the respondent No. 4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate legally and validly.

6. In the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition dated 30-5-2010, it has been stated that the respondent No. 4 collected a photocopy of the bainapatra for sale of a portion of the Waqf property and it transpired that the bainapatra was entered into between one Zafar Ahmed and his mother Alhaj Saera Khatun on the one hand and Mohammad Idris (petitioner) and others on the other hand.

7. In the Affidavit-in-Reply dated 7-6-2010, it has been mentioned that the property referred to in the bainapatra is vague and nebulous. Moreover, the alleged bainapatra has not been acted upon and no sale deed has been executed in favour of Zafar Ahmed. The payment of Taka 2,850 by way of subscription to the office of the Waqf Administrator by the respondent No. 4 prior to his appointment as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate is indicative of his mala fide intention. The respondent No. 4 has no right to meddle into the affairs of the Waqf Estate which was created for the benefit and welfare of the descendants of the wakif.

8. At the outset, Mr. Mostafa Niaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits' that admittedly the wakif Sheikh Ahmed Ali Chowdhury created the Waqf-Al-Awlad, namely, Md Taqui Choudhury Waqf Estate on 22-11-1901 and in the Waqf deed, there is clear mode of appointment of Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate from amongst the descendants of the wakif and the petitioner, being admittedly a descendant of the wakif, has the indefeasible right to be appointed as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in terms of the Waqf deed; but the sudden appointment of the respondent No.4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate under section 44 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 runs counter to the stipulation of the deed of Waqf in that regard and that being so, the impugned order dated 10-8-2009 is without lawful authority.

9. Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad further submits that it is an indisputable fact that the respondent No.4 is a stranger and is not related to the family of the wakif and since he is a busybody, his appointment as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate is unlawful.

10. Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad next submits that admittedly the last Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate Md Ali Chowdhury died on 17-4-2007 and thereafter for about two years, the petitioner failed to make any application to the Waqf Administrator formally for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Waqf deed, but the fact remains that he managed the affairs thereof unofficially during the interregnum.

11. Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad also submits that it is an admitted fact that the petitioner was not given any opportunity of being heard prior to issuance of the impugned order dated 10-8-2009; albeit his application dated 30-7-2009 was very much before the Waqf Administrator for consideration at the relevant time and as the impugned order was passed in violation of the principle of natural justice, the same is ex-facie without lawful authority.

12. Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad further submits that by way of making the application dated 30-7-2009 to the Waqf Administrator for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate, the petitioner invoked Section 51 of the Waqf Ordinance and since no rival claimant was found among the descendants of the wakif, the delay of about 2(two) years in the matter of invocation of Section 51 of the Ordinance will not be fatal to the merit of the case.

13. In support of his submissions, Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad has relied upon the decisions in the cases of Serajuddin Shah (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Religious Affairs and others reported in 51 DLR 479 and Md Abdul Jabbar Mondal vs The Administrator of Waqf & others reported in 10 MLR (AD) 169.

14. On the other hand, Mr Majumder Saiful Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4, submits that there is no legal requirement for hearing the petitioner under Section 44 of the Waqf Ordinance prior to issuance of the impugned order dated 10-8-2009 particularly when the petitioner was admittedly present at the time of holding of the inquiry by the Waqf Inspector and in that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the principle of natural justice was not substantially complied with.

15. Mr Majumder Saiful Islam also submits that the power of the Waqf Administrator to appoint an Official Mutawalli under Section 44 of the Ordinance, through unfettered, yet he assigned a reason in the impugned order for appointment of the respondent No.4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate and that being so, it is very difficult to find fault therewith.

16. Mr Majumder Saiful Islam further submits that after the death of the last Mutawalli on 17-4-2007, the Waqf Estate was virtually left uncared for bordering on extinction and given this panorama, the respondent No. 4 made an application to the Waqf Administrator on 12-4-2009 for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate and after causing an inquiry into the allegations raised by the respondent No. 4, the Waqf Administrator was satisfied as to the veracity of those allegations and ultimately he passed the impugned order dated 10-8-2009 on the basis of the recommendation made by the Waqf Inspector contained in his report dated 3-8-2009 and such being the state of affairs, no exception can be taken to the impugned appointment of the respondent No. 4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

17. Mr Majumder Safiul Islam next submits that it is true that the respondent No. 4 is not a kith of the wakif's family; but that does not pose as an impediment to his appointment as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate under Section 44 of the Ordinance and by that reason, he was appointed as Official Mutawalli by the Waqf Administrator to save it from extinction.

18. Majumder Saiful Islam also submits that the respondent no. 4 is "any other person" adverted to in section 51 of the Ordinance and after a long lapse of about 2(two) years from the date of death of the last Mutawalli, he had to invoke the provisions of section 51 under compelling circumstances and being left with no other option and the Waqf Administrator, relying on the report of the Waqf Inspector, appointed him as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

19. Mr Majumder Saiful Islam next submits that since immediate action was necessary to save the Waqf Estate from Extinction, the Waqf Administrator had to pass the impugned order without hearing the petitioner in person and as this is an exceptional circumstance, the non-adherence to the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem" will not vitiate the impugned order dated 108-2009.

20. In support of his submissions, Mr. Majumder Saiful Islam has drawn our attention to the decision in the case of Ali Ahsan Boni vs Muksumul Hakeem reported in 5 BLC 84.

21. We have heard the submissions of Mr. Mostafa Niaz Mohammad and the counter-submissions of Mr. Majumder Saiful Islam and perused the Writ Petition, Affidavit-in-Opposition, Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition, Affidavit-in-Reply and relevant Annexures annexed thereto.

22. It is an admitted fact that Md Taqui Chowdhury Waqf Estate was found on 22-12-1901 by the wakif Sheikh Ahmed Ali Chowdhury and the character of the Waqf is Waqf-al-Awlad. As per the stipulations embodied in the deed of Waqf, the first Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate was Mr Abdul Majid Chowdhury, a son of wakif. The second Mutawalli of the Estate was Mr Golam Rabbani Chowdhury and the third Mutawalli was Golam Sobhan Chowdhury, sons of the wakif. The 4th Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate was Md Ali Chowdhury, a son of Golam Rabbani Chowdhury and a grand-son of the Wakif Sheikh Ahmed Ali Chowdhury who died on 17-4-2007.

23. It is also admitted that after the death of the last Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate on 17-4-2007, the petitioner, or for that matter, any other descendant of the wakif did not make any application to the Waqf Administrator for appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate for about 2(two) years. Presumably finding no other alternative, the respondent No.4 Mr Shah Alam, though an outsider, made an application to the Waqf Administrator on 12-4-2009 (Annexure-'B') for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate. The record shows that after filing of the application by the respondent No. 4 on 12-4-2009, the petitioner made an application dated 30-7-2009 (Annexure-'C') to the Waqf Administrator for his appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in terms of the Waqf deed. So the factual position is that without any justifiable reason, the petitioner slept over the matter and purportedly managed the affairs of the Waqf Estate unofficially during the interregnum. In the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that the filing of the application dated 30-7-2009 to the Waqf Administrator by the petitioner is an after-thought. This conduct of the petitioner is deprecated.

24. Section 51 (1) of the Waqf Ordinance is as follows:

"51. Notification of Changes in Enrolled Waqf—(1) In the Case of any change in the management of an enrolled Waqf due to the death, retirement or removal of the Mutawalli, the prospective Mutawalli who is eligible or who considers himself to be eligible to succeed to the office of Mutawalli in terms of the Waqf deed or according to the custom or usage of the Waqf, shall forthwith, and any other person may, notify the change to the Administrator."

25. Undeniably, the petitioner being a prospective Mutawalli did not notify the change in the management of the Waqf Estate to the Administrator of Waqf due to the death of the last Mutawalli Md Ali Chowdhury forthwith as mandated by section 51 of the Ordinance. Anyway, in the facts and circumstances of the case, we are at one with the contention of Mr Majumder Safiul Islam that the respondent No. 4 falls within the ambit of the phrase "any other person" referred to in section 51 of the Ordinance. In such a situation, it cannot be said that the respondent No.4 is a busybody. So we opine that he rightly and legally made the application dated 12-4-2009 to the Waqf Administrator, having regard to section 51 of the Ordinance.

26. The impugned order dated 10-8-2009 was admittedly passed by the Waqf Administrator under section 44 of the Waqf Ordinance. Section 44 runs thus:

"44. Appointment of Official Mutawalli-Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance or in any other law for the time being in force or in any deed or instrument, the Administrator may, where considered necessary, appoint an official Mutawalli on such terms and conditions as to remuneration and other matters as the Administrator thinks fit for the administration and management of a Waqf property and institution attached there."

27. Now let us scan the impugned order dated 10-8-2009. From a bare reading of the same, it seems that in the interest of proper management of the administration of the Waqf Estate, the respondent No.4 was appointed as Official Mutawalli. It also appears that at the time of passing of the Impugned order dated 10-8-2009 by the Waqf Administrator, the application dated 30-7-2009 filed by the petitioner for his appointment as Mutawalli in terms of the Waqf deed was very much before him, but he passed the impugned order without giving him any opportunity of being heard. Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad has emphatically contended that the impugned order is without lawful authority in view of non-adherence to the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem" In this connection, the contention of Mr Majumder Saiful Islam is that since the petitioner was physically present at the time of inquiry held by the Waqf Inspector, the principle of natural justice was substantially complied with before passing of the impugned order. But it should be borne in mind that the Waqf Inspector is not the decision making authority. He was just entrusted with the duty of holding of the inquiry into the allegations leveled against the descendants of the wakif. As per the relevant provisions of the Waqf Ordinance, the decision making authority is the Waqf Administrator. Had the Waqf Administrator afforded the petitioner an opportunity of being heard before issuance of the impugned order, probably the petitioner would have no legs to stand upon.

28. Be that as it may, the principles of natural Justice are applied to administrative process to ensure procedure fairness and to free it from arbitrariness. Violation of these principles result in jurisdictional errors. Thus in a sense, violation of these principles constitutes procedural ultra vires. It is, however, impossible to give an exact connotation of these principles as its contents are flexible and variable depending on the circumstances of each case, i.e., the nature of the function of the public functionary, the rules under which he has to act and the subject-matter he has to deal with. These principles are classified into two categories-(i) a man cannot be condemned unheard (audi alteram partem) and (ii) a man cannot be the judge in his own cause (nemodebet esse judex in propria causa). The contents of these principles vary with the varying circumstances and those cannot be petrified or fitted into rigid moulds. They are flexible and turn on the facts and circumstances of each case. In applying these principles, there is a need to balance the competing interest of administrative justice and the exigencies of efficient administration. These principles were applied originally to Courts of Justice and now extend to any person or body deciding issues affecting the right or interests of individuals where a reasonable citizen would have legitimate expectation that the decision-making process would be Subject to some rules of fair procedure. These rules apply, even though there may be no positive words in the statute requiring their application.

29. Lord Atkin in R vs Electricity Commissioners ([1924] 1 KB 171) observed that the rules of natural justice applied to anybody of persons having legal authority to determine questions affecting the rights of subject, and having the duty to act judicially. The expression having the duty to act judicially was used in England to limit the application of the rules to decision-making bodies similar in nature to a Court of law.

Lord Reid, however, freed these rules from the bondage in the landmark case of Ridge v Baldwin ([1964] AC 40). But even before this decision, the rules of natural justice were being applied in our country to administrative proceedings which might affect the person, property or other rights of the parties concerned in the dispute. In all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be observed if the proceedings might result in consequences affecting the person or property or other right of the parties concerned.

30. In England, the application of the principles of natural justice have been expanded by introducing the concept of 'fairness'. In Re Infant H (K) ([1967] 1 All E.R. 226), it was held that whether the function discharged is quasi-judicial or administrative, the authority must act fairly. It is sometimes thought that the concept of 'acting fairly' and 'natural justice' are different things, but this is wrong as Lord Scarman correctly observes that the Courts have extended the requirement of natural justice, namely, the duty to act fairly, so that it is required of a purely administrative act (Council of Civil Service Union v Minister for the Civil Service (19841 3 All ER 935). Speaking about the concept, the 'acting fairly' doctrine has at least proved useful as a device for evading some of the previous confusions. The Courts now have two strings to their bow. An administrative act may be held to be subject to the requirements of natural justice either because it affect rights or interests and therefore involves a duty to act judicially, in accordance with the classic authority and Ridge v Baldwin; or it may simply be held that in our modern approach, it automatically involves a duty to act fairly and in accordance with natural justice. The Indian Supreme Court has adopted this principle holding "this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands" (Swadeshi Cotton Mills vs India, AIR 1981 SC 818).

31. It has been stated in "Administrative Law" by HWR Wade, 5th edition at page-465: "For the purpose of natural Justice, the question which matters is not whether the claimant has some legal right, but whether the legal power is being exercised over him to his disadvantage. It is not a matter of property or of vested interests, but simply of the exercise of Governmental power in a manner which is fair ..." In the American jurisdiction, the right-privilege dichotomy was used to deny due process hearing where no right was involved. But starting with Gonzalez v Freeman (334 F 2d 570), the Courts gradually shifted in favour of the privilege cases and in the words of Professor Schwartz, "The privilege-right dichotomy is in the process of being completely eroded" ("Administrative Law", 1976, Page-230). Article 31 of our Constitution incorporating the concept of procedural due process, the English decisions expanding the frontiers of natural justice are fully applicable in Bangladesh.

32. In English law, the rules of natural justice perform a function, within a limited filed, similar to the concept of procedural due process as it exists in the American jurisdiction. Following the English decisions, the Courts of this sub-continent have held that the principles of natural Justice should be deemed incorporated in every statute unless it is excluded expressly or by necessary implication by any statute.

33. The basic principle of fair procedure is that before taking any action against a man, the authority should give him notice of the case and afford him a fair opportunity to answer the case against him and to submit his own case. The person sought to be affected must know the allegation and the materials to be used against him and he must be given a fair opportunity to correct or contradict them. The right to a fair hearing is now of universal application whenever a decision affecting the rights or interest of a man is made. But such a notice is not required where the action does not affect the complaining party.

34. Reverting to the case in hand, the impugned order of the Waqfs Administrator has affected the complaining party, that is to say, the petitioner. From this point of view, it was incumbent upon the Waqf Administrator to adhere to the principle of 'Audi Alteram Partem" before issuance of the impugned order affecting his right or interest in relation to the Waqf Estate due to the admitted position that he is a descendant of the wakif.

<u>35. From the foregoing discussions and in the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears to us that no opportunity was afforded to the petitioner to controvert the allegations leveled against him and other descendants of the wakif's family. As a matter of fact, the petitioner did not have a fair deal before the Waqf Administrator especially when his application for appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate was pending before the Waqf Administrator prior to issuance of the impugned order. As admittedly the petitioner was condemned unheard, the impugned order, as we see it, is without lawful authority and of no legal effect.</u>

36. In our view, the power vested by section 44 of the Waqf Ordinance in the Waqf Administrator is an extra-ordinary power and this power should be exercised by him sparingly 'where considered necessary' by adherence to the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem". In the instant case, this having not been done, the impugned order appointing the respondent No. 4 as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate is a nullity in the eye of law.

37. As to the decisions reliedcisc by Mr Mostafa Niaz Mohammad and Mr Majumder Saiful Islam, we feel constrained to hold that those have no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of the present case inasmuch as those of the cited cases our quite distinguishable. Of course, we are in agreement with the interpretation of the provisions of section 44 of the Ordinance given therein.

38. In view of what have been discussed above and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, we find merit in the Rule. The Rule, therefore, succeeds.

Accordingly, the Rue is made absolute without any order as to costs. The Impugned appointment of the respondent No. 4 Md Shah Alam @ Md Saha Alam Chowdhury as Official Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate under section 44 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 issued by the Waqf Administrator under Memo No. O. Pro./Cha. Uo/170/09 dated 10-8-2009 (Annexure-'D') is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. However, the Waqf Administrator will be at liberty to hear the parties concerned and give a decision afresh with regard to appointment of the Mutawalli of the Waqf State in accordance with law.

End.

AM Amin Uddin with Munshi Moniruzzaman, Advocates-----For the Petitioner. 
Forrukh Rahman, Advocate-----For the Respondent No. 1.
